text.0_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: Malbim on Judges — The Questions (1–3) Why had they not asked until now, “Who shall go up first?” And why did he say to Shimon rather than to another tribe?
text.0_Chapter, 0_Verse, 1_Comment: And they asked. During the lifetime of Joshua they did not need to inquire by means of the Urim and Tumim, for Joshua arranged everything according to the word of Hashem, as our Sages said (Eruvin 63a), as it is written, “And he shall stand before Eleazar the priest” — yet we do not find that Joshua needed it. But after his death they needed to inquire by means of the Urim and Tumim. (a) Who should go up? For during the lifetime of Joshua he was the one who commanded the people; now they asked who should go up first. (b) At first they conquered all together; now each tribe needed to conquer its own portion, as it says (Joshua 13), “I Myself will dispossess them; only cast it by lot for an inheritance.” Therefore they asked who should conquer first — for if the first were not successful, the Canaanite would say that with Joshua’s death their valor had weakened. And because in the portion of each tribe there remained nations that they had not yet conquered, he relates here how they fought against them.
text.0_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: Judah shall go up. In accordance with his preeminence, and because he received his portion first.
text.0_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: And he said to Shimon his brother. For the inheritance of the tribe of Shimon lay within the territory of the tribe of Judah (Joshua 19).
text.0_Chapter, 2_Verse, 1_Comment: Go up with me in my lot. To conquer my portion. And it is possible that Judah was to conquer in the hill country; therefore he said, “Go up with me,” whereas Shimon was to conquer in the plain; therefore he said, “and I will go.” And similarly below (v. 17), “And Judah went with Shimon his brother.”
text.0_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: The Questions (4) After stating that Hashem delivered the Canaanite into their hand and they defeated them at Bezek, how can it then say again that they fought and struck the Canaanite?
text.0_Chapter, 3_Verse, 1_Comment:
And they struck them at Bezek. At first the camps went out with their commanders and arrayed themselves around Bezek, and there they struck ten thousand men. And when it says “at Bezek,” it means around Bezek, as in: “And it came to pass, when Joshua was by Jericho” (Joshua 5).

(“Adoni-Bezek” the first time is accented on the last syllable [milra], and this indicates that the yod is not additional; rather, the yod strengthens the name, as is found in Scripture. But the second and third occurrences of “Adoni-Bezek” are accented on the penultimate syllable [mil‘el], which is a sign that the yod is additional — for by then he was no longer a lord.)
text.0_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: And they found. Later, when they came near to capture the city itself, they found Adoni-Bezek there. He had stayed within the city to defend it when needed, unlike the king of Ai, who went out from the city and left it exposed.
text.0_Chapter, 4_Verse, 1_Comment: And they fought against him. Again; and there they struck the Canaanites a second time, who had locked themselves within the city behind doors and bars.
text.0_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: And he fled. For he saw that the city had been taken. “And they cut off” — Hashem placed it in their hearts to do to him what they had not done to any of their other enemies. This was somewhat against the laws of Israel, since the seven nations were to be slain by the sword, not subjected to this kind of mutilation. Rather, Hashem repaid him measure for measure.
text.0_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: And he said. He perceived in this the judgment of Heaven — that he was repaid measure for measure. And because he admitted his wrongdoing and acknowledged Hashem’s punishment, he died in the normal course on the road.
text.0_Chapter, 6_Verse, 1_Comment: And they brought him to Jerusalem. For from that place they proceeded to wage war against Jerusalem, and they took him along with them; and there he died.
text.0_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: The Questions (8–22) The Abarbanel asked: If the intention here was to recount the wars that the children of Judah waged after the death of Joshua, why did it see fit to mention afterward the war of Hebron and Debir and the matter of Achsah, when the capture of Hebron has already been recorded in the Book of Joshua, and there it is attributed to Caleb? And why is the matter of Achsah mentioned a second time? And why does it again state that Hebron was given to Caleb? With regard to what is written, “But the Jebusite the children of Benjamin could not dispossess,” this raises difficulty in three respects.
text.0_Chapter, 7_Verse, 1_Comment: And they fought. It has already been mentioned in the Book of Joshua (15:63), “But the Jebusite, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the children of Judah could not dispossess; and the Jebusite dwelt with the children of Judah in Jerusalem to this day.” It is clear that they had already fought in Jerusalem and did not capture it. And below (v. 21) it says: “But the Jebusite, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the children of Benjamin did not dispossess; and the Jebusite dwelt with the children of Benjamin in Jerusalem to this day.”
text.0_Chapter, 7_Verse, 2_Comment: In my view, since Adoni-Zedek king of Jerusalem was the first of the five kings who gathered against Gibeon and there fell (Joshua 10), they surely devised plans to capture his city, just as they then captured the cities of the five kings. And they went, as opportunity allowed, to wage war — and Judah was the one who fought. For Jerusalem was in the portion of Benjamin, yet a strip within it belonged to Judah (as above in ch. 15); and from this perspective he too had a claim to its territory. Thus, during the lifetime of Joshua they were unable to dispossess its inhabitants, who were Jebusites, and they dwelled among Judah “until this day” — meaning until the end of Joshua’s lifetime, when he wrote his book. After the death of Joshua, wars arose between them and the inhabitants of the city; they captured it and burned the city in punishment for having rebelled and fought against them. Yet despite capturing the city, they did not capture the stronghold, which was later called the Fortress of Zion, and which was not taken until the days of David; and there too a Jebusite dwelled, as it says (II Samuel 5:7–8). Judah did not fight there, since it was not in their portion, and Benjamin did not begin to fight there at all. Concerning this it says, “The children of Benjamin did not dispossess” — meaning they did not fight at all — and he dwelled with the children of Benjamin “until this day” (that is, until the end of Samuel’s lifetime, who wrote the Book of Judges). And this is close to the view of the Abarbanel.
text.0_Chapter, 7_Verse, 3_Comment: And they sent the city into fire. The commentators interpreted this as “they sent fire into the city.” But this is not required, for we find the same formulation elsewhere (Judges 20:48; 1 Kings 8:12; Psalms 74:7): “They have sent Your sanctuary into fire.” That is, through the fire they sent the city from existence into destruction.
text.0_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: And afterward they went down. Since the mountain of Jerusalem was higher than the surrounding mountains, it says “they went down” — first to fight in the hill country, and from there to the Negev and the Shephelah.
text.0_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: And Judah went. This conquest was already mentioned in the Book of Joshua (ch. 15), and there it is explained that Caleb dispossessed the Anakim, and this occurred during Joshua’s lifetime. Here, however, it recounts together everything that Judah conquered. That is to say: Judah had already gone to the Canaanite who dwelled in Hebron while Joshua was still alive. And although there the matter is attributed to Caleb, he was the head of the tribe, and his tribe went with him; and from this perspective it may be attributed to both. For Hebron itself was given to the Levites, while the field of the city and its surrounding villages were given to Caleb; therefore both took part in its dispossession.
text.0_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: And he went from there. This narrative, and likewise the story of Achsah, is recorded in Joshua (ibid.). That is, it had already occurred during Joshua’s lifetime. The Sages were evidently troubled by the repetition of this story, and by the fact that it is inserted here along with the note that the children of the Kenite went up from the City of Palms — something that seems entirely unrelated.
text.0_Chapter, 10_Verse, 1_Comment: And they expounded it in Temurah (17a): that three thousand laws were forgotten during the days of mourning for Moses, and Othniel son of Kenaz restored them through his dialectical reasoning. And when she said, “You have given me the land of the Negev,” it means a person dried of all material good, possessing nothing but Torah. And that the children of the Kenite left the luxuriance of Jericho, which Joshua had given them, and went to Othniel son of Kenaz to study Torah.  They wisely understood that the repetition of the matter indicates that this time it alludes to allegorical themes set in golden rhetoric. For we find that Debir is called Kiriath-Sepher (Joshua 15:49), and from this they derived that this city was then designated as a “city of the book,” meaning that students gathered there to meditate upon and review the Book of the Torah, and there was a great academy there. It was also called Kiriath-Sannah, after “the will of the One who dwells in the bush,” and because Moses received the Torah from Sinai. And Othniel was the head of the academy.  He “struck Kiriath-Sepher” — and in the language of the Sages, striking refers to victory in dialectical debate, as in “the war of Torah.” Thus it says, “When you sit to fight with a ruler,” “Your arrows are sharp,” and similar verses that are expounded concerning the war of Torah. And “striking” refers to one who wins the battle and establishes the halakhah, as it says in Berakhot (18b) regarding “And he went down and struck the lion in the pit on a snowy day,” which is expounded: “the school of Rav in the winter day.” Thus Othniel prevailed — whether in the literal war against the Canaanite at Kiriath-Sepher (as mentioned in Joshua), or in the second, Torah-based victory (as mentioned here).  And since Achsah saw that the land of the Negev had fallen to her in two senses:  (1) that the land itself was dry and thirsty for water — this is mentioned in Joshua;  (2) that her husband had turned toward the Negev — for “one who wishes to become wise should go south” —  and this was all his desire and delight, and it would not produce sustenance for his household, therefore she said, “You have given me” (using נתתני instead of נתת לי), meaning that I myself have become like the land of the Negev through my husband. Therefore she requested a blessing and a field for livelihood. And he gave her upper springs and lower springs:  (1) to water her dry land;  (2) and also as a hint that you already have a man who draws living waters from the source of blessing — both upper and lower — from Divine wisdom and from human wisdom.
text.0_Chapter, 10_Verse, 2_Comment: As our Sages said in the Midrash: “One to whom the secrets of the upper and the lower realms have been revealed may request something from Me.” And according to this, he relates here — in the language of allegory and poetic expression — that when he became established and spread much Torah, as he requested in I Chronicles (4:10; 2:55) according to the homiletical interpretation of the Sages, the children of the Kenite went up to him, to the wilderness of Judah near there. And he settled this people in an academy of wisdom.
text.0_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: And the children of the Kenite. They were tent-dwellers, traveling from place to place, and they were at peace with Israel. And when Judah fought against the Canaanite, they went up from the City of Palms, which was in the place of the battle, and settled in the wilderness of Judah. And he settled this people in a covenant of peace and tranquility. And just as Saul did when he fought against Amalek, when he said to the Kenite, “Go, depart, go down from among the Amalekite…” (I Samuel 15:6), so it was now.
text.0_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: And he went. In fulfillment of the agreement stated above (v. 3).
text.0_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: And it was. Until now it has related that Judah, who went up after the death of Joshua to fight according to the word of Hashem, succeeded, acted valiantly, and that Hashem was with him. From this point until the end of the chapter it begins to recount that afterward they did not act according to the command of Hashem and did not dispossess the inhabitants of the land, even though they saw that Hashem was with them. This serves as the introduction to what is stated in the next chapter, that the angel of Hashem went up to Bochim to rebuke them for this. It then recounts how each tribe sinned in this matter, beginning with Judah. It says: although Hashem was with Judah and he dispossessed the hill country, it would therefore have been easy for him to descend from the mountain to the valley and conquer the inhabitants of the valley, as it says (Joshua 17:18), “For the mountain shall be yours… and its outgoings shall be yours, for you shall dispossess the valley.” It is thus clear that after conquering the hill country it would have been very easy to conquer the valley. Nevertheless, he did not dispossess the inhabitants of the valley; that is, he did not conquer the hill country with the intention of afterward conquering the inhabitants of the valley, because when he saw that they had iron chariots he became discouraged and was afraid to fight against them. For even their intention in conquering the hill country was not to dispossess the Canaanite entirely from their portion, but only because…
text.0_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: And they gave Hebron to Caleb. They were obligated to support Caleb, for this had been granted to him by Moses; and he drove out the three sons of Anak. Yet they did not set their intention on dispossessing the surrounding territory completely.
text.0_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: And the Jebusite. Meaning that Benjamin too was lax in this commandment and failed to dispossess the Jebusite from its territory. This verse has already been explained above (v. 8).
text.0_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: And the house of Joseph also went up. They were negligent in the conquest of the land; and in order to magnify their guilt, he first states that the house of Joseph also went up to capture Bethel. And at that time they had clear proof and evidence that Hashem was with them — for…
text.0_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: The Questions (23) Why was it necessary to recount this? Would it not have been enough simply to state that they captured the city of Bethel?
text.0_Chapter, 22_Verse, 1_Comment: And the house of Joseph spied out Bethel. The camp had not yet approached Bethel itself; rather, they sent to scout the land round about. For the verb tur (“to scout”) is usually connected with the word et, as in “to scout the land,” but here it appears with the preposition b, because they did not scout Bethel itself but in Bethel, that is, in the region of Bethel. It is explained that there is a difference between a tar (scout) and a meragel (spy): the spy seeks the vulnerable points of the land and the place easiest to conquer, whereas the scout seeks what is good (as in “to scout out a resting place for them”). Thus they searched in the surroundings of Bethel for a suitable place for the camp to encamp, since they intended to lay siege and remain around Bethel for many days. (It also says vayaturu in the causative form, meaning that they sent scouts to scout and did not scout themselves, as Rashi explains.) And “the name of the city” means that this was not the Bethel near Ai that belonged to Benjamin, but Bethel-Luz, as explained above (Joshua 16:2).
text.0_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: And they saw. Meanwhile, the watchmen — whom the camp had posted around the city so that no one might escape — saw a man coming out of the city. Though they were few, since the main force had moved away to scout the land, they nonetheless showed boldness and bravery.
text.0_Chapter, 23_Verse, 1_Comment: And they said to him, “Please show us the entrance to the city.” Meaning not the obvious gate, but a concealed access point.
text.0_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: And he showed them… and they struck. The watchmen alone captured the city. From this they ought to have recognized that Hashem was with them — that one could chase a thousand. “And the man…” — this is added in passing: first, to indicate that they fulfilled their promise, which was upright and proper; and second, so that one should not mistakenly identify this Luz with the Luz located in the land of the Hittites.
text.0_Chapter, 26_Verse, 0_Comment: The Questions (27) Was this not already mentioned in the Book of Joshua (ch. 17)?
text.0_Chapter, 26_Verse, 1_Comment: And they did not dispossess. Meaning that despite having seen that Hashem was with them, the house of Joseph — namely Manasseh and Ephraim — still failed to dispossess their allotted territory. Manasseh did not drive out Beth-shean and the surrounding cities. This had already been mentioned in Joshua (ch. 17), where it states that “the children of Manasseh could not dispossess Beth-shean,” and that was during Joshua’s lifetime. But now they were able — yet they were unwilling.
text.0_Chapter, 27_Verse, 0_Comment: And it came to pass. Even though Israel became strong over them, they were content to levy tribute from them and did not dispossess them, as the Torah had commanded.
text.0_Chapter, 28_Verse, 0_Comment: And Ephraim. Of the house of Joseph, Ephraim did not drive out the inhabitants of Gezer, nor did he place them under tribute; instead, he lived among them in a covenant of fraternity — in violation of Hashem’s command, Who said, “You shall not make a covenant with them,” and “They shall not dwell among you, lest they cause you to sin against Me.”
text.0_Chapter, 29_Verse, 0_Comment: Zebulun. He enumerates the tribes according to the sequence of their territorial allotments: after the house of Joseph came Zebulun, then Asher, Naphtali, and Dan — since Shimon and Issachar had successfully dispossessed their portions.
text.0_Chapter, 31_Verse, 0_Comment: And the Asherite dwelled among the Canaanite. For the Canaanite constituted the majority, and Asher lived among them; and the same was true of Naphtali.
text.0_Chapter, 33_Verse, 0_Comment: And they pressed. And this failure was even more evident in Dan, for at first the Amorite pressed them into the hill country, and afterward…
text.0_Chapter, 34_Verse, 0_Comment:
And the Amorite was determined. He began moving upward from the valley into the hill country, settling in Mount Heres, as well as Aijalon and Shaalbim. The tribe of Dan by itself could not overcome them until the house of Joseph came to assist; then the power of the house of Joseph prevailed.

Nevertheless, they merely imposed tribute. Even after witnessing open hostility, when they should have learned and utterly dispossessed them, they refrained from doing so. They were satisfied with extracting tribute and defining the Amorite’s border.
text.0_Chapter, 35_Verse, 0_Comment: That the border of the Amorite extended from the ascent of Akrabbim, from Sela and upward. As though two nations had entered into a treaty and fixed for each one the limits of his territory. This was exceedingly evil in the eyes of Hashem; therefore He sent an angel to rebuke them for it, as will be described in the next chapter.
text.1_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: The Questions (2) Why does the phrase “I will bring you up” appear in the future tense rather than in the past? (11) Why does it revert here to recount the death of Joshua and the elders, which has already been recorded at the end of the Book of Joshua? — From verse 11 until the end of the chapter there are duplications and apparent redundancies, most of which seem to bear no direct connection to this context.
text.1_Chapter, 0_Verse, 1_Comment: And he went up. After they entered into a covenant with the inhabitants of the land, the angel of Hashem ascended — meaning a prophet serving in Hashem’s mission — in order to rebuke them for it.
text.1_Chapter, 0_Verse, 2_Comment: And He said, “I will bring you up.” This rebuke revolves around two matters: (a) the evil inherent in the deed itself, as in “Your wickedness shall chastise you,” and (b) the harm that results from it. Regarding the first, He says: “Did I not say, ‘I will bring you up’?” — that is to say: (1) the elevation from the lowest degradation, the affliction of Egypt; (2) the bringing you to the highest exaltation, namely, “and I will bring you to the land.” And I said — meaning, through this I declared — that you should recognize this everlasting kindness, for which you were obligated to render Me gratitude and service. And on this basis, I said, “I will not annul My covenant with you forever” — but only on condition…
text.1_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: And you shall not make a covenant with the inhabitants of this land. For such a covenant with Hashem’s enemies contradicts the covenant between Me and you; it is impossible that devotion to God coexist with attachment to His enemies and blasphemers. And now, since you have not listened to My voice and have forgotten all My kindness toward you — what have you done? Is not such an act inherently evil, as it says, “Know and see that it is evil and bitter that you have forsaken Hashem your God”?
text.1_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: And also. (He now clarifies the second point.) Your actions will inevitably bring you harm, for therefore I have declared, “I will not expel them from before you.” They will injure you in two ways: socially and politically, as snares in your midst; and spiritually, as their gods will become a trap for you. Thus He demonstrated that they sinned both (1) against intrinsic good, and (2) against their own well-being.
text.1_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: And it was. At that time they were moved to weeping, for they realized the folly of what they had done.
text.1_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: And he sent. The entire previous narrative took place while the elders who outlived Joshua were still alive. During their days the people continued to serve Hashem, though they were negligent in completing the conquest of the land. The angel rebuked them, they regretted their actions, wept, and sacrificed to Hashem. Now the text turns to what happened after the elders died. It introduces this by recalling that Joshua had originally sent the people to take possession of the land in accordance with the Torah’s command, and that they remained faithful in Divine service during his lifetime.
text.1_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: And they served. In this way they upheld their wholeness and served Hashem throughout the days of Joshua and the elders who followed him. Because the elders had personally witnessed the deeds of Hashem, they taught the people and directed them along righteous paths.
text.1_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: (From verse 11 through verse 20 constitutes a parenthetical passage, functioning as an introduction and thematic preface to the entire book and to all the accounts of the period of the Judges.)
text.1_Chapter, 10_Verse, 1_Comment: And they did. He explains that they collapsed in three stages, one after another: (a) first, they did evil in the eyes of Hashem, meaning that they sinned against the commandments of the Torah; (b) afterward, they reached the extreme of rebellion, to the point that they served the Baals. He now clarifies that even within this rebellion of idolatry there were two stages: for there is one who serves idolatry in association (with God), and there is one who completely forgets the God who made him. At first they served in association. And this is what it says —
text.1_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: And they forsook Hashem, the God of their fathers. (In my view, throughout Scripture there is a distinction between when the name “Hashem” is mentioned alone — in which case it speaks of Him as Creator of the world and its continual renewer — and when the name “God” is mentioned with a possessive qualifier, such as “the God of Israel” or “the God of their fathers” — in which case it speaks of Him in terms of the relationship He has with Israel and their fathers, whom He chose as His portion and over whom He exercised special Providence.) For this reason, they were forbidden to serve [other powers] in association, since they are not placed under any ministering power or star, but only under the Providence of Hashem — as it says, “whom Hashem allotted to all the nations… but you Hashem has taken.” When they served in association, although they did not forsake Hashem in His essential aspect — for they still believed that He is the Creator and Renewer of the world — nevertheless they forsook Hashem as the God of Israel or as the God of their fathers; that is, they abandoned Him insofar as He is the God of Israel and of their fathers, by virtue of which they are under His direct providential governance and have no foreign god with Him. Thus it says, “And they forsook” — first they forsook “Hashem, the God of their fathers,” meaning that they began to serve in association and thereby abandoned the God of their fathers who brought them out of the land of Egypt, who from then onward exercised special Providence over them and designated them as His portion. “And they went after other gods” — and by this they provoked Hashem, in that they joined the Name of Heaven with something else. Afterward, they collapsed even further and descended terribly.
text.1_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: And they forsook Hashem. They abandoned Him even in His aspect as Hashem, the Creator of all being — for they denied Hashem, saying, “He is not,” and they worshiped the Baal and the Ashtaroth.
text.1_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: And His anger burned. As they transgressed in three degrees, so their punishment advanced in three corresponding degrees: first, He delivered them into the hands of raiders, who despoiled their wealth and goods.
text.1_Chapter, 13_Verse, 1_Comment: (b) Then, “He sold them into the hands of their surrounding enemies,” that is, enemies who opposed them simply as hostile neighbors. “He sold them” means that He handed them over — for once He removed His special Providence, their protective covering was gone, and they were abandoned to the forces of nature and circumstance. Consequently, they could no longer withstand enemies who were stronger by natural means.
text.1_Chapter, 13_Verse, 2_Comment: (c) And afterward He further punished them actively, not merely by withdrawing His Providence, until…
text.1_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: Wherever they went out, the hand of Hashem was against them for harm. That is to say, at first, when there was only concealment of the Divine countenance, the harm did not come by the hand of Hashem, but arose naturally on its own. Now, however, He punished them actively and by His own hand. Previously, when it was merely concealment of the Divine presence, it was conceivable that at times they might still succeed by natural means against an enemy weaker by nature. But now, when He punished them actively with His hand, then wherever they went out — even when, according to natural circumstances, they ought to have prevailed — the hand of Hashem was against them so that they would not succeed, as He had spoken to them, that when they served idolatry He would punish them directly. And thus He continued to deal harshly with them until they were greatly distressed, recognized the evil they had done, and began to return.
text.1_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: And He raised up. I have already written that this entire passage, from verse 10 until the end of the chapter, serves as a general introduction to the entire book. It recounts the condition of Israel throughout all the days of the Judges, until Samuel the prophet, who wrote the book. During that period their sin persisted in one of the three stages mentioned above, and their punishment likewise in one of the three kinds of punishments described above. Now it relates how the Judges arose in each generation to deliver Israel. First, it states in general terms: “And Hashem raised up judges, and they saved them” — meaning that whenever they were in distress, He raised up judges for them; and those judges who arose delivered them from the hand of their plunderers. In this respect, all the judges were alike: Israel attained deliverance through them. However, there was a difference in the duration of the deliverance. We find judges whose deliverance lasted throughout the entire lifetime of the judge, such as Othniel, Deborah, and others. And we find judges during whose lifetime the enemies returned to dominate, such as Ehud, Samson, and others. He explains that this depended upon the generation: if they listened to the voice of the judge throughout his lifetime, then they were delivered for all the days of the judge’s life, and only after his death did they return to wickedness. But at times they rebelled and quickly turned aside even while the judge was still alive, and the enemy ruled over them during the judge’s lifetime. And this is what it says —
text.1_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: And also. Meaning that sometimes they failed to heed even their judges, for they turned aside quickly during the judge’s lifetime. Thus they deviated from the path their fathers had walked — the path of obeying Hashem’s commandments — since their fathers were accustomed to listen to their prophets and judges, as it says, “The people served Hashem all the days of Joshua and all the days of the elders.” But they did not act likewise; and in such cases the enemy gained strength even during the judge’s life.
text.1_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: And Joshua died. Joshua passed away, and that entire generation was gathered to its fathers. A new generation arose that did not know Hashem — neither by intellectual understanding nor by firsthand experience of His acts. From that point they began to abandon the ways of righteousness and to follow paths of darkness.
text.1_Chapter, 17_Verse, 1_Comment: And when. That is to say, at times He raised up judges, and Hashem was with the judge, and he delivered them all the days of the judge’s life. And this too depended upon the conduct of the generation, for Hashem relented because of their groaning from those who oppressed them. For they stood in their righteousness throughout the days of the judge and cried out to Hashem, and He relented from the harm during all the days of the judge. And regarding the phrase “their oppressors and their crushers”: the oppressor presses them with tribute and servitude, while the crusher crowds them, constricting their space, as it says, “and one shall not press another” (Joel 2). Yet even so…
text.1_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: And when the judge died, they turned back and became more corrupt than their fathers. This was the cause that, after the judge’s death, they were handed over to spoil and devastation.
text.1_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: And the anger burned. After presenting this introduction from verse 11 until here, he returns to what he concluded in verse 10: “And another generation arose after them who did not know Hashem,” etc. Therefore, the anger of Hashem burned against Israel. For when Hashem saw that they had collapsed from their faith, His anger burned against those generations, and He said: “Because they have transgressed My covenant (and have not listened to My voice…).” Above (v. 2) it says, “you have not listened to My voice.” There is a distinction between “listening to the voice” and “listening in the voice”: listening “to the voice” means accepting the command or words in themselves, whereas listening “in the voice” refers to heeding the argument and reasoning through intellectual consideration — as in “Hear the voice of my adversaries” (Jeremiah 18), “Listen to the sound of the shofar” (Jeremiah 6), meaning their arguments and the testimony of the shofar that signals impending calamity. And it adds that they did not set their heart to listen on the basis of argument and proof.
text.1_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: I likewise will no longer drive out any of them from before you. Instead, the nations will remain in the Land as thorns among you.
text.1_Chapter, 20_Verse, 1_Comment: Which Joshua left. This is a parenthetical statement — meaning that what Joshua left and did not dispossess during his lifetime was already by Divine design, and it was…
text.1_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: In order to test. For He desired to test the generation after Joshua — whether they would keep the way of Hashem by dispossessing the nations and refraining from making a covenant with them. And for this reason…
text.1_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: And Hashem left these nations, so as not to dispossess them quickly. Thus the days of conquest extended until after the death of Joshua, in order to see whether the generation that followed him would keep the Torah of Hashem by dispossessing them and refraining from making a covenant with them. And all this is a parenthetical statement, from which he derives what follows: since they did not stand in the test and did not dispossess them — as he explained at length in chapter 1 — therefore, when the anger of Hashem burned, He decreed that He would no longer dispossess anyone from before them. They were no longer able to prevail over them, just as Joshua had warned them (23:12–13): “If you turn back… know for certain that Hashem will no longer drive out these nations before you, and they shall be a snare to you until you perish…” — and this was fulfilled after his death.
text.2_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: And these are the nations. He now enumerates specifically the nations whom Hashem left to test Israel — the generation that had not known the wars of Canaan nor witnessed them firsthand.
text.2_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: Only. That is to say, the purpose of the test had two aspects: (a) “Only in order that the coming generations might know” — those who would be required to learn warfare and the tactics of battle, which the earlier generations had not known, since the Canaanites had been driven out before them by Hashem through miracles. Through this they would recognize the power of the miracle and understand what they had caused by their wrongful deeds, as it says, “O God, we have heard with our ears… the work You performed in their days… for not by their sword did they inherit the land…” (Psalms 44). And the word “only” indicates that for this very purpose He left them. Therefore He left them…
text.2_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: The five rulers of the Philistines, etc. From among them Judah took Gaza, Ekron, and Ashkelon after Joshua’s death; but some they did not conquer and thus had to continue fighting against them.
text.2_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: And they were. The second objective was to test Israel by means of them, to see whether they would heed Hashem’s commandments — refraining from intermarriage and from worshiping their gods.
text.2_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: And the children of Israel. They failed in both of these tests. Regarding the first — that they should learn to wage war — they did not battle them, but instead lived among them and entered into covenants with them. And regarding the second — that they should refrain from intermarriage…
text.2_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: And they took their daughters… and they also worshiped their gods. (In this whole exposition my interpretation aligns closely with that of the Abarbanel.)
text.2_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: And they did. Up to this point he has presented a general introduction to all the narratives of the book — what occurred from after the death of Joshua throughout all the days of the Judges. Now he returns to recount the particulars: the story of each judge and what took place in his days. He says that the children of Israel began to do evil in the sight of Hashem, until they forgot Him and until they served the Baals. And through this…
text.2_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: And the anger of Hashem burned… and He sold them into the hand of Cushan. (As was explained above in chapter 2, from verse 11 through 16.) And afterward…
text.2_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: And they cried out… and Hashem raised up a deliverer. As explained above from verse 17 and following.
text.2_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: And they again did evil. As was stated there: “And when the judge died, they returned and corrupted themselves.” “And Hashem strengthened Eglon…” — because they did evil; that is to say, Eglon was weak in himself, and according to natural circumstances they would have prevailed over him. But because they did evil, Hashem strengthened him until he defeated them through Divine Providence, as it says there (2:15), “Wherever they went out, the hand of Hashem was against them for harm.” And also, by doing evil they caused him to be strengthened, for by this he incited their neighbors to mistreat them, saying: “Their God has forsaken them and no longer goes out with their armies, for they have rebelled against Him.” And through this…
text.2_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: And they cried out… and He raised up for them a deliverer. As was stated in the introduction (above 2:17). And behold, Othniel judged them also in matters of religion; therefore it says, “a deliverer for the children of Israel, and he delivered them.” But Ehud only saved them from distress; therefore it says, “for them a deliverer,” for the Spirit of Hashem did not come upon him as it did upon Othniel. Rather, it was through his being left-handed, etc. — that is to say: (a) Because he was left-handed, he was able to conceal the sword on his right side, and they did not detect it, since it is not customary to grasp a sword on the right side in that manner. (b) And because they sent tribute by his hand, he found opportunity to approach the king. And it explains that this was by virtue of his being left-handed.
text.2_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: He fashioned for himself a two-edged dagger to ensure effective penetration, and he made it short so that it would not be seen.
text.2_Chapter, 15_Verse, 1_Comment: And he strapped it… on his right thigh. Since he was left-handed; and because they sent the tribute by him.
text.2_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: And he came near, etc. And the phrase “Now Eglon was a robust man” is an introduction to what is stated in verse 22 — meaning that he was corpulent, as in the expression “ten fattened oxen.”
text.2_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: And he sent. He accompanied them on their way, and he did so for two reasons: first, that they themselves would not be endangered; and second, so that they would not become suspicious when he came back, as if he had merely forgotten something.
text.2_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: And they went out. Eglon was in the antechamber, and from there the men went out. And since it is not customary for anyone to approach the king, Eglon entered the inner chamber; and this is what it says —
text.2_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: And he was sitting… alone. That is to say, separated by himself. And Ehud came and drew near to him and said, “I have a message from God for you.” And he rose; and while he was occupied with rising, Ehud reached out…
text.2_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: And the Spirit of Hashem came upon him. (a) A spirit of justice and courage to judge Israel and to restore them to the ways of Hashem; (b) and through their return to the true ordinances of Hashem, he went out to war and Hashem helped him — not only at that moment, but his power prevailed completely. Until —
text.2_Chapter, 20_Verse, 1_Comment: Thus the land was at peace for forty years, which is the category described above (2:18): “He delivered them from their enemies all the days of the judge.” And he died, etc.
text.2_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: For he did not withdraw the blade, so that his garments would not be stained. And the excrement came forth; and because of the odor, his servants thought that he was covering his feet.
text.2_Chapter, 21_Verse, 1_Comment: (And some interpret “parshdonah” as meaning that he went out to the area where the cavalry stood. However, since it says, “And Ehud went out by the vestibule,” it is evident that the first “and he went out” does not refer to Ehud — and so the Targum understands it. The word itself is compound: “peresh” (excrement) and “shdonah.”)
text.2_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: And he secured the doors of the inner room; and because there was no one in the outer chamber, they thought that the king himself had locked the door. (“He locked” indicates fastening with a bolt; and “the vestibule” means the portico or outer hall before the house.)
text.2_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: And his servants came to the outer hall. And the word “mesikh” (vocalized with a tzeirei vowel) means “covering his feet.”
text.2_Chapter, 23_Verse, 1_Comment: And thus it is taught in the Mishnah: “Anyone who ‘covers his feet’ must immerse.”
text.2_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: And they waited until they were ashamed. There is a distinction between the terms “lingering” (mithmahmeah), “delaying” (boshesh), and “being late” (achar). “Lingering” is the opposite of haste — one is not quick and eager, but delays. “Delaying” refers to tarrying longer than is appropriate. “Being late” refers to arriving after an established time. And “bosh,” from the hollow verbs, is related to “boshesh,” from the doubled verbs. At first they waited during his lingering, for they thought that he was covering his feet, and it is customary to linger and delay. But afterward, when he delayed beyond the proper measure, they became ashamed — and then they opened the door with a key. But…
text.2_Chapter, 25_Verse, 0_Comment: And Ehud had already fled while they were lingering. He calculated only the customary delay, not expecting that they would hesitate beyond the proper measure. Thus he made his escape within the normal interval of their waiting.
text.2_Chapter, 26_Verse, 0_Comment: And he assembled to himself the children of Ammon, etc. First he defeated them in war, and afterward he seized from them the City of Palms. Since Jericho was under a ban not to be rebuilt, they constructed a nearby settlement but refrained from naming it Jericho — which was likewise prohibited — and instead called it the City of Palms, after the palm trees that flourished there. Hiel the Bethelite was later punished for rebuilding Jericho on its original site and restoring its former name.
text.2_Chapter, 26_Verse, 1_Comment: And afterward, they were subjugated and became subject to tribute under him.
text.2_Chapter, 27_Verse, 0_Comment: And they permitted no one to pass over. Since Moab was stationed at Jericho, the City of Palms, on this side of the Jordan.
text.2_Chapter, 29_Verse, 0_Comment: And Moab was humbled on that day. The salvation did not last throughout his lifetime, but only for that day (as Deborah declares in her song: “In the days of Shamgar the roads were deserted”). It was only a partial deliverance — sufficient to free them from servitude.
text.2_Chapter, 30_Verse, 0_Comment: And after him was Shamgar… and he also saved. This too was only a partial salvation, reflecting the first pattern described in the book’s introduction (2:17): “Even their judges they did not heed.” Hence it does not say of him, “He judged Israel” (as noted above, v. 15).
text.3_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: And they continued to do evil. This happened while Ehud was still alive, as stated earlier; and when Ehud died — since his merit shielded them as long as he lived. Thus it does not say here, as it does above, “And Othniel died, and they again did evil” (and likewise later 8:33; 10:6; 11:15), for in this case their wrongdoing began during his lifetime.
text.3_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: And He sold them. Previously they had fallen into the hands of Aram and Moab, who were not among the seven Canaanite nations; but now they were delivered into the hand of the king of Canaan itself, fulfilling the warning, “They shall be a snare to you.” He had once ruled in Hazor — a city conquered by Joshua — but now resided in Harosheth-hagoyim, a fortified stronghold, preserving an old hostility toward Israel.
text.3_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: And they cried out. In the earlier instances (3:9, 15) the text uses “ויזעקו,” but here it uses “ויצעקו,” since “a cry” (צעקה) denotes a stronger outcry than “a lament” (זעקה). This intensification is due to three factors: (a) he possessed nine hundred iron chariots, leaving them no realistic prospect of victory; (b) he oppressed them with severity — interpreted by the Sages as verbal abuse and blasphemy; and (c) the oppression endured for twenty years.
text.3_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: And Deborah. He explains that four conditions for redemption were now assembled: (a) the people’s outcry to Hashem; (b) Deborah’s merit, having attained prophecy — unlike earlier saviors — along with her natural character as “the wife of Lapidoth,” suggesting energetic, fiery action; (c) her active leadership in reforming the nation, as she judged Israel (with “shoftah” understood as a present participle in the kal form, though some interpret it as a complete past verb of a quadriliteral root).
text.3_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: And she. (d) The merit of the people themselves — unlike the other judges who needed to travel among the nation to administer justice (as it says of Samuel, “He went in circuit to Bethel…”), Deborah remained seated beneath the palm, known as the Palm of Deborah (situated between Ramah and Bethel), and the Israelites came to her voluntarily for judgment.
text.3_Chapter, 4_Verse, 1_Comment: Concerning this, the Sages offered a parable: As the palm tree has only one core, so Israel then had a single heart devoted to their Father in Heaven. And likewise they taught: Just as the palm’s shade is slight, so the number of Torah scholars was small at that time; otherwise the people would not have journeyed from distant regions to seek judgment from a woman.
text.3_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: And she sent. Following these preparations — through the merit of the leader and the generation — she addressed him: first, to make clear that her words were prophetic, as indicated by the phrase, “Has not Hashem commanded?” Second, the Divine directive was that he gather men to Mount Tabor, numbering ten thousand, specifically from the tribes of Zebulun and Naphtali. The Sages have offered explanations for the selection of these two tribes at that moment.
text.3_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: And then “I will draw toward you” — through Hashem’s Providence, He will draw Sisera and all his forces to the Kishon River, and there He will deliver him into your hand through miraculous intervention.
text.3_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: The Questions (8) How was it possible for him to say, “If you will not go with me, I will not go,” once she had spoken to him in the name of Hashem — since one who rebels against a prophet’s command is deserving of death? And what is the meaning of, “For the honor shall not be yours,” etc.?
text.3_Chapter, 7_Verse, 1_Comment: And Barak said to her, “If you go with me.” This was not out of doubt in her prophecy, nor rebellion against her command — for one who rebels against a prophet is deserving of death. Rather, since he was commanded to gather ten thousand men, he reasoned that if she did not accompany him, the people would not trust his word, and he would go for nothing. Moreover, because she had told him the victory would be miraculous, he assumed that his merit alone was not sufficient to warrant such a miracle; only if she went with him would the miracle occur through her merit.
text.3_Chapter, 7_Verse, 2_Comment: This is reflected in the Midrash: Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Nehemiah offer two interpretations. Rabbi Yehudah explains, “If you go with me to Kedesh, I will go with you to Hazor,” aligning with the first reason — that she accompany him in assembling the people from Kedesh. Rabbi Nehemiah explains, “If you go with me to the song, I will go with you to battle,” corresponding to the second reason — that only through her merit would the song of victory be sung over the miracle.
text.3_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: And she said, “I will indeed go with you.” Meaning, both to Kedesh to assemble the army and to the battlefield.
text.3_Chapter, 8_Verse, 1_Comment: Yet the honor shall not be yours in this campaign. For if you had gone independently, the victory would have brought you distinction — both because the people would have followed your leadership, and because Sisera would have been delivered into your hand. But now it will be otherwise: “Hashem will deliver Sisera into the hand of a woman.” The entire episode will be credited to a woman — its beginning, since the army’s mobilization will be through Deborah, and its conclusion, since Sisera’s death will come through Jael. Had you gone forth on your own in confidence, Sisera would have fallen to you.
text.3_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: And he advanced on foot. That is, through his own agency (as in the phrase “Hashem has blessed you on my account”), and not due to Deborah. Alternatively, in its simple sense, he possessed no cavalry or chariots to oppose the nine hundred iron chariots.
text.3_Chapter, 9_Verse, 1_Comment: And she ascended with him. In fulfillment of her words, “I will indeed go.” Thus it first records that she arose and went to Kedesh, and here it notes that she went up to Mount Tabor.
text.3_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: And Heber the Kenite. This is preparatory to the fulfillment of the statement, “Into the hand of a woman Hashem will deliver Sisera.” It was providential that Heber separated then from his kinsmen — who had settled in the wilderness of Judah (as noted earlier in 1:16) — and moved his tent near Kedesh, positioning himself for the coming moment of salvation.
text.3_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: And he called together. So as to realize the words, “I will draw Sisera and his chariots to the Brook Kishon,” Hashem inspired him to: (a) mobilize all his chariots and his whole army, despite the fact that logic would suggest confronting such a weak force with only a limited number; and (b) to move them toward the Kishon River.
text.3_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: Rise, for this is the day. Delay not for another time, since Hashem has already advanced ahead of you and has begun striking his forces.
text.3_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: And Hashem routed… before Barak. Abarbanel interprets this to mean that the confusion occurred even before Barak reached them — Hashem made them hear the sound of chariots and cavalry, causing panic, so that Sisera had already taken flight.
text.3_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: And Barak gave chase. Meaning that he did not engage in a full battle; rather, he pursued the retreating forces, and the whole camp fell as casualties.
text.3_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: And Sisera. Abarbanel questions how Jael could have performed such a deed — killing Sisera after there was peace between him and her husband’s household, and after he had entered her tent — seemingly in violation of accepted norms. I respond, following his reasoning: the peace between Jabin and the house of Heber was part of a broader covenant with the Kenites who dwelled in the wilderness of Judah, as the verse states. But once Heber separated from his kinsmen and settled among Israel, the covenant of the Kenites no longer bound him, since he had withdrawn from that collective.
text.3_Chapter, 16_Verse, 1_Comment: A second explanation, according to Abarbanel, is that Sisera fled into Jael’s tent, and a woman is not subject to the political obligations of state treaties; she acted on her own, not as her husband’s representative. Yet such arguments are unnecessary, since the house of Heber was counted among Israel — and how could they fail to fight for their nation and their God?
text.3_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: And he said, “Is there any man here?” For it is improper etiquette for someone to enter a woman’s tent if no man is present. Therefore he would inquire whether a man of the household was there; and you are to answer, “There is none,” so that no outsider will come in. The word “stand” is grammatically an infinitive functioning as a command.
text.3_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: And she struck it in. She held the mallet in one hand and the tent peg in the other; yet she lacked the physical strength to drive it through by her own power. Therefore, by Divine assistance, the peg descended into the ground by its weight, penetrating and passing through. And since he had fallen into deep sleep from the milk he drank, being fatigued and faint, he died at once.
text.3_Chapter, 44_Verse, 0_Comment: And he was humbled. At once, on that very day; though later he resumed fighting, the power of Israel intensified against him until he was cut off. Consequently, peace endured throughout Deborah’s lifetime, because they upheld their righteousness as long as she lived — in fulfillment of what was said earlier (2:18): “He saved them from their enemies all the days of the judge.”
text.4_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: When Israel was ungoverned. She declares that when Israel had become undisciplined — either by casting off restraint, or through weakness (as in, “for the people were unrestrained”) — so that chaos abounded; then, if volunteers arose from among the people to act courageously, this could not be explained naturally but only as the work of God. Hence, “Bless Hashem,” for it was from Him that this came.
text.4_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: Hear, O kings. Along with your rulers, the advisors of state. (It is established in my view that “hearing” applies to matters of greater significance, while “hearkening” applies to lesser matters, as explained in Isaiah 1.) O kings, do not suppose that this triumph was due to natural causes; rather, “I, to Hashem — I will sing.” I ascribe this victory to Hashem alone, and to Him I offer praise.
text.4_Chapter, 2_Verse, 1_Comment: There is a difference between “shir” (song) and “zemer” (psalm). “Zemer” denotes a higher form of praise than “shir,” which is why Scripture consistently says, “Sing to Him, chant to Him,” or “I will sing and I will chant,” with the chant intensifying the song. I have explained that “zemer” is used particularly when praising God for acts of Providence, miracles, or extraordinary intervention.
text.4_Chapter, 2_Verse, 2_Comment: There is a difference between the name “Hashem” and the title “the God of Israel.” The latter consistently refers to His particular Providence over Israel, through which He raises them by miraculous intervention. Thus she declares that she will sing in recognition of Him as Hashem — Creator and universal Governor — and she will chant in recognition of Him as the God of Israel, who guides them through extraordinary and miraculous Providence.
text.4_Chapter, 2_Verse, 3_Comment: These two verses function as a preface to the Song itself; from here onward the actual song commences.
text.4_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: Hashem, when You went forth from Seir. These two verses lead into the statement “in the days of Shamgar,” forming a contrast between the early era of Israel’s might and the later decline in Shamgar’s time. The poet recalls that when Israel entered the land, having encircled Edom, Hashem their King went before them from Seir toward Moab (the surrounding regions poetically termed “the field of Edom”), and then proceeded toward the territories of Sihon, Og, and Canaan. At that time, the earth quaked — as if all existence trembled: earth and heaven alike; even the celestial hosts melted before them, and the clouds above poured forth rain.
text.4_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: And the mountains melted. They dissolved downward until all was liquefied. “Before Hashem — this is Sinai” means that they melted before Hashem who came forth from Mount Sinai and endowed His people with power; before Hashem as the God of Israel, manifest through His intimate Providence and the miracles He wrought on their behalf.
text.4_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: In the days of Shamgar. Observe the stark contrast in Shamgar’s era and afterward in Jael’s time: the main roads fell into disuse — meaning the trade caravans ceased (as in “a caravan of Ishmaelites,” referring to organized travelers). Even solitary travelers who used narrow paths (distinguishing between the broad road, “derekh,” and the smaller track, “netiv”) resorted to crooked routes. Fear prevented them from using the straight highways; instead they detoured along winding side paths that branched off from the main road toward villages. They abandoned direct roads and took only circuitous ones.
text.4_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: And likewise, “the open settlements ceased.” The people withdrew into fortified cities out of fear of the enemy. “In Israel they ceased” — indicating that, just as when Israel first entered the land villages and roads had once ceased — then it was the Canaanites who confined themselves within strongholds in fear of Israel. But now the situation was reversed: it was Israel whose rural settlements disappeared, not the Canaanites, because the Canaanite had prevailed over them.
text.4_Chapter, 6_Verse, 1_Comment: Until I, Deborah, arose. This condition persisted through the days of Shamgar, until she stood up.
text.4_Chapter, 6_Verse, 2_Comment: That I arose as a mother in Israel. She uses figurative language, as if Israel had ceased to function as a people and were now newly reborn; and she stood as the mother who brought the whole nation forth again.
text.4_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: He chose. At Israel’s initial entry into the land, the advance guard — the forty thousand armed men from Reuben and Gad — crossed before the nation (Joshua 4). Yet in the present crisis, none of that former vanguard appeared; instead, the fighters were from Zebulun and Naphtali. The poet therefore speaks loftily: the forty thousand once chosen by God to wage war in the open field did not fight now at the city gates. With fortified cities now under threat, God needed to appoint new warriors. The meaning is that God selected fresh combatants for a different kind of warfare — defense of gates and strongholds — because none of the earlier champions came forward. Among those original forty thousand not even shield or spear was seen, as if their prior selection had been for open battle, not for urban defense. (The term “lacham” has troubled commentators, since grammatically the verb would require a different vocalization; in my interpretation it is a noun, meaning “warfare at the gates.”)
text.4_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: My heart. Therefore I directed my heart toward the leaders of Israel — the willing ones among the people, the ten thousand who marched with Barak — that they might bless Hashem, for salvation came through a small number, without power and without battle in the usual sense.
text.4_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: You who ride. He addresses three strata within the nation: first, the affluent merchants riding white donkeys; second, those seated in judgment — the leaders and scholars; and third, the poor who travel on foot in search of sustenance. Let all of you together declare and recount the mighty deeds of God.
text.4_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: From the sound. At the watering places along the Kishon, Hashem produced a resounding noise that to Sisera seemed like the crash of great forces — as though vast armies were approaching. Because of this, they proclaim the just deeds of Hashem on behalf of Israel. “His righteous acts toward the open settlements” — in poetic language, when Israel retreated to the fortified gates out of fear, it was then that Hashem manifested Himself in the unfortified villages, without walls or bars — meaning that at that moment He laid bare His mighty arm in open salvation.
text.4_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: Awake, awake. Stir yourself in recollection of the magnitude of this wondrous deliverance.
text.4_Chapter, 11_Verse, 1_Comment: Rise, Barak, and carry off your captives. He was not required to fight, only to gather the spoils of the defeated foe. In other words, Deborah’s role was in song, and Barak’s in collecting captives and booty — the victory itself was not achieved by their strength.
text.4_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: Then. She clarifies the marked contrast between the earlier salvation brought about by Ehud, which followed a natural course, and this present salvation, which came directly from Hashem. Thus “Then” refers back to the era of Ehud.
text.4_Chapter, 12_Verse, 1_Comment: A remnant went down for the mighty. The “remnant” refers to Ehud, who survived after slaying Eglon. The phrase “for the mighty” means that he acted with the aid of mighty warriors. Ehud subdued Moab with the support of strong men who joined him, as described when he sounded the shofar and Israel descended with him from the hills. Thus he prevailed over a weakened, scattered Moab through human strength. In contrast, in my case it was Hashem who descended on my behalf. Neither I nor mighty warriors accomplished the victory; Hashem Himself acted. And this was not against a feeble people, but against true warriors — the army of Sisera. (The verb “descended” comes from the root meaning “to subdue,” in an intensive form.)
text.4_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: From Meni. He clarifies who the “mighty” were in the earlier verse: they were from Ephraim, who joined Ehud; their lineage traced to Amalek, and they struck Amalek, who had allied with Moab (Judges 3:14). “After you” refers to Ehud — Benjamin followed after him among his people, since Ehud was of that tribe. These were powerful, heroic fighters. But in this war it was not seasoned warriors who came. From Machir descended lawgivers — scholars and judges, not soldiers. And from Zebulun came those who handle the scribe’s staff — writers and teachers, not men bearing shield and sword.
text.4_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: Similarly, the leaders of Issachar who accompanied Deborah were men learned in Torah. And the tribe of Issachar that marched with Barak went down into the valley on foot, having no cavalry, no chariots, and no trained warriors for battle.
text.4_Chapter, 14_Verse, 1_Comment: At the divisions. The poet reflects with sorrow upon the two tribes, Reuben and Dan, who did not come to the war. For in the days of Joshua, Reuben marched at the head of the camps, and Dan served as the rear guard for all the camps; yet now they did not appear. And if you examine the boundaries of the land, you will find that all the tribes were close to the field of battle, for Mount Tabor lay within the territory of Issachar. To its south were the portions of Judah, Simeon, the sons of Joseph, and Benjamin. And since Sisera had spread his forces against Issachar, Zebulun, and Naphtali—against whom he fought—he could easily have fallen upon any of the other tribes without obstacle. For the territory of Gad and half of Manasseh bordered Issachar across the Jordan; to the south it bordered the territories of Joseph, Benjamin, and Judah; and to the northwest were Zebulun and Naphtali, whose inheritances touched one another, as it says regarding the inheritance of Asher (Joshua 19:27), “it reached Zebulun,” and regarding the inheritance of Naphtali (ibid., v. 34), “it reached Zebulun from the south, and it reached Asher on the west, and Judah by the Jordan toward the sunrise.” Only the territories of Reuben and Dan were separated. For if the enemy had wished to attack the territory of Reuben, he would first have had to cross the Jordan into Gilead and pass through the regions of Gad and half of Manasseh. Likewise, if he had wished to attack Dan, whose territory lay in the southwestern corner, he would have had to pass through Asher. Therefore she said, “At the divisions of Reuben”: that Reuben divided himself and did not come to the army—even though he had no fear that the enemy would fall upon him—“great were the searchings of heart.” This phrase means deep engravings and terrible impressions upon the heart, that is, a profound breaking of the heart.
text.4_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: Why did you sit still? You dwell on the frontier like a warrior, for one who sits on the border is responsible for restraining the enemy from entering the land and for being constantly ready for the day of battle. Yet when distress came and your strength failed, why did you sit among the sheepfolds? Was it in order to listen to the whistling of the flocks you had gathered, as it says, “And the children of Reuben had very great livestock”? Was this why you remained at the border? But you might reply, “At the divisions of Reuben there were great searchings of heart.” That is to say, it is hardly necessary to inquire further about this, for the investigations of the heart are greater than the matter under discussion — since the reason is evident: Reuben said, “Why should I be afraid? Surely…”
text.4_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: Gilead remained across the Jordan. for Gilead lives beside me, guarding my land and standing as a barrier between me and the enemy. Therefore he did not come and did not share in the distress of his brothers. And likewise, “Why did Dan remain by the ships?” Why did Dan occupy himself with trade and gather ships, and not come to help? This too has an evident reason: he said in his heart that since Asher dwells along the seashore and occupies its inlets, Asher stands between him and the enemy and guards the breaches of his land from the enemy’s approach. Therefore he did not come.
text.4_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: Zebulun. While the others held back, Zebulun alone scorned his life even to death, and Naphtali likewise exposed his life on the high places of the field of battle. Thus she concludes her point: the victory came through a small number and without human power.
text.4_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: They came. Just as in Joshua’s era Jabin of Hazor assembled the Canaanite kings at the waters of Merom (Joshua 11), so now he gathered kings once more and encamped by the waters of Megiddo. The poet intentionally fuses past and present: what happened now mirrors what happened then. The kings came and fought alongside Sisera, just as their predecessors once fought with Hazor’s king. “They took no plunder of silver” — Jabin’s allies were not mercenaries; they did not fight for wages, just as in earlier days they had come without payment.
text.4_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: Similarly, from the heavens they fought — the stars from their pathways. The stars that had previously aided Israel in Joshua’s battles already possessed established routes — for “mesillah” signifies a prepared and accustomed road. From those same celestial tracks first laid in earlier times, they now battled Sisera. The poet’s image is symmetrical: as Sisera summoned allies from antiquity, Israel likewise received reinforcements from ancient cosmic powers.
text.4_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: Similarly, the River Kishon that carried them off is called the “river of antiquity,” for it had, in poetic conception, already swept away such armies in ancient days. The poet fuses the waters of Merom and the Kishon into one continuous symbolic stream.
text.4_Chapter, 20_Verse, 1_Comment: My soul, tread down the mighty force. That is, my soul, tread upon this strength — meaning that you should step with your feet upon these powerful waters and cross over them.
text.4_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: Thus the meaning is: My soul, march powerfully across the river when the horses’ hooves pounded from the furious charge of Sisera’s warriors. The poet imagines the river’s waves as gallant heroes racing against Sisera’s chariots, striking at their horses’ legs. At that very instant — when the flooding stream overwhelmed Sisera’s army and the crashing sound was heard — Barak and his forces crossed the river on foot.
text.4_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment:
They came. Just as in Joshua’s era Jabin of Hazor assembled the Canaanite kings at the waters of Merom (Joshua 11), so now he gathered kings once more and encamped by the waters of Megiddo. The poet intentionally fuses past and present: what happened now mirrors what happened then. The kings came and fought alongside Sisera, just as their predecessors once fought with Hazor’s king.

“They took no plunder of silver” — Jabin’s allies were not mercenaries; they did not fight for wages, just as in earlier days they had come without payment.
text.4_Chapter, 25_Verse, 0_Comment: Her hand. As explained earlier (4:21), she grasped the tent peg in one hand and the hammer in the other, intending to strike; however, she lacked the physical strength to drive it in fully. Through Divine intervention, the peg sank into his temple on its own. Thus, “her hand reached for the peg, and her right hand for the hammer.” Both her hands were straining and fatigued (note that “hand” can appear in masculine grammatical form, as elsewhere in Scripture). When it says she struck Sisera, it implies that her blow itself produced only a slight impression; nevertheless, through the crushing effect, even that small impact resulted in the peg piercing through his temple completely. Some commentators understand “weary” to refer to Sisera, but that interpretation does not align with proper grammar.
text.4_Chapter, 26_Verse, 0_Comment: Between. Initially he knelt between her legs and lay down — understood by the Sages as implying intimacy. Then, in that same place between her legs, he knelt, fell, and died. The point is that precisely where he bent in desire, there he collapsed in ruin and met his death.
text.4_Chapter, 27_Verse, 0_Comment: Through the window. There is a difference between a “window” and a “lattice”: the lattice is an elaborately constructed opening. Here it refers to a magical or divinatory window through which Sisera’s mother sought omens to learn his fate. Initially she peered through the window; later she perceived through the lattice — and then she began to cry out in lamentation. According to this explanation, she saw in her vision Sisera fallen to the ground, a woman standing over him striking his head, blood flowing, and slain warriors with reddened necks. Hence the verse unfolds in stages: first she looks out the window asking, “Why is his chariot delayed?” and afterward she wails through the lattice, “Why are his chariot wheels slow?”
text.4_Chapter, 27_Verse, 1_Comment: There is a difference between “boshesh” (tarrying) and “achar” (being late). “Boshesh” implies an unusual delay beyond what is normal, while “achar” denotes missing a definite, expected time of arrival. Thus, once the appointed time had clearly passed, she cried out, “Why have they been late?” She even added, “the steps of his chariots” — meaning that even if the chariot itself were taken, surely some messenger should have come to report the outcome. These thoughts arose as she peered into her window of divination.
text.4_Chapter, 28_Verse, 0_Comment: Her wise noblewomen responded. These “wise” attendants attempted to interpret the divination in an auspicious manner, and even Sisera’s mother echoed her own earlier statements so as to cast the situation in a hopeful light.
text.4_Chapter, 29_Verse, 0_Comment: Have they not found and divided the spoil? The wise women reinterpret the grim vision: the bloodied man seen lying on the ground is not Sisera, but a symbolic representation of the spoil itself. The divination clothed the plunder in the form of a man. The woman standing over his head signifies captive women — the choicest part of the spoils. The blood on his head symbolizes dyed and embroidered garments destined for Sisera. The reddened necks represent richly woven fabrics, metaphorically forming the “neck” of this imagined man of spoil. In other words, the omen did not depict death but abundance. The divination embodied the plunder as a symbolic human figure in the visionary scene.
text.4_Chapter, 30_Verse, 0_Comment: Thus. Thus may all Your enemies be destroyed, O Hashem; but those who love Him shall resemble the sun in its rising, advancing in strength and radiance until full daylight, like a sun unobscured by clouds and unshadowed by gloom.
text.4_Chapter, 30_Verse, 1_Comment: And the land had tranquility. Because they remained righteous throughout the lifetime of Deborah.
text.5_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: And they did. Previously Scripture stated, “They again did evil,” indicating a continuation of prior wrongdoing. But now, because in Deborah’s time they had fully repented and only afterward began to sin afresh, it says merely, “They did.” In this spirit the Sages taught that through the Song their sins were pardoned.
text.5_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: And the power of Midian intensified. With each incursion it became greater, until Israel was compelled to construct hidden tunnels and caves — places so confined that light pierced them only through narrow holes. Others explain that these were beacon-fires set upon the mountains to be lit when the enemy arrived, so that they might preserve their possessions, similar to the early practice of lighting signal torches (Rosh Hashanah 22b).
text.5_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: The Questions (3–5) Why does the text repeat itself — “Midian went up,” “they came up against him,” “they encamped against them”? And similarly, why are the details described in seemingly redundant phrases?
text.5_Chapter, 2_Verse, 1_Comment: And they advanced upon him. Meaning, upon the planted fields.
text.5_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: And they camped against them. Meaning, against the people directly. He clarifies: by attacking the crops they ruined the land’s yield; and by stationing themselves against the inhabitants they left no means of survival.
text.5_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: For they and their livestock ascended. They advanced against the fields, while their tents spread over the people. Both they and their camels were without number, because their chief aim in coming was to devastate.
text.5_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: And when they cried out on account of Midian. Their cry was not over their wrongdoing, but over their distress. They protested the affliction without acknowledging that it was the consequence of sin. For that reason, a prophet was sent to admonish them.
text.5_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: A man, a prophet. Because later an angel is sent, this messenger is described simply as “a man.” He declared, “So says Hashem: your own actions have caused this calamity.” And he proceeds to explain —
text.5_Chapter, 7_Verse, 1_Comment: (1) I brought you up out of Egypt. Accompanied by miraculous signs and wonders, so that you would acknowledge My majesty and might, and be filled with reverent fear.
text.5_Chapter, 7_Verse, 2_Comment: (2) And I delivered you from the house of slavery. This should have awakened gratitude within you — and taught you that you belong to Me as My servants.
text.5_Chapter, 7_Verse, 3_Comment: (3) And I rescued you. This should have taught you that you continue to rely on Me.
text.5_Chapter, 7_Verse, 4_Comment: (4) And I expelled them from before you. If they were driven out because of their corrupt practices, how could you adopt those same practices? And despite this, you did not heed My voice.
text.5_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: And the angel of Hashem came. Once the prophet had admonished them, the angel of Hashem appeared to bring salvation — fulfilling the verse, “In all their affliction He was afflicted, and the angel of His presence saved them.”
text.5_Chapter, 10_Verse, 1_Comment: Which belonged to Joash. Referring to the oak owned by Joash; or possibly to Ophrah of Joash, distinguishing it from another Ophrah in Benjamin’s territory (Joshua 18:23). Gideon, Joash’s son, was fit for Divine inspiration because heavenly influence descends only upon one prepared to receive it. Even partial readiness draws abundant blessing. Two qualifications were necessary: first, some merit — which would attract further assistance (“He who seeks purity is helped”); second, innate courage, enabling the spirit of Hashem — strength and valor — to rest upon him. Gideon had merit through honoring his father, indicated by the verse identifying him as “his son.” He also demonstrated courage by threshing wheat in hiding from Midian — an act revealing inner boldness and readiness for battle.
text.5_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: And he appeared to him. On account of this latent strength the angel revealed himself to Gideon, informing him that Hashem was with him and that he was a valiant warrior — meaning that Divine grace and sanctity would be poured upon him, together with abundant bravery.
text.5_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: If Hashem is with us. Gideon thought their suffering resulted from Divine concealment — that God had withdrawn and left them to natural forces, as in the verse, “Is it not because my God is not among me that these evils have found me?” Therefore he asks, “If Hashem is with us, why has all this happened to us?” — implying that events seem to have unfolded as though by chance.
text.5_Chapter, 12_Verse, 1_Comment: And where are all His miracles? When He exercised His Providence over us, He wrought signs that transcended the natural order.
text.5_Chapter, 12_Verse, 2_Comment: As our fathers recounted to us. Today we see no miraculous signs — so where are those wonders? It appears that He has abandoned us. And if you argue that our sins are the cause — did not Hashem bring us out of Egypt when we were steeped in Egyptian impurity? If He redeemed us then, though we were not yet fully loyal to Him, how can it be that now, after He has chosen us as His people, He has cast us off and given us into Midian’s hand? That would imply He no longer exercises Providence over us.
text.5_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: The Questions (14) Why does the verse state, “And Hashem turned to him,” rather than saying that the angel — who had been speaking with him up to this point — turned to him?
text.5_Chapter, 13_Verse, 1_Comment: And Hashem turned to him. Until now the angel had been speaking with him, but now Hashem turned to him in prophetic speech (for the angel serves as an intermediary to Him, and precedes the revelation before the word of Hashem is disclosed — as happened when Joshua was in Jericho). And He said, “Go in this your strength,” meaning: either the strength already found in him — the strength of valor — as shown by what was said about him preparing to flee from Midian, upon which this existing strength was now infused with abundant Divine influence sufficient to save Israel. Or, it refers to the strength of his argument — for after it was seen that he contends over the withdrawal of Divine Providence from Israel, this is a sign that the matter burns within his heart, and that he is therefore prepared for their salvation.
text.5_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: With what shall I save Israel?
