At first he thought that the deliverance would come through natural means, since the command had come by way of an angel — and this indicates warfare conducted through natural agency, as it says, “Behold, I send an angel before you,” and as explained there. Therefore he asked: What will be the means for this? If it is through a large army — behold, my thousand (clan) is the poorest in Manasseh. And if it is that Israel will listen to my voice — I am the youngest in my father’s house?!
text.5_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment:
And Hashem said to him: For I will be with you.
Therefore the deliverance will be miraculous — not by the strength of an army,
but you shall strike Midian as though he were a single man.
text.5_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: The Questions (17) The sign was needed in order to confirm that He would fulfill His promise to save them — not to prove that He was speaking with him, for that requires no sign. And how could bringing a gift serve as a sign?
text.5_Chapter, 16_Verse, 1_Comment: And he said to him: “If now I have found favor in Your eyes, then perform for me a sign that You are speaking with me.” This may be understood in two ways: First, he was uncertain whether the speech came from God Himself without intermediary — which would indicate a miraculous salvation requiring no multitude or army, for there is no restraint to Hashem to save by many or by few — or whether it came through an angel, in which case the salvation too would come through intermediary means, suggesting deliverance through natural instruments: a large force and war. Thus he said: “If now I have found favor in Your eyes.” For that Hashem Himself should go in their midst without intermediary indicates the finding of favor, as it says, “If I have found favor in Your eyes, let Hashem go in our midst,” and “By what then shall it be known that I have found favor in Your eyes? Is it not by Your going with us?” Therefore he requested a sign — that he might know that You are speaking with me without intermediary. For there is an angel who is merely a messenger sent by God, and there is one within whom the Divine manifestation itself is clothed. And this sign would be through the offering. For if he is merely a messenger performing Hashem’s mission and his Master is not with him, he would not accept a burnt offering or meal offering, since “he who sacrifices to gods shall be utterly destroyed — except to Hashem alone.” As the angel of Hashem said to Manoah: “If you offer a burnt offering, you must offer it to Hashem.” In that case, he would either refuse it, or eat it, as did the angels with Abraham. But he would not permit a sacrifice to be offered to him. If he accepts a sacrifice from his hand, this would be the sign and proof that Hashem dwells within him. The second matter is this: Even if Gideon knew that God Himself was speaking with him, he requested a sign from another perspective. There is a difference between speech that comes from God to a prophet in the capacity of mission, and speech that comes from God to individuals. Good promises delivered through a prophet in the form of mission are never retracted, even if the people later worsen their deeds, as it says: “The prophet who speaks in the name of Hashem — if the word does not come to pass — that is the word Hashem did not speak.” But good promises given to individuals not in the capacity of mission may indeed change for the worse if the recipient later corrupts his conduct.
text.5_Chapter, 16_Verse, 2_Comment: And as the Rambam said: However, even a word of Hashem spoken to individuals — if it is accompanied by some sign or wonder — will not change under any circumstance. This was the matter of the sign given at the Covenant Between the Pieces and similar events — that once the Divine word was sealed with a sign, the matter would no longer be altered.
text.5_Chapter, 16_Verse, 3_Comment: And as the Ramban explains in many places, this is what he meant when he said: “And perform for me a sign that You are speaking with me.” That is, since You are speaking with me alone, and I am not a messenger to the people, it is therefore possible that the matter might change because of sin — as Jacob feared, “perhaps sin will cause [the promise not to be fulfilled]” (Berakhot 4a). Therefore I request a sign, so that the matter will necessarily come to pass in every circumstance. And the sign was that He accepted the offering from him in a miraculous manner, by fire. Thus he said: “Do not depart from here…”
text.5_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: And Gideon came and prepared a kid of the goats, etc. According to the first explanation that we gave — that Gideon was uncertain whether the offering would be accepted as a burnt-offering to Hashem, or whether it would be eaten, as the angels did with Abraham — therefore he prepared a young goat, which was suitable either for offering up or for eating. He also prepared broth in a pot and meat in a basket, which were likewise fit either for being offered up or for being eaten. And he brought it out to him beneath the terebinth tree, to see what he would do with it.
text.5_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: (20–21) Why at first is he called “the angel of God,” and afterward “the angel of Hashem”?
text.5_Chapter, 19_Verse, 1_Comment:
And the angel of God said to him… and the angel of Hashem stretched out the tip of the staff.
We have already explained that an angel cannot receive a sacrifice, for “he who sacrifices to any god shall be destroyed,” unless Hashem Himself dwells within him and the offering is to Hashem alone. Therefore, in the speaking and commanding it was through an intermediary angel, and thus he is called “the angel of God.” But at the moment he stretched out the tip of the staff to receive the offering, it was necessarily that Hashem Himself was dwelling within him and accepting the sacrifice. Therefore in this act he is not called “the angel of God,” for one who sacrifices to a being called god would be liable, but rather “the angel of Hashem.”
text.5_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: And Gideon saw that he was the angel of Hashem. Then he knew that he was not merely an “angel of God,” which would indicate a messenger-angel without Hashem dwelling within him — for the term “God” can also be used of an angel — but rather that he was the “angel of Hashem,” which signifies that Hashem was dwelling within him.
text.5_Chapter, 21_Verse, 1_Comment:
And Gideon said, “Alas, Hashem God! for therefore I have seen…”
That is to say: “For no man can see Hashem and live.” It is impossible for a human being to behold Hashem while still enclosed within the body; such vision can occur only at the moment of death.
text.5_Chapter, 21_Verse, 2_Comment: And as it is said (Sifra, Vayikra, ch. 2): “In their lifetime they do not see, but at their death they see the Shechinah,” as it is written, “For to Me every knee shall bow.” Therefore he thought that he would die.  And according to the commentators who explain that he was uncertain whether it was a prophet or an angel — the thought arose in his mind that it is impossible for a human being to see an angel, whose essence is purely spiritual and separate from matter. How then could a man, clothed in physical substance, behold such a being? Only at the moment of death — when the soul, which is spiritual, becomes prepared to separate from its bodily shell — does it resemble the angel, who appears clothed in form yet is ready at once to divest himself of it. And then, the like can behold the like.
text.5_Chapter, 21_Verse, 3_Comment: And this is what he meant when he said, “Alas! for therefore I have seen” — that is, because of this likeness between myself and the angel, for my soul is now prepared to depart from the prison of the body; therefore I have seen God face to face. For the “faces” resemble one another in their condition in this respect, and thus he thought that he was destined to die.
text.5_Chapter, 21_Verse, 4_Comment: (And especially it may be said that Gideon — and likewise Manoah — were afraid because they saw him at the very moment he vanished from their sight. For at that instant, when he divests himself of his bodily form, it is impossible for a living person to behold him. Concerning this Elijah said, “If you see me when I am taken from you.” And this is what is meant by “And Gideon saw that he was the angel of Hashem” — for he saw him in his very essence as an angel, since until then he had appeared to him in the form of a man.) Therefore he was afraid.
text.5_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: And Hashem said to him, “Peace be to you.” Peace is the opposite of death, whose cause is the separation and conflict of the elements. When there is peace among the foundations of the body and between body and soul, there is no destruction — as it is said, “Behold, I give him My covenant of peace.” This peace was also the cause that he was able to see the angel, for the material substance did not hinder the soul from perception. Therefore, “Do not fear; you shall not die” — neither the death of the body nor the death of the soul — for your sins have been forgiven, as it is said, “Peace, peace to him who is far and to him who is near, says Hashem, and I will heal him.”
text.5_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: And he built there an altar. After he saw that a miracle had been performed in that place, he built an altar. And he called it “Hashem is Peace.” According to the plain meaning, it means that he called Hashem “Peace” (and so is the opinion of the master of the cantillation marks, placing the disjunctive accent on the Name). That is to say, since the people of his town were idol worshipers and he feared they might interfere with his actions — as indeed they later destroyed the second altar that was built afterward — this altar he called “Hashem is Peace,” for Hashem granted it peace, that the townsmen did not destroy it. And it remains to this day in Ophrah as a memorial of the miracle.
text.5_Chapter, 23_Verse, 1_Comment: And the commentator explains that Gideon called the altar “Hashem is Peace,” meaning: May Hashem establish peace for us. That is, he recognized that Hashem is the peace of all the worlds — the thread that strings together all parts of existence, binding them and sustaining them. As explained in Isaiah (45:7) on the verse “Who makes peace,” and for this reason He is called “King to whom peace belongs.”
text.5_Chapter, 23_Verse, 2_Comment: And our Sages said concerning this (Shabbat 12b): “Here the Name itself is called ‘Peace.’” And there is, in my view, an intellectual matter in this which I have explained elsewhere.
text.5_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: (25–26) He did not explain what he was to do with the first bull, for he commanded him only to offer the second bull. And the phrase “and build on the top of this stronghold in proper arrangement” has no clear meaning — for does one build upon the arrangement? One prepares the arrangement upon an altar already built, not the reverse.
text.5_Chapter, 24_Verse, 1_Comment: And it came to pass that night. By day he had built the altar, but it is not stated that he offered a sacrifice upon it, for he feared to offer one by day because of the townsmen. Therefore he intended to offer it at night, as it is said (v. 27), “And it was when he feared…” and so he did it by night. When he turned in his thoughts to consider what he should offer — whether a ram, a lamb, or a goat — Hashem said to him: “Take the bull of your father.” That is, you shall offer that one. Therefore it did not explicitly state that he was to sacrifice it, for this was an answer to his doubt about what he should bring — Hashem replied: “The bull that belongs to your father you shall offer.” Then He added and commanded him something new: that he should take the second bull, seven years old. This second bull belonged not to his father but to the townsmen, and it had been fattened for seven years. When Midian began to rule over Israel, they had vowed to offer this bull to idolatry when they would be delivered from Midian, and they had fattened it throughout the seven years of Midian’s rule. He then explained what he was to do with the second bull: after he would offer the first bull upon the altar, he was to demolish the altar of Baal and cut down the Asherah that was upon it.
text.5_Chapter, 25_Verse, 0_Comment: And you shall build an altar. From the stones of the altar of Baal that was demolished he was to build an altar to Hashem. “On the top of this stronghold, in proper arrangement” — he commanded him to build the second altar upon the first altar that he had built upon the rock, so that one altar would be constructed upon another. This is the meaning of “on the top of this stronghold,” that is, that the first altar was firm and strong enough to build upon it. And that the second altar should be upon the arrangement — that is, upon the place where he had offered the first bull. “And you shall take the second bull and offer it as a burnt offering with the wood of the Asherah” — so that the stones of the altar of idolatry would become for Hashem, and the wood of the Asherah would serve as fuel, and the bull would be for a burnt offering. All this was to demonstrate that Hashem would redeem them from Midian, and also that he was prepared to risk his life to sanctify the Name and to show that there is no substance in idolatry.
text.5_Chapter, 25_Verse, 1_Comment: And our Sages said: Seven things were permitted on that night.
text.5_Chapter, 26_Verse, 0_Comment: And Gideon took ten men. For he needed first to offer the first bull, and afterward to build an altar upon the arrangement; and had he done it alone, it would have taken until daylight. Therefore he took men to assist him. And it explains that he was afraid to do it by day.
text.5_Chapter, 27_Verse, 0_Comment: And behold, the altar was torn down. There is a difference between demolition and tearing down: one who demolishes dismantles the structure, but one who tears down shatters each stone into fragments. In truth, he did not tear it down but only demolished it, as it is said, “and you shall demolish the altar of Baal,” for he took the stones intact and built with them for Hashem. But they, not knowing that he had rebuilt an altar from those stones, assumed that he had smashed and shattered it.
text.5_Chapter, 27_Verse, 1_Comment: And the bull was offered. The word “et” here means “with,” that is, the Asherah together with the bull was offered upon the altar that had been built. (And without doubt the townsmen destroyed the altar that had been built above, but the lower altar they were unable to demolish; therefore it was called a stronghold. And it was by the Providence of Hashem that it was called “Peace,” as explained above.)
text.5_Chapter, 30_Verse, 0_Comment: (31) Why the repetition: “Will you contend for Baal?” and “Will you save him?” And how could he say, “Whoever contends for him shall be put to death by morning” — who would put him to death? Were not all the people zealous for Baal and ready to contend on his behalf?
text.5_Chapter, 30_Verse, 1_Comment: And Joash said. He said to them: Either way, your claim collapses. If you think that Baal has the power to avenge his own honor, but simply chooses not to contend — then why should you contend for Baal, if he does not plead his own cause? And if you think that he wishes to contend but lacks the power — then why should you save him, if he cannot save himself? Therefore, whoever contends for him shall be put to death by morning.
text.5_Chapter, 30_Verse, 2_Comment: Why did he wait all night and remain silent? If he truly had power, he should have killed Gideon by morning — yet Gideon lives. This proves that he has no power. And if you reply that he does not wish to contend, that too is false — for if he were truly a god, he would surely plead his own cause because his altar was torn down; he would not remain silent over such a matter. Rather, he is no god, he has no power, and there is nothing in him.
text.5_Chapter, 31_Verse, 0_Comment: And he called him. So that they would understand from this that Baal is vanity, he called him by this name — meaning “let Baal contend,” thereby openly denying Baal and serving Hashem. In this way the higher purpose was fulfilled: through this act they were distanced from idolatry. And this was a preparation for the deliverance that had been promised, for it is impossible for them to be saved while they still believe in Baal.
text.5_Chapter, 33_Verse, 0_Comment: And the spirit of Hashem. This was a spirit of might, as the Guide explains — the first level of prophecy, when the spirit of God rests upon a man to deliver an entire nation. And he sounded the shofar. As a signal for them to assemble for war; and Abiezer — his clan and his town — were summoned.
text.5_Chapter, 35_Verse, 0_Comment: (36–40) Why did he ask for a sign after he had already been given a sign with fire? And why did he now request two signs? And according to proper language usage, he should have said, “If there shall be dryness upon all the earth and dew upon the fleece”; and in the first instance it says, “And it was so.”
text.5_Chapter, 35_Verse, 1_Comment: And Gideon said. He did not request the sign in order to know whether God was able to save — for such a test is forbidden, as it indicates a lack of faith, as Rabbeinu Saadia explained. Rather, he saw that that generation was unworthy of deliverance. Although the people of his town had abandoned Baal, the other tribes were still bowing to him, like those who knelt upon their knees. Therefore he sought a sign whether his small merit would suffice for this salvation. He asked for two signs, because a wonder is not complete unless it is tested from two sides. At first he reasoned that dew would naturally remain longer upon the ground, since by its nature and coolness it retains moisture more steadily. Afterwards he reasoned the opposite — that the fleece, by its softness and absorbent quality, might draw the dew more strongly to itself, as the author of the Akedah explains. Therefore in the first sign it says, “And he wrung the fleece,” for the main wonder there was that the dew remained upon it afterward; since the initial attraction of dew to fleece could be natural. In the second sign it says, “And there was dryness upon the fleece,” for the primary wonder was that it was dry from the outset and did not draw the dew at all despite its absorbent nature. And these two signs were also necessary according to the allegorical meaning. For at first he doubted whether his small merit would suffice that Israel be saved even though they were idol worshipers; therefore he said, “If You will save Israel by my hand,” meaning by my merit. And his merit began at the threshing floor, where the angel had appeared to him.
text.5_Chapter, 36_Verse, 0_Comment: And he said. He placed a fleece of wool on the threshing floor and tested it with dew — for dew is a metaphor for the Divine influx descending from above, as it is said, “I will be as the dew to Israel,” and “My head is filled with dew.” “If there shall be dew upon the fleece alone, while upon all the earth there is dryness” — that is, even if all the land, meaning all Israel, is unworthy of the heavenly dew and remains dry — nevertheless, if by my merit I draw down the dew, then I shall know that You will save Israel by my hand and through my merit.
text.5_Chapter, 37_Verse, 0_Comment: And it was so; and he rose early… and wrung the fleece. Our Sages explained that it does not state that there was dryness upon all the earth, because there is a covenant with the dew that it is never withheld. Thus, the wonder consisted only in the abundance of dew upon the fleece. This sign was still close to nature — it was an increase and excess of dew. Yet Hashem had promised him two things: (1) that He would save the people by his hand, and (2) that He would save them by his hand alone, without a great army, in a miraculous manner. Concerning this second point he sought another sign — one fully miraculous — to assure him that his small merit would suffice for a miracle. Therefore he said, “Let me test, I pray, once more.” As I have explained elsewhere, there is a difference between a test (nisayon) and an examination (bechinah): a test seeks to determine whether one can rise to a higher level than his current state. So too here — he wished to see whether he would ascend from a sign near nature to a sign wholly miraculous, namely, that the fleece alone would be dry. That is entirely against nature. According to the principles of language, one ordinarily places first what is primary in the statement. Thus he should have said, “If upon all the earth there is dryness and upon the fleece there is dew.” But according to what we have explained, both signs centered on the fleece. For even in the first instance he knew that dew could not be entirely withheld; rather, he tested whether there would be such abundance upon the fleece that, relative to it, the earth would appear dry. Therefore the wording is as stated.
text.5_Chapter, 39_Verse, 0_Comment: And God did so that night. For in the second sign there was no room at all for nature; it was purely the finger of God. And the two signs were necessary also according to the allegory. At first he defeated the camp of Midian by himself, and to this the first sign corresponded. Afterwards, “all the men of Israel cried out and pursued,” and they achieved the final victory without him, as it is said (8:2), “What was I able to do compared to you?” This was symbolized by the second sign: although there was dryness upon the fleece — that is, Gideon’s strength alone did not suffice to complete the victory — yet there was dew upon the ground, meaning that the Divine blessing rested upon the rest of Israel, and through them the deliverance was completed.
text.6_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: North of the Hill of Moreh. En-Harod was to the south of the Hill of Moreh, while the camp was to the north in the valley.
text.6_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: The people who are with you are too many. Hashem desired that it be evident that He had wrought the victory by miracle. For if there were many people, they would say that they themselves had prevailed.
text.6_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: (3) What is meant by “let him return and depart early”? And why here does it say, “and there returned of the people,” whereas in verse 8 it says, “and he sent every man to his tent”?
text.6_Chapter, 2_Verse, 1_Comment: Whoever is fearful and trembling. The Divine influx rests only upon those who are prepared and worthy of it. Here two qualifications were required: (1) preparation of courage, and (2) preparation of holiness to receive the Divine matter — for this victory would be girded with valor and accomplished by a miracle, adorned with Divine strength. Therefore he first commanded that the fearful and fainthearted return, for they were not prepared for courage. And afterward he separated those who knelt upon their knees, who were unworthy of the miracle.
text.6_Chapter, 2_Verse, 2_Comment: Let him return and depart early. That is, let him return at once and lodge at Mount Gilead, and in the morning go to his home. He did not command them to go home immediately, because he knew that the deliverance would occur at night, and these men would pursue from Mount Gilead after the fleeing enemy. For this reason he used the expression “depart early” (yitzpor), which also implies flying swiftly like birds after the enemy. But regarding those who knelt upon their knees, he commanded that they go immediately to their homes, for these were idol worshipers, and he did not wish them to participate in the war at all — not even in the pursuit.
text.6_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: (4) Why did he conduct a second test? What is meant by “and I will refine him for you”? Why the doubled expression: “everyone of whom I say… this one shall go,” and “everyone of whom I say… this one shall not go”? And in the first case it says “shall go with you,” but in the second it says “shall not go” without the words “with you”?
text.6_Chapter, 3_Verse, 1_Comment: The people are still too many. At first it said, “The people who are with you are too many,” for the earlier ones were not idol worshipers and were aligned with him — they were with him in spirit. But these, who were idol worshipers, were not truly with him.
text.6_Chapter, 3_Verse, 2_Comment: And I will refine them for you. That is, I will determine who is fit to go with you. Whoever is worthy shall go with you — meaning, according to your intention before Hashem in this war. But of whoever I say, “This one shall not go,” he shall not go at all — not only that he will not go with you in the proper spirit and intention, but he will not go at all, for when he sees the battle he will turn back, being without faith.
text.6_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: Everyone who laps. That is, one who brings the water with his hand to his mouth is called “lapping,” whereas one who kneels fills his mouth directly from the water.
text.6_Chapter, 4_Verse, 1_Comment: And according to our Sages, those who knelt were accustomed to kneel before their reflection (as an act connected to idolatry). Moreover, kneeling indicates a gluttonous impulse to drink all at once and a weakening of the limbs, as explained in the Akedah. Therefore he commanded that those who knelt be set aside, for they would not go. And those who lapped with the tongue — that is, those who brought the water with their hands to their mouths — they were the ones who went. Rashi, however, explains this matter in a different way.
text.6_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: And all the rest. At first it said, “and ten thousand remained,” and as I have explained elsewhere, what “remains” is something intentional and purposeful. But “the rest” refers to what is unnecessary and superfluous.
text.6_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: (8) Why does it state again, “and the camp of Midian was below him in the valley,” when this had already been said in verse 1?
text.6_Chapter, 7_Verse, 1_Comment: And they took. The three hundred men took the provisions of those who were departing; therefore there were found in their hands three hundred jars and shofars. “And the camp of Midian was below him” — this had already been mentioned in verse 1, but now he had ascended the mountain, and the camp was beneath him.
text.6_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: Go down… into the camp… and if you are afraid… go down… to the camp. “In the camp” means to descend upon the camp to conquer it; but “to the camp” means to stand at a distance and hear what they are saying. Therefore it says, “And if you are afraid” — that is, since it is impossible to bestow upon you a spirit of might if fear remains in your heart — “go down, you yourself, to the camp.” And afterward, “your hands shall be strengthened, and you shall go down into the camp” — to fight. To the edge of the armed men. That is, the armed ones, for not all were armed; only those stationed at the edge stood on guard.
text.6_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: (13) What is the meaning of the dream in its details? (17) Why the repetition: “From me you shall see and so shall you do,” and “and it shall be, as I do, so shall you do”?
text.6_Chapter, 12_Verse, 1_Comment: And behold, a cake of barley bread. It was then the sixteenth of Nisan, the time of the barley harvest, and they had come to plunder the harvest of the fields, which was barley bread. He saw a cake — and heard the sound, the clatter of the barley bread they had come to seize — rolling and overturning in the camp of Midian. Instead of Israel hiding from them as before, it was now reversed: the barley cake came to rule over their enemies. And it came as far as the tent — that is, into the very camp where the tents stood.
text.6_Chapter, 12_Verse, 2_Comment: And it struck it and it fell. This represents that the slain would fall in battle. “And it overturned it upward” — this was a second vision: afterward they would flee from the valley to the surrounding hills, and there the tent would collapse completely. And therefore it says, “And his fellow answered and said…”
text.6_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: And he divided. He describes eight of his stratagems: (1) He divided them into three companies, to attack from three directions. (2) He placed shofars in all their hands, to terrify them with the blast of war. (3) Torches — to frighten them with pillars of fire and smoke. (4) Empty jars — so that the torches would suddenly appear, and that a loud crashing sound would be heard when the jars were shattered.
text.6_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: And he said, “From me you shall see, and so shall you do.” (5) They were not to act until he acted — for since he was coming to the edge of the camp, he would be the one to begin.
text.6_Chapter, 16_Verse, 1_Comment: (6) “And it shall be, as I do, so shall you do” — that everything he would do, they were to do exactly as he did. And he explains:
text.6_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: And I will blow the shofar… and you shall also blow the shofars. (7) The blasts were to surround the entire camp, so that they would think there were many battalions — for in every battalion one blows the shofar. And they would imagine themselves encircled, since the sound would travel all around them.
text.6_Chapter, 17_Verse, 1_Comment: (8) That they should cry out, “A sword for Hashem and for Gideon” — that is, there is here a miraculous element attributed to Hashem, and a natural element attributed to Gideon.
text.6_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: (19–23) Why does it repeat: “and they blew the shofars,” “and the three companies blew the shofars,” and “and the three hundred blew the shofars”? First it says “and they blew,” and afterward “and they held the shofars to blow”? And why the repetition: “and the camp ran,” “and they fled,” and “and the camp fled”?
text.6_Chapter, 18_Verse, 1_Comment: And they came… at the beginning of the middle watch. At that time most were asleep; only those who had just risen to relieve the guards were awake. Thus those going off duty were lying down to sleep, and those coming on duty still had drowsiness upon their eyelids. And they blew. Gideon and his men blew first. And then—
text.6_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: And the three companies blew. As he had said, “From me you shall see, and so shall you do.”
text.6_Chapter, 19_Verse, 3_Comment: And they held. Here he begins to describe the confusion that arose in the enemy camp. At the moment when they held the torches in their left hands and the shofars in their right hands to blow — while not all had yet blown, but were preparing themselves to do so — at that moment they cried out, “A sword for Hashem and for Gideon.”
text.6_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: And they stood. That is, each man still stood in his place around the camp, and from this alone a commotion already arose within the enemy camp. And all the camp ran. They began to run — some in one direction and some in another — out of confusion and panic. And they shouted and fled. Some of them raised a battle cry, while others began to flee, for great confusion had arisen among them.
text.6_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: And they blew. But when all three hundred shofars began actually to sound, then Hashem set every man’s sword against his fellow. For since some were shouting a battle cry and others were fleeing, those who shouted assumed that those who fled were enemies. This confusion spread throughout the entire camp, and thus the whole camp fled, scattering in every direction.
text.6_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: And he cried out. As I mentioned earlier (v. 3), he instructed those whom he had first sent away to lodge at Mount Gilead so that they would be ready to pursue. And they came, were summoned, and pursued.
text.6_Chapter, 48_Verse, 0_Comment: And likewise he sent messengers to the hill country of Ephraim to seize the waters; and they captured the waters and seized the two kings of Midian. And the phrase “and they pursued to Midian” — whereas it should have said “after Midian” or “Midian” — means that they pursued them face to face, for by capturing the waters they came before them and cut them off.
text.7_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: (1) Did he not send messengers throughout all the hill country of Ephraim?
text.7_Chapter, 0_Verse, 1_Comment: What is this thing that you have done to us? For at first he sent messengers to Manasseh, Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali (6:35), but not to Ephraim. Only now did he send messengers to the hill country of Ephraim — and this was a great disgrace to them. This is what they meant by saying, “by not calling us when you went to fight,” but only afterward, at the conclusion of the battle. (The word “kerot” is an infinitive form compounded from patterns of verbs with weak letters, like “galut Yerushalayim,” “kero mikra.”)
text.7_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: (2–3) Why the repetition: “What have I done now compared to you?” and “What was I able to do compared to you?”
text.7_Chapter, 1_Verse, 1_Comment: And he said. He answered: Why do you contend with me? If it is because I took the honor for myself in being the one to begin — you are the ones who completed it. “What have I done now compared to you?” At this point, at the conclusion, I have done nothing in comparison to you. (He said “now,” for he still hoped to capture Zebah and Zalmunna; as yet he had not accomplished that.) And though I was the one who gathered the vintage — who began — yet the gleanings which you gathered at the end are better than the first harvest. Thus, in terms of the deed itself, your actions are greater, even though they came afterward.
text.7_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: This is secondly from the aspect of might: was it not into your hands that God delivered the princes of Midian? In this you displayed extraordinary valor, so great that it was attributed to Hashem, that He gave them into your hand. And what was I able to do compared to you? This was something I was not capable of doing. Through this, their anger was softened.
text.7_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions: (5–17) What did he say to the men of Sukkot, and why did the officers of Sukkot answer him? They said, “Have the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already been delivered into your hand, that we should give bread to your army?” In verse 15 it mentions that they said, “Should we give bread to your weary men?” In verses 15–16 it states that he came to the men of Sukkot, that he took the elders of the city, and that he disciplined the men of Sukkot, which implies that he did not discipline the elders — for if he had, it should have said “and he disciplined them.” Why, then, did he not strike the elders? And why did he kill the men of Penuel but not the men of Sukkot?
text.7_Chapter, 4_Verse, 1_Comment: And he said to the men of Sukkot. They were obligated to give them bread for two reasons: (a) on account of the commandment of charity, since they were weary and hungry, and this commandment rests upon the entire people; (b) on account of obligation, since they were an army at war pursuing the enemy, and this responsibility rests upon the officers to provide from the levy, as it serves the public good. Because they were weary and in pursuit, Gideon first turned to the people — as it says, “And he said to the men of Sukkot” — and he gave the reason that they should provide bread because they were weary, and therefore should give on account of the commandment of charity. He further added that they were engaged in a mitzvah, pursuing Zebah and Zalmunna.
text.7_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: And the officers of Sukkot said. It is understood that the people did not wish to give to him on account of charity, because his men were weary. He then turned to the officers that they should give on account of obligation, as he stated at the end of his words that he was pursuing Zebah and Zalmunna. The officers responded: “Are the palms of Zebah and Zalmunna now in your hand, that we should give bread to your army?” You want us to give because they are your army — that is, a military force — for which the obligation rests upon the officers. But you have not yet defeated the enemy, and it is understood that they feared that if they were to give on this basis, they would be punished if the enemy prevailed. (And the word “and he said” indicates that one of the officers answered on behalf of them all.)
text.7_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: When I return in peace, I will tear down this tower. That is to say, they have no excuse to claim that they fear the enemy, since they trust in their strong tower; therefore he would tear down the tower — measure for measure.
text.7_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: From Maaleh-Haḥeres. That is, he fell upon the camp at night, just as in the first instance he had thrown them into panic at night; and when the sun rose upon the land, he returned. That is to say, he turned back because the sun had risen, for his men were few and could wage battle only at night.
text.7_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: And he took the elders of the city and the thorns… and he disciplined with them. That is to say, by means of them — he commanded that the elders discipline the men of Sukkot with thorns because they had withheld bread out of hardness of heart.
text.7_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: And he tore down the tower of Penuel. As stated above; and he killed the men of the city, for they had no excuse as the men of Sukkot did, as explained earlier.
text.7_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: The Questions(18) Their response, “As you are, so were they,” does not constitute a valid defense
text.7_Chapter, 17_Verse, 1_Comment: Where are the men whom you killed at Tabor? When Zebah and Zalmunna fled to cross the Jordan, they passed through Tabor, and there they killed Gideon’s brothers. Now, according to the laws of the state, captured kings are not executed in war unless there is a charge against them — such as kings who had submitted and then rebelled. Therefore, it would not have been proper to kill Zebah and Zalmunna (who were rulers of the land) without judgment. Thus he tried them for killing his brothers. They responded, “As you are, so were they — each one,” meaning that they were liable to death just as you are, for they rebelled against us as you have. “For we saw them like the form of royal sons” — that is, they conducted themselves with royal bearing, and therefore we regarded them as rebels against us and liable to death in our judgment. Just as if we had captured you, you would have been liable to death for rebellion, so they thought they were his sons, royal princes, and therefore liable to death for their father’s rebellion according to the laws of Midian.
text.7_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: And he said, “They were my brothers, the sons of my mother.” That is to say, they were not my sons but my brothers; they did not rebel, and you killed them without cause. Had you let them live, I would not have killed you without judgment.
text.7_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: And he said to Jether. Because he was the blood-avenger for the killing of his father’s brothers.
text.7_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: For as a man is, so is his might. Valor must correspond to the person who performs the act of valor, and this act of bravery — to kill kings of the land — befits you.
text.7_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: Rule over us. They said to him: (a) that he should rule because he is worthy of it and they would derive benefit from him; (b) that his sons should also rule, on the grounds that “you have saved us,” etc.
text.7_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: And he said… I will not rule… That is to say, whether the benefit comes from me or the salvation — all is attributed to Hashem, and He shall rule over you.
text.7_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: I would request… After stating that he did not pursue authority, it now relates that he also despised personal gain; for by law half of the spoil rightfully came to him, yet he did not take it, except for a small amount, and only as a gift.
text.7_Chapter, 23_Verse, 1_Comment: For they were Ishmaelites. That is, the Midianites conducted themselves like the Ishmaelites and mingled with them, as it says, “And Midianite men passed by… and they sold Joseph to the Ishmaelites” (Genesis 37), as explained by Radak.
text.7_Chapter, 25_Verse, 0_Comment: Aside from the crescent ornaments. These constituted spoil in their own right, and thus they remained in his possession.
text.7_Chapter, 26_Verse, 0_Comment: And he made. From the earrings he made an ephod, an ornament as a memorial of the miracle; and after his death his brothers went astray after it. It became a snare to Gideon and to his household, and because they stumbled on account of it, he was punished in that his sons were killed.
text.7_Chapter, 27_Verse, 0_Comment: Forty years. Including the seven years of oppression.
text.7_Chapter, 28_Verse, 0_Comment: And he recorded for himself the officers of Sukkot… and he came to the men of Sukkot. He saw that the officers of Sukkot were not deserving of punishment, for they argued correctly that they were not yet obligated to provide him with provisions as a levy, and they were also afraid to do so. However, the men of Sukkot — from whom he had requested bread on account of their weariness — were deserving of punishment. Therefore, he came to the men of Sukkot, not to the officers. He explained the reason for the punishment on the grounds that they had taunted him: “Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in your hand, that we should give bread to your weary men?” He did not cite the wording of the officers — “that we should give bread to your army” — for that was not a taunt, since they were not yet established as an army to be supported by a levy. But the men of Sukkot, who said “your weary men,” to whom he had asked charity for exhausted individuals and not provisions for an army — this was a taunt.
text.7_Chapter, 28_Verse, 1_Comment: And he dwelt in his house. For he no longer needed to wage war, since there was no adversary.
text.7_Chapter, 32_Verse, 0_Comment: And when he died, they returned. As it says above, “And it came to pass when the judge died…” (Judges 2:19).
text.7_Chapter, 68_Verse, 0_Comment: And they did not remember… Hashem, nor did they show kindness to the house of Jerubbaal… That is to say, this deliverance had a miraculous, Divine element, and it was fitting that they remember Hashem; yet they did not remember Hashem, for they attributed it to a natural cause and to Gideon’s valor. And if so, they should at least have remembered Gideon for all the good he had done — but instead they repaid evil for good, as will be related shortly. The text repeats “the house of Jerubbaal, Gideon,” to indicate that they did not show kindness to Gideon as the house of Jerubbaal — that is, one who contended with Baal — even though after his death they themselves began to sacrifice to Baal.
text.8_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: What is better for you? He said that they should speak to the people that this is for the public good: for if the sons of Jerubbaal were to rule, all of them would necessarily rule, since they are equal — all being sons of Jerubbaal — and their claim to authority would be equal; and this would not be good for the community. Secondly, it would also be for their own benefit, since he is of their family.
text.8_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: And he inclined their hearts. Not because it was for the public good, nor because they remembered what they had pledged to Jerubbaal — “Rule over us, you and your son as well” — but rather because they said, “He is our brother.”
text.8_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: And they gave to him. In this way the leaders of Shechem became partners in the act of murder, for they assisted him with money.
text.8_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: May God hear you. He is the Judge, and He will judge between us.
text.8_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions(8–15) What did he intend with this parable? Why did he choose the vine, the olive, and the fig from among all the fruit trees? Why, regarding the fig and the vine, did he say “Come, reign,” but regarding the olive he said “Reign” without the word “come”? Why in all the cases did it say “the trees said,” yet with the bramble it says “all the trees said”?
text.8_Chapter, 7_Verse, 1_Comment: The trees went forth. The trees went repeatedly to anoint a king over themselves. The parable refers to human beings (for “man is the tree of the field”), who went to establish for themselves a ruler and governor. It is the way of those seeking a king to seek out the one most worthy and most distinguished for advancing the perfection of the community. Such a choice is not made by the masses, but by their leaders and sages, who have the authority to choose. Therefore it does not say at the outset “all the trees,” but simply “the trees went” — meaning the select trees that bear fruit, who represent the distinguished among the people.
text.8_Chapter, 7_Verse, 2_Comment: Now purposes are divided into three categories: the good, the pleasant, and the useful.
text.8_Chapter, 7_Verse, 3_Comment: The pursuit of what is pleasant is an activity of the animal faculty of sense, while the pursuit of what is useful stems from the intellect. At first, the choosers are the elders and the sages, and they seek the absolute good. Thus the parable relates that they said to the olive, “Reign over us,” for the olive represents the good, since it produces oil for illumination — a metaphor for the light of wisdom and Torah — and light is called good. They agreed that such a godly person is worthy of kingship; therefore they did not say, “Come, reign,” for he need not go or move toward it, since kingship properly belongs to him by virtue of his own essence.
text.8_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: And the olive said to them. But such a fortunate and elevated man does not desire authority, for it would interrupt his spiritual perfection, making him a servant to the people, overseeing their affairs. As it is said, “Do I grant you authority?” Therefore he replied, “Shall I cease my richness?” — meaning the attainment of wisdom and the abundance of prophecy, through which God and men are honored, for the manifestation of the Divine spirit is called “honor” in Scripture — and go to sway over the trees, to occupy myself with their needs?!
text.8_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: And the trees said to the fig tree. After the group of sages and men of virtue did not find one who was good in their eyes, they ceased seeking; then another group arose — the wealthy — who seek what is pleasant for bodily life, and they wished to appoint someone useful according to the end they desired. This is symbolized by the fig, whose fruit is sweet and pleasing to the taste. They said, “Come, you,” meaning that although they knew kingship properly belongs to a man of spirit, nevertheless, “come” and exert yourself until you reign. This represents their seeking a wealthy and mighty man who could sustain them with luxuries and pleasant living.
text.8_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: And the fig tree said to them. But even such a person, who possesses some imagined personal enjoyment, would not wish to abandon it for the sake of the people, as it is said, “In that day he shall swear, saying, I will not be a healer; in my house there is neither bread nor clothing.” Thus it said, “Shall I cease my sweetness?” — and it did not say that it benefits God or man, for in truth the category of the pleasant has no real benefit at all.
text.8_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: And the trees said to the vine. Then a third group arose, intermediate between the two, seeking to choose a person who stands between the good and the pleasant — namely, the useful — symbolized by the vine, for wine gladdens the heart of man, and its rich fragrance brings alertness and vitality.
text.8_Chapter, 11_Verse, 1_Comment: And they said, “At the head of all remedies is wine,” meaning that they would choose a man wise in governance and of upright character, who would lead them in paths of justice and adjudicate their cases for the well-being of civic life.
text.8_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: And the vine said to them. But even the vine — representing the statesman endowed with civic wisdom — would not wish to abandon his perfection, for within him is something that gladdens both God and men: the goodness of character that yields righteousness, kindness, and compassion, in which God rejoices, and the excellence of governance in which people rejoice. How, then, could he go and sway over the trees?!
text.8_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: And all the trees said to the bramble. Then the leaders of the people — the sages, the wealthy, and the officials — ceased seeking a king; the fruit-bearing trees no longer sought one, for they had found none suitable. At that point all the trees arose — meaning the barren trees, which are the majority — and they sought a king. Since they themselves had no purpose or fruit, they chose the bramble, the worst of them all and devoid of any benefit. Its only advantage over the other barren trees was that none could approach it, for it was full of spears, arrows, and painful thorns, as it is said, “But the sons of Belial are all like thorns thrust away.” The parable teaches that after the distinguished members of the people ceased seeking a king, the entire multitude gathered to appoint over themselves a man lacking all perfection, the worst among them, whose only distinction was that he was filled with murder, spear, and lance.
text.8_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: And the bramble said. He accepts the kingship and seeks after it, for by means of it he loses no perfection; rather, his heart swells if their heart is sincere toward him. Therefore he conditions with them: “If in truth and sincerity you anoint me… come, take refuge in my shade.” Yet it is known that the bramble has no shade at all, and is the lowest of them all. That is to say: abandon your exalted stature — you lofty and elevated cedars of Lebanon — and humble yourselves to sit beneath me in a low and degraded place; my painful thorns will be your shade and refuge. And if not — if you rebel against me — then do not imagine that from my lowly station I cannot harm you. On the contrary: since the bramble is readily kindled by fire, that fire will consume the cedars of Lebanon.
text.8_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (16–19): Why does it repeat, “If you have acted well…” and “If you have acted according to the recompense of his hands,” and then repeat the matter again in verse 19?
text.8_Chapter, 15_Verse, 1_Comment: And now. He begins to explain the parable: when Gideon died, among his sons were those who were wise and sought the good, like shoots of olive trees; and there were the wealthy who sought what is pleasant, like the fig tree that ripens its early fruit; and those wise in governance who sought what is useful, like a desirable vineyard. These refused kingship and did not pursue it. But you, the lesser masses of the people, went to the bramble, in whom there is neither good, nor pleasantness, nor usefulness — only that he is like a thorn and thistle to destroy his brothers. He then makes a condition with them:
text.8_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: Who fought for you. Even if he had not succeeded in the war, you would still have owed him gratitude for having risked his life on your behalf. And regarding what was said, “If you have acted according to the recompense of his hands,” he explains: “and he delivered you from the hand of Midian” — and from this you were obligated to repay him, measure for measure, good in return for good. And where is that recompense? Behold…
text.8_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: But you rose up against my father’s house and killed his sons. This was neither goodness nor recompense. And you made the son of his maidservant king — not out of gratitude or repayment, but only because he is your brother.
text.8_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: And if. After explaining the opposite of “If you have acted well” and “If you have acted according to the recompense of his hands,” he now explains the opposite of “If you have acted in truth and integrity.” He adds that if this had truly been done in truth and integrity, then on this very day — after his sons have been killed — you would have no remaining claim or merit.
text.8_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: But if not. As is indeed the case — that it was not fitting for the murderer of his father’s house to inherit his honor — then your end will be like the end of the trees: from the bramble shall go forth fire, and so forth.
text.8_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: And he ruled. It does not say “and he judged,” for he did not judge but ruled by force. (The word vayasar is in the simple (qal) form of a weak verb, like vayasar eleha.)
text.8_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (25): Why did they set ambushers to rob travelers on the road?
text.8_Chapter, 24_Verse, 1_Comment: And they set. At first they placed ambushers to kill him on the road by which he would pass; but the ambushers did not focus on their objective — to lie in wait for Abimelech himself — and instead they robbed passersby. Through this the conspiracy became known and was reported to Abimelech, and he refrained from passing there and remained in Arumah. (And this was from Hashem, so that before the bramble would be burned, it would first consume the cedars of Lebanon.)
text.8_Chapter, 25_Verse, 0_Comment: And Gaal son of Ebed came. Hashem brought about a second turn of events, that Gaal came to Shechem, and the people of Shechem trusted in his strength, that he would fight against Abimelech. Because of this they went out to gather their vineyards, whereas previously they had feared to go out. It was their custom to hold celebrations and feasts at the time of the grape harvest, and there they openly cursed Abimelech.
text.8_Chapter, 27_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (28): The commentators were pressed regarding the intent of this verse:
text.8_Chapter, 27_Verse, 1_Comment: And Gaal son of Ebed said. He stood at the head of those speaking and said: “Who is Abimelech, and who is Shechem, that we should serve him?” That is to say, what connection does Abimelech have with Shechem that they should be obligated to serve him? Is he not the son of Jerubbaal on his father’s side — and primary lineage follows the father — and his father was not from Shechem? He added, “and Zebul his officer” — if you serve Abimelech, must you also serve his officer? The meaning is: “that we should serve him and Zebul his officer.” He continued: “Serve the men of Hamor, the father of Shechem.” He meant: you foolish ones, like donkeys, you should serve the men of Hamor, the father of Shechem. Thus he called Abimelech by the name Hamor, who was the ancient father of Shechem, and he is now the ruler in his place. It also contains a mockery, for the donkey is the most foolish of animals. That is to say: if you wish, serve the men of Hamor — namely Zebul and the men of Abimelech. But why should we serve him — I and my brothers? We were not born in Shechem, nor are we subject to Hamor, prince of Shechem.
text.8_Chapter, 27_Verse, 2_Comment: It may also be explained that he referred to Abimelech disparagingly as “Shechem,” meaning that he seeks authority on the grounds that he is the son of the ruler of the land — just as Shechem was the son of Hamor the Hivite, prince of the land in earlier times. Thus he said: “Who is Abimelech, and who is Shechem, the prince of the land, that we should serve him?”  “Is he not the son of Jerubbaal — and Zebul his officer?” That is, he is not certainly the son of Jerubbaal, since he is the son of his concubine, and it is the way of a concubine to be unfaithful; his mother also consorted with Zebul his officer, so that he may be the son of Jerubbaal or the son of Zebul — it is uncertain which of them is his true father, and he is attributed to both.  He further said: if you wish to serve him because his father was ruler of the land, then serve the men of Hamor, the father of Shechem, who preceded him in rulership — and why should we serve him? According to this reasoning, the descendants of Hamor have the prior claim to authority.
text.8_Chapter, 28_Verse, 0_Comment: Who would grant. If I were ruler here, I would remove him from kingship. And he said concerning Abimelech: command that whoever hears should inform Abimelech to increase his forces and come out to battle, for the people have conspired against him.
text.8_Chapter, 30_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (31): The commentators were strained in explaining the phrase “they are besieging the city against you”:
text.8_Chapter, 30_Verse, 1_Comment: In Tormah. That is, the city of Arumah, where Abimelech was.
text.8_Chapter, 30_Verse, 2_Comment: Behold, Gaal… and his brothers are coming to Shechem. That is to say, they intend to settle there.
text.8_Chapter, 30_Verse, 3_Comment: And behold, they are besieging the city against you. He informed him that they had agreed among themselves to go out the next morning to lay siege to the city of Arumah. This is what he meant by saying, “Increase your forces and come out” — that is, come out from the city where you are, for there they intend to place you under siege.
text.8_Chapter, 31_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (32–40): Zebul’s advice to lie in wait in the field at night seems to lack reason — why the ambush? By day he would come and they would go out to him. And regarding what it says, “and you shall spread out against the city,” Abimelech did not do so on this occasion. From where did he know that Gaal and the people would come out to him — perhaps they would remain shut inside the city?
text.8_Chapter, 31_Verse, 1_Comment: And now he counseled wisely. That he should arise at night and lie in ambush against them in the field.
text.8_Chapter, 32_Verse, 0_Comment: And in the morning. Rise early and spread out against the city of Shechem, for Gaal and the men of the force will go out to you at Arumah and will not be in the city, and you will easily capture it. Thus, “you shall do to him as your hand finds” — namely, that he divided the people into four companies, some to stand at the gate of the city so as not to allow them to return, and some to fight in the field. However, his plan was thwarted, as will be explained.
text.8_Chapter, 33_Verse, 0_Comment: And Abimelech arose. He followed his counsel, and they lay in ambush… in four companies, for he thought that two companies would stand at the entrance of the city gate, and two companies would strike all who were in the field.
text.8_Chapter, 34_Verse, 0_Comment: And Gaal went out. And so it was: Gaal went out with the men of Shechem at dawn to go toward Arumah, but he did not depart immediately; rather, he stood with his men at the entrance of the city gate to arrange his ranks. In the meantime, Abimelech rose from the ambush, thinking that Gaal had already set out on his way and was in the field.
text.8_Chapter, 35_Verse, 0_Comment: And Gaal saw and said, “Behold, people are coming down.” Because of this he did not move far from the gate, and Zebul sought to mislead him by saying that it was merely the shadow of the mountains.
text.8_Chapter, 36_Verse, 0_Comment: But Gaal insisted that he saw it was indeed a people, and that they were divided into companies, and he pointed out their location; and his intention was to return to the city.
text.8_Chapter, 40_Verse, 0_Comment: And he drove out. In the meantime the authority of the governor of the city prevailed, for he too had supporters; and moreover, after the men of Shechem had fallen slain, they agreed to drive Gaal out of the city.
text.8_Chapter, 41_Verse, 0_Comment: And the people went out into the field. For their work, since it was then the time of the grape harvest, and they had already despaired of the war.
text.8_Chapter, 42_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (43–44): Why does it repeat “and he struck them… and he struck them”?
text.8_Chapter, 42_Verse, 1_Comment: And he divided them. Now he succeeded according to Zebul’s counsel in the first stage, for he divided his people into three companies; and when he saw that the people were going out from the city and had separated themselves from it, he began to strike them, and while he was striking them—
text.8_Chapter, 45_Verse, 0_Comment: And they heard. After the counsel of Hashem was fulfilled in Shechem, He brought it about that the fire of the bramble would also consume Beth-millo, the inhabitants of Shechem. For near Shechem there was a strong tower that could not have been captured; yet Hashem caused that they did not go there to seek refuge. Instead, they gathered in the chamber of the house of El-berith, which was made of wood, to take counsel there and to make a covenant concerning their rebellion.
text.8_Chapter, 46_Verse, 0_Comment: And God sent an evil spirit. This was a providential punishment, so that the violence done to the seventy…
text.8_Chapter, 46_Verse, 1_Comment: And it was told to Abimelech. That they had come out from the tower; and then he cut down trees and set fire to the stronghold, which was made of wood. It was from Hashem that they left the stone tower to take refuge beneath wooden beams, and thus was fulfilled what was said: “Fire shall go forth from Abimelech and consume the leaders of Shechem and Beth-millo.”
text.8_Chapter, 52_Verse, 0_Comment: Now it relates how there was likewise fulfilled what was said, “and fire shall go forth from the leaders of Shechem and consume Abimelech,” in that a woman killed him. A piece of a millstone is a fragment of stone from the upper millstone, and it was measure for measure — just as he had killed his brothers upon one stone.
text.8_Chapter, 55_Verse, 0_Comment: And he returned. This concludes the account of how Jotham’s curse was fulfilled in all its details.
text.8_Chapter, 77_Verse, 0_Comment: And Zebul said to him. Then Zebul sought to draw him out of the city by stirring within him the desire for battle; he said to him:
text.8_Chapter, 88_Verse, 0_Comment: They spread out. Abimelech and the people who were with him — some of them stood at the entrance of the city gate to prevent the stricken from returning to the city, and the two companies struck all who were in the field, who were scattered throughout many fields; afterward Abimelech destroyed the city.
text.9_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: To save Israel. For Abimelech did not save them, but merely ruled over them by force.
text.9_Chapter, 0_Verse, 1_Comment: Ben Dodo. That was his name. Radak writes that some explain it to mean “the son of his uncle,” that is, Abimelech’s cousin, the son of his father’s brother — see there. And how, then, was he a man of Issachar?!
text.9_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: They would be called Havvoth-Jair. That is, Jair son of Manasseh went and captured their settlements [the villages of Gilead] and called them Havvoth-Jair. Following the model of that earlier Jair’s valor, this later Jair likewise gave his cities—collectively—the appellation “Havvoth-Jair.” There is a distinction between the verb “to call” when it is followed by the word “et” and when it is followed by a lamed: when “call” is followed by “et,” it denotes the assigning of an intrinsic, proper name; when it is followed by a lamed, it denotes an additional designation attached to an already existing name. In the case of the first Jair, their essential name was “Havvoth-Jair,” and therefore it says, “and he called them (et).” But in the case of this Jair, it was only a secondary designation, and therefore it says, “they were called for them,” for this was not their essential name.
text.9_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: And they again did evil. For until now, during the lifetime of the judges, they served Hashem; as it says, “And it came to pass, when the judge died…” (above, chapter 2).
text.9_Chapter, 5_Verse, 1_Comment: And they did not serve Him. Not even in partnership.
text.9_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (8): The phrase “in that year” is difficult to understand:
text.9_Chapter, 7_Verse, 1_Comment: And they oppressed and crushed… in that year. That is to say: (a) they were punished immediately; (b) already in the very first year the hardship of the oppression began, and it continued for eighteen years.
text.9_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (10): The vav of “and we have forsaken” appears superfluous:
text.9_Chapter, 9_Verse, 1_Comment: And have we forsaken. That is to say, they thought that although they had served the Baalim, they had not abandoned Hashem, for they regarded Baal as an intermediary between themselves and Hashem. Thus they said: Even if we have sinned, have we truly forsaken our God and served the Baalim?! — in astonishment. Did we not consider Baal merely as a mediator between us and Hashem?
text.9_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (11): Had He not yet delivered them from the children of Ammon and the Philistines?
text.9_Chapter, 10_Verse, 1_Comment: And Hashem said. He made this known to them through a prophet, so that they would not say that they had not sinned. He said to them: “Was it not from Egypt and from the Amorite”—that is, just as I delivered you in earlier times from Egypt and from the Amorite—so too from the children of Ammon and from the Philistines who are now oppressing you, I am able to deliver you. (And therefore it says “from the children of Ammon” without a connecting vav, for it means: just as from Egypt, so from the children of Ammon.)
text.9_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: And the Sidonians. That is to say, lest you claim that you thought I performed wonders only in ancient times and not in later generations — behold, the Sidonians, Amalek, and Maon oppressed you in more recent generations; and you cried out to Me, and I delivered you from their hand.
text.9_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: And as for what you said, “Have we truly forsaken Hashem?” — the answer is that you have indeed forsaken Me and have served other gods, not as you claim. Therefore I will no longer continue to save you.
text.9_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: Go and cry out to the gods. Since you have chosen them, it is fitting that they should save you in your time of distress — not I.
text.9_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (15–17): What is meant by “Do to us whatever is good in Your eyes,” since He did not wish to save them? The phrase “and His soul grew short” has troubled the commentators. It is also difficult that it says the children of Ammon encamped in Gilead, which seems to contradict what was stated earlier that they crossed the Jordan. Furthermore, in chapter 11, verse 29, it says that Jephthah crossed the Jordan, implying that the children of Ammon had returned to their land and he fought them in their own cities.
text.9_Chapter, 14_Verse, 1_Comment: And they said, “We have sinned.” They confessed their sin, yet they said: Why should You punish us through the hand of man? Do to us Yourself whatever is good in Your eyes — as it says, “Let us fall now into the hand of Hashem, but let me not fall into the hand of man.” Therefore they said, “Only deliver us from the hand of man.”
text.9_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: And His soul grew short over the suffering of Israel. Through their repentance, His spirit and will could no longer endure the suffering of Israel — that it should continue or be prolonged — and that the enemy should again cross the Jordan to extend and increase their affliction.
text.9_Chapter, 15_Verse, 1_Comment: And in the Guide of the Perplexed (Part I, chapter 48) it is explained: “That is to say, the will of God could no longer endure or behold the suffering and distress of Israel.”
text.9_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: And they cried out. This too was from Hashem: that the children of Ammon, who had already crossed the Jordan to fight against Judah and Benjamin (as stated above, verse 9), turned back and encamped in Gilead, where they had oppressed them for eighteen years. In this way their suffering was shortened, so that it would not spread to all the tribes.
text.9_Chapter, 16_Verse, 1_Comment: And the children of Israel assembled. But the children of Israel had already assembled when he crossed the Jordan; and Gilead, which had been under subjugation, also sought a leader for itself.
text.10_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: And Gilead begot Jephthah. That is to say, nevertheless everyone knew that Gilead had fathered him, for she was designated to him as a concubine.
text.10_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: And the wife of Gilead bore. That is to say, she was his wife through marriage canopy and betrothal.
text.10_Chapter, 1_Verse, 1_Comment: And they said to him, “You shall not inherit.” This was not in accordance with the law: (a) for the son of a concubine inherits a portion along with the other sons; (b) and their driving Jephthah out of the city was clear injustice.
text.10_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: And he fled. This indicates that they sought to kill him, so that he was compelled to flee, and that the elders of the city did not administer justice.
text.10_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: And it came to pass after days. This injustice continued for many days, until the children of Ammon went to war.
text.10_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: And it came to pass when they fought. That is to say, they did not restore Jephthah out of justice, but only because they needed him.
text.10_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (6–11): In verse 6 they said “commander,” but in verse 8 they said “head”? At first they said “and we will fight,” and afterward “and I will fight”? What is the force of the argument, “Did you not hate me?” — for even so, would they not seek his help if they expected benefit from him? And what did they mean by “Therefore now…” — how does this follow from what preceded? What is new in “I will be your head” — had they not already agreed to this? And what did they mean by replying, “According to your words, so shall we do,” since they had already said the same to him? Until now they conditioned that if he fought and was victorious, then he would be head; how, then, did they appoint him head immediately, before he had won and before he had fought?
text.10_Chapter, 5_Verse, 1_Comment: Come and be our commander. There is a distinction between “head” and “commander.” A commander is one who stands at the edge of the camp because of his importance and superiority — whether in valor, wealth, or wisdom — even though he is not the head or ruler over them, as in “Come, be our commander.” They did not initially speak with him about his reward after the war, but only about the present. They asked that he stand at their edge on account of his prominence, since he was mightier than all of them; therefore they said, “and we will fight against the children of Ammon,” in the plural. For the commander is not the head to whom the action is attributed alone, since in war all are equal with him — he merely stands at their forefront.
text.10_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: And Jephthah said. He replied to them: How can you say that I should be your commander on account of my distinction, as though you had not summoned me out of need but out of esteem and affection? Did you not hate me, and drive me from my father’s house, for I was lowly and despised in your eyes? Moreover, had you come to me in a time of peace, I might have forgiven the past; but you have come to me now only when you are in distress. Thus it was not remorse for what you did, nor love and respect, that moved you — but necessity alone. Why, then, should I go to help you for nothing, without gain—as though there were a covenant of friendship between us, when in truth there is none?
text.10_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: And they said… therefore now we have returned to you. That is to say, it is true, as you have spoken, that formerly we hated you and wronged you; but for that very reason we have now come back to you, so that you will not go on our account out of love or affection, but will receive your compensation — for you shall go with us and fight, and you will be the one who wages the battle, and the victory will be attributed to your name. From this it follows that after you prevail, you shall be our head, in accordance with the law that the victor in war and the deliverer of the people — even if he be among the lowly of the nation — is appointed head and ruler.
text.10_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: And Jephthah said. He replied to them: Even now you have shown me no sign of affection or indication of remorse for the past; it appears as though I am going with my enemies to help them merely for payment. For what you have promised — that after the war and victory you will appoint me as head — is not something that depends upon your agreement, since it would follow of itself. If you bring me back… and Hashem delivers them before me, I shall become your head on my own, even against your will, according to the law of the victor. What, then, are you promising me?
text.10_Chapter, 8_Verse, 1_Comment: His intention is clear: he desired that they appoint him head immediately, so that from the outset he would not go merely as a commander but as head — as he later said to the king of the children of Ammon, “What is there between me and you, that you have come to fight against my land?” — which he spoke from the position of one who was already ruler and lord of the land.
text.10_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: And they said… according to your word, so shall we do. That is to say, they would appoint him head immediately upon his arrival in Gilead.
text.10_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: As it says, “And he went… and they appointed him over them as head and commander.” They chose him immediately as head, and also as commander on account of his distinction. “And Jephthah spoke all his words before Hashem” — he stipulated with them the laws of authority, defining the extent of his rule, just as Samuel spoke to them of the ordinances of kingship when he anointed Saul.
text.10_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: What is there between me and you? For a war that arises between two kings — if conducted according to the norms of kingship and not by way of oppression — must necessarily have some cause, such as a dispute, a claim, or the like; and often they can reach an understanding between them peacefully before war breaks out. He therefore asked that he inform him of the reason for the war, and what he sought from him.
text.10_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: And the king of the children of Ammon said… because Israel took my land… He informed him that he had a claim to the land, which had belonged to Moab in earlier times before Sihon conquered it, and he demanded that the cities be returned to their original owners. (Apparently, the king of the children of Ammon then ruled also over the land of Moab.) He argued on behalf of Moab that Israel had taken its land, and also that what they had taken from Sihon had included territory that had belonged to his own people — as it is said (Joshua 12), “Sihon… from Aroer… to the border of the children of Ammon,” and there (Joshua 13:25), “And their border was Jazer… and half the land of the children of Ammon.”
text.10_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: Thus said Jephthah. He advanced four arguments: (a) that Israel did not take anything from the land of Moab or from the children of Ammon — for he would have a claim only if Israel had taken it directly from him without intermediary. On the contrary, when they sent messengers to the king of Moab and to the king of Edom and they did not consent to let them pass through their territory (even though this could have been grounds for war), Israel turned away from their land and did not enter the border of Moab, for the Arnon was the boundary of Moab in those days.
text.10_Chapter, 14_Verse, 1_Comment: (Second argument:) The lands he mentioned were conquered from Sihon, who at that time ruled over them; and even this was not done unlawfully so that he could claim against them. For when they sent messengers also to Sihon, Sihon himself initiated war against them. It was not enough for him that he did not allow them to pass through his land, but “Sihon did not trust Israel to pass through his border” — that is, he would not even permit them to go along the edge of his territory and circumvent it, as they had done around the land of Edom and Moab, for he did not trust them. Therefore he gathered his people and fought against them, so that he was the one who began the war; and Hashem delivered him into the hand of Israel, and they took his land, which was the land of the Amorites — not the land of Moab, for those territories were at that time under Amorite rule.
text.10_Chapter, 14_Verse, 2_Comment: (Third argument:) “And now Hashem, the God of Israel, has dispossessed…” That is to say, the war of Israel at that time was a Divine matter, and all the nations knew this — that Hashem had driven them out. If Hashem, to whom the whole earth belongs, dispossessed the Amorite, how can you dispossess him? “Is it not that which Chemosh your god gives you to possess?” What right have you to speak against that which is the wonder of God and His Providence?
text.10_Chapter, 14_Verse, 3_Comment: (Fourth argument:) And now, are you any better…? Balak was king at that time and remained silent; and after him many kings arose, and three hundred years have already passed during which Israel has dwelt in and possessed the land — and you were silent. This constitutes a strong presumption of ownership and carries a legal claim. So too Abarbanel explains these verses along these lines.
text.10_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: Is it not that which Chemosh your god gives you to possess? What right have you to speak against that which is among the wonders of God and His Providence?
text.10_Chapter, 26_Verse, 0_Comment: And I have not sinned against you. That is to say, since you have no claim to the land, no cause for war can be imagined except if one had wronged the other in honor or the like — and this has not occurred, for I have not sinned against you. Therefore, you are doing me wrong by waging war against me, which is evil against the laws of kings and the customs of nations. And if there is no arbiter between us, let Hashem the Judge decide…
text.10_Chapter, 28_Verse, 0_Comment: And he passed through Gilead. It was already stated that the king of the children of Ammon had encamped in Gilead; accordingly, it was Jephthah’s strategy to pass through Gilead by way of Mizpeh of Gilead toward the land of the children of Ammon. While the king of the children of Ammon and his camp were stationed in Gilead, it was easy to strike their territory and inflict a heavy blow upon the cities of Ammon, and through this they were subdued, for they were compelled to return to defend their cities.
text.10_Chapter, 30_Verse, 0_Comment: And it shall be Hashem’s. That is to say: either it shall be for Hashem, if it is not fit for a sacrifice; or, if it is fit for sacrifice, then I will offer it up as a burnt offering — as explained by Radak.
text.10_Chapter, 32_Verse, 0_Comment: Thus said Jephthah. He advanced four arguments:
text.10_Chapter, 33_Verse, 0_Comment: And she was his only one. Since the term “only” can be used even when there are other children who are not regarded as significant, such as the sons of concubines — as in the case of Isaac, “your son, your only one,” although he had Ishmael — therefore it says “she alone was his only one,” and explains: “he had none besides her,” meaning that no son or daughter had been born to Jephthah.
