text.10_Chapter, 34_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (35–40): Why did he not go to have his vow annulled, for one may find grounds and express regret? Had the law of annulment of vows been forgotten by them? Moreover, according to the law it was not a valid vow at all, since a human being is not fit to be offered as a burnt offering:
text.10_Chapter, 34_Verse, 1_Comment: Alas, my daughter. It appears that he wished to reconsider and seek release from his vow, since he had grounds for regret. Thus he said: “Alas, my daughter! Have you indeed brought me low? Are you the cause of my trouble? How can I do this thing to you, when I have opened my mouth to Hashem and cannot turn back?” — in astonishment. Are not vows made to Hashem subject to annulment through grounds and regret? They are not like promises made to human beings, which one is obligated to fulfill; for one who vows to Hashem has the possibility of release.
text.10_Chapter, 35_Verse, 0_Comment: And she said to him. She replied that this matter is not like other vows, which through prior regret a sage uproots from the outset; but in your case there is no regret from the beginning, only regret now — after Hashem has taken vengeance for you upon your enemies, since through the vow you were victorious over them, and it is impossible for you to have regret over the essence of the vow from the beginning. This caused Jephthah’s error, for he did not go to the sages to seek release from his vow; yet in truth this is a mistaken argument, for even regret arising now can at least uproot the vow from that point onward.
text.10_Chapter, 36_Verse, 0_Comment: And I will weep for my virginity. That she would set herself apart and withdraw, not marrying a man but devoting herself to the service of Hashem — and this is what she meant when she said…
text.10_Chapter, 38_Verse, 0_Comment: And he fulfilled his vow to her… and she had not known a man. In this way he carried out his vow — in that she did not know a man, but remained secluded and unmarried until her death; and according to his understanding, this was a mitzvah. But the view of the Sages is that he actually offered her up as a burnt offering.
text.10_Chapter, 39_Verse, 0_Comment: To recount for four days. They would go to speak with her and relate her story, and afterward she would return to her seclusion; but according to the Sages, “to recount” means to lament and chant dirges over her death.
text.11_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (1–3): Why did the children of Ephraim gather together, and what wrong had he done to them? And Jephthah’s reply contains obscurity and repetition:
text.11_Chapter, 0_Verse, 1_Comment: And the men of Ephraim cried out. Ephraim was angered that Gilead had chosen a head and commander as leader over the house of Joseph because they had won the war. They argued: Why did you not call us to fight? They even sought to burn his house, for they did not consent to his leadership, as will be explained in verse 4. They claimed precedence over Manasseh within the house of Joseph, as it says, “And he set Ephraim before Manasseh,” and on this basis they brought charges against him.
text.11_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: And Jephthah said. He advanced three arguments:
text.11_Chapter, 1_Verse, 1_Comment: (a) I and my people had a dispute with the children of Ammon. It was I who was the party to the dispute, for the children of Ammon had oppressed the people of Gilead for eighteen years, and the obligation of the war rested upon us alone.
text.11_Chapter, 1_Verse, 2_Comment: (b) And I cried out to you — all those days we cried out, and you did not come to save us.
text.11_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: (c) And I saw that you were not delivering us, for had you intended to help, the time for that had long since passed; therefore I put my life in my hand, placing myself in great danger, and Hashem delivered them into my hand by Providence. Why then have you come up against me this day to fight against me? That is to say, to help you did not come all that time — only now you have come up to fight against me?!
text.11_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: And Jephthah gathered. When he saw that their spirit was not softened by his gentle words — for they said — it explains the cause of the war: the children of Ephraim claimed that the men of Gilead had presumptuously chosen a judge as though they were the principal part of the house of Joseph. They argued against them, saying, “You are fugitives of Ephraim,” meaning that Ephraim is the primary tribe, together with half of Manasseh, who received their inheritance alongside it as one portion and lot, as stated in the book of Joshua. But you, Gilead, who took your possession beyond the Jordan, are fugitives from the tribe, for your proper place was within Ephraim, within Manasseh; instead, you went off in flight to the other side of the Jordan. How then do you dare to choose a commander, ruler, and governor?
text.12_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: Barren and had not borne. For it is possible to speak of a barren woman who had previously borne before becoming barren, and it is also possible that one has not borne for some other reason; therefore it repeats the expression.
text.12_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: And now, please beware, of things that naturally cause harm to a pregnant woman; and beyond that, do not drink, etc. And what it says, “anything unclean,” refers to matters forbidden to a Nazirite.
text.12_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: For behold, you are pregnant. It is as though you are already pregnant now, such that you must take care immediately.
text.12_Chapter, 4_Verse, 1_Comment: And the Sages (Midrash Rabbah, Naso 10:16) said that there was already seminal seed within her, and at the very moment the angel spoke with her she conceived. Thus he first said “and you shall conceive” in the future tense, and afterward “for behold, you are pregnant” — at that very moment. Therefore it says “and you are bearing” (with a ḥolam), a form combining the present with the past reversed, indicating that she was already prepared to give birth.
text.12_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: A man of God came to me, for she was uncertain whether he was a man or an angel; that is to say, insofar as he was clothed in physical form he was a man of God, but in terms of his awe-inspiring presence he was like an angel — and this is what she meant by “like the appearance of an angel”, because he was very awesome.
text.12_Chapter, 5_Verse, 1_Comment: And I did not ask him from where he was. For it was customary to ask a person about his place of origin, and in response he would state his name, as it says, “And Micah said to him, ‘From where do you come?’ and he said, ‘I am a Levite.’”
text.12_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (7–13): Why did she not relate that he said to her, “Behold, you are barren”? Likewise, why did she not mention “a razor shall not come upon his head,” nor “and he shall begin to save Israel”? Why did the angel come to the woman and not to Manoah himself? And why did Manoah request that he return again to instruct them regarding the conduct of the child, when he had already instructed them, and the angel added nothing in the second appearance beyond what he had said the first time?
text.12_Chapter, 6_Verse, 1_Comment: And he said to me, “Behold, you are pregnant.” As for his statement to her, “You are barren,” she did not relate it for the sake of peace (Vayikra Rabbah, Tzav 9). Likewise, she did not mention, “a razor shall not come upon his head,” because this is included in what she said, “for the child shall be a Nazirite to God.” Nor did she repeat, “and he shall begin to save Israel,” since at that time the Philistines ruled, and she feared lest the matter become known and they kill the child who would be born. She added, “until the day of his death,” though the angel did not state this explicitly, for he knew that before his death he would profane his Nazirite status.
text.12_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: And instruct us what we shall do for the child who will be born. That is to say, the angel explained only the conduct required of the woman, but did not teach them the conduct required of the child (especially since she had not told him that a razor should not come upon his head). Therefore he requested that the angel come again to instruct them regarding the child’s conduct — particularly since this was a new form of Nazirite status (for Samson’s Nazirite vow differed in its laws, in that he became impure through contact with the dead, yet did not lighten his hair with a razor).
text.12_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: Now let your words come to pass — what shall be the rule for the child? That is to say, in the first instance you declared the rule concerning the woman and her conduct; now instruct us: (a) the rule of the child — how he is to conduct himself; and (b) his deeds — since you designated him even before birth, he will surely perform great things; therefore inform us of his actions and mighty deeds.
text.12_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: Of all that I said to the woman, she shall observe. That is to say, there is no need for me to inform you of the rule for the child, for you may ask those who know the law and they will teach you the laws of his Nazirite status (and therefore they said that Manoah was an ignoramus); I came only to warn the woman, for that was something new.
text.12_Chapter, 12_Verse, 1_Comment: As for the reason the angel did not come to Manoah: Abarbanel explains that she was more prepared than he to behold the angel. It may also be said that Samson’s Nazirite status was not a vow subject to annulment, for it was established by the angel; had it been instituted by the father, it would have been a regular vow — since a father may place his son under a Nazirite vow — and its law would have been different.
text.12_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: Please let us detain you. Since he did not know whether he was a prophet or an angel, he said: if you are a prophet, let us detain you and you may dine with us; and if you are an angel, we shall prepare before you a kid of the goats as an offering.
text.12_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: And he answered, “If you detain me” for a meal, I will not eat; but if you prepare a burnt offering, offer it to Hashem, for one who sacrifices to any god other than Hashem alone shall be devoted to destruction. It explains that Manoah was uncertain and did not clearly know that he was an angel of Hashem; therefore he hesitated in his words, whether to detain him for a meal or to bring an offering.
text.12_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: And Manoah said… What is your name? That is to say, Manoah, who thought he was a prophet of God, assumed that a prophet would not trouble himself to go and prophesy unless he expected some reward — money or food — or sought honor, so that when his words came to pass he would be regarded as a prophet. Since Manoah had wished to invite him to a meal and he refused to eat, he still supposed that perhaps he acted for the sake of honor; but this would not be possible unless he disclosed his name, so that when his prophecy would be fulfilled they could publicize that he was the seer and prophet. Therefore he said, “What is your name?” so that when your word comes to pass and your prophecy is fulfilled, we will honor you.
text.12_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: And he said… Why do you ask my name? I do not seek honor or glory from man, for I am an angel. Moreover, my name is wondrous — unknown to those who dwell in flesh. And since an angel’s name corresponds to his mission, and he was sent at this moment to perform wonders, as it says, “and he does wondrously,” therefore at this time his name was Wondrous.
text.12_Chapter, 17_Verse, 1_Comment: And the Sages, in Bamidbar Rabbah (Naso 10:19), explained that his name was “Wondrous” in connection with the Nazirite vow, as it is written, “When a man shall clearly utter a vow of a Nazirite” (ki yafli lindor neder).
text.12_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: And he took. Then he offered it to Hashem, as it had been said, “offer it to Hashem.” Thus it says, “and he offered it upon the rock to Hashem, and he did wondrously.” The angel performed wonders, bringing down fire upon the altar, and they saw this with their own eyes.
text.12_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: And he ascended… in the flame of the altar. This too they saw with their own eyes. It is clear that seeing the angel at the moment of his departure was a far greater matter than seeing him while he was clothed in physical form; for when he casts off the garment in which he had materialized and returns to his spiritual state, the eye of flesh cannot behold him. As it is said (II Kings 2:10), “If you see me taken from you, it shall be so for you,” for at the moment of his being taken from the physical, Elisha could not see him unless he possessed a double portion of his spirit. Therefore he said, “We shall surely die, for we have seen God.”
text.12_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: And the angel of Hashem did not appear again… then Manoah knew that he was the angel of Hashem. For until that point there still remained some doubt in his mind — perhaps he was a wonder-working man performing extraordinary acts, and he hoped that he would descend from the altar and return to them. But once he vanished from their sight, they knew that he was an angel and had returned to his place.
text.12_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: And he said… “We shall surely die.” I have already explained the reason for this fear above (6:22), in connection with Gideon.
text.12_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: And his wife said to him. She gave him three reasons: (a) If Hashem had desired to kill us, He would not have accepted from our hand a burnt offering and a meal offering, for that is a sign of favor and love, not of anger and punishment. (b) Nor would He have shown us all these wonders; does one perform miracles for those who are to be slain? (c) And at this time He would not have announced to us such a message — one that necessarily implies that I shall live and bear a son.
text.12_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: To stir him. That the spirit of might would begin to move him from time to time, in the camp of Dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol; for we find Zorah and Eshtaol listed in the territory of Judah (Joshua 15:33) and also in the territory of Dan (Joshua 19:42). Thus it clarifies that this was in the portion of Dan.
text.13_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (1–4): Why did Hashem bring it about that Samson, a Nazirite of God, should take a wife from the daughters of the Philistines? Was it not possible to provide another cause for Samson to provoke the Philistines without compromising his sanctity?
text.13_Chapter, 0_Verse, 1_Comment: And he saw a woman in Timnah. The narrative introduces this to show that it was arranged by Hashem, for he merely saw her with his eyes and did not speak with her; he might have thought that perhaps she would not please him once he spoke with her, or perhaps she or her father would not consent, or perhaps she would not agree to convert. Yet despite all this…
text.13_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: And he went up and told his father and his mother and said, “I have seen a woman.” That is to say, I have not spoken with her — I have only seen her; and now, take her for me — meaning, make efforts that she consent to this.
text.13_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: And his father and his mother said to him. They replied to him: (a) Is there not a woman among the daughters of your brothers, or at least among your own people? (b) Why do you go to take a wife from the Philistines, who are our enemies? (c) from the uncircumcised? And he said, “Take her for me” — her and no other; and certainly he intended that she convert, since he asked that they take her for him as a wife, which implies marriage in the proper manner.
text.13_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: And his father and his mother. They sought to restrain him from this, not knowing that it was from Hashem, for He was seeking an occasion to take vengeance upon the Philistines. And as to why Hashem did not arrange another cause for this, it answers that the Philistines ruled over Israel; had he openly provoked them, they would have poured out their wrath upon Israel. Therefore it was arranged that they would think Samson’s hostility arose because of his wife, not because he was angered by their dominion over his Israelite brothers.
text.13_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (5–6): Did he not go together with his father and mother? How then did the young lion encounter him while he was alone, such that his father and mother were unaware of it?
text.13_Chapter, 4_Verse, 1_Comment: And they came to the vineyards of Timnah. Apparently it was the season of the first grapes, and as they were walking along the path of the vineyards, Samson turned aside from the road — as it is said, “Go around, go around, we say to the Nazirite: do not approach the vineyard.” Being alone, a young lion came roaring toward him. As the Sages said: it is a tradition that a lion does not attack two people — it was only because he was by himself.
text.13_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: And the spirit of Hashem rushed upon him. In this there was a twofold display of might:
text.13_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: And he went down and spoke to the woman. Now he spoke with her to see whether she would please him also in terms of her intellect and character, and to learn of her affection for him — and she was pleasing in his eyes in this respect as well.
text.13_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: And he turned aside to see the carcass of the lion. On this occasion there were no grapes in the vineyard, and he had no need to deviate from the path; rather, he turned aside from the road to see the carcass of the lion. For one who sees the place where a miracle was performed for him is required to bless, and he turned there to give thanks to Hashem for His kindness.
text.13_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: And he took it down into his hands. Because he went to take a wife from the Philistines, he stumbled and ate impure honey — as the Sages said: he desired something impure…
text.13_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: And his father went down to the woman. Such was the custom there: the father of the groom would inform her so that she might prepare herself, and the groom would make a seven-day feast in his own house while he was still a young man, at his own expense. Thus it says, “And Samson made a feast there, for so the young men used to do” — that is, this was the custom there for young men — apart from the seven days of celebration that the bride would hold after the marriage.
text.13_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (12): Since on the seventh day they said to Samson’s wife, “Entice your husband,” had not the seven days of the feast already ended? How then does it say that she wept throughout the seven days? The riddle itself could not possibly be told by anyone, for who could foresee that bees had made honey in the carcass of a dead lion? This is not something they could discover. And why does it repeat, “If you tell it and find it”? ``
text.13_Chapter, 11_Verse, 1_Comment: And Samson said to them, “Let me now put forth a riddle to you; if you can indeed declare it to me within the seven days of the feast.” The primary explanation follows that of the Efodi: they were given time until the end of the seven days of the wedding feast that followed the marriage, such that during the first seven days they investigated and inquired, and during the latter seven — which are called simply “the days of the feast” — that was the time to declare it.
text.13_Chapter, 11_Verse, 2_Comment: This riddle was something entirely impossible for a person to solve, for were they prophets to know that he had slain a young lion, and that there a swarm of bees had nested and produced honey? Rather, he hinted to them the means of discovering the riddle by saying, “and find it” — meaning, search in the city and its surroundings; there you will find something strong from which sweetness came forth, for after searching you will find the carcass of the lion and the honey. Even so, in comparison to this, the pledge was of unequal value.
text.13_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: And they could not declare the riddle for three days. That is to say, during the first three days of the initial seven days of the celebration, they examined it, inquired, and investigated; and when they did not find its solution, they concluded that it was something hidden and despaired of further searching. Yet they had not yet gone to Samson’s wife to persuade her to entice him to reveal it, for she was not yet his wife until the seventh day, and she could not ask him to disclose his secrets.
text.13_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: And it came to pass on the seventh day. That is to say, from the day he presented them with the riddle — this was the end of the days of the young men’s feast and the day of the marriage, and the beginning of the final seven days of celebration — at which time she was Samson’s wife and could inquire into his secrets. Thus it says, “And they said to Samson’s wife.” They did not ask her to reveal the riddle herself, for she would have replied, “Shall I cause my husband to give you thirty changes of garments?” Rather, they asked that she entice him so that he would reveal the riddle to them — as it says, “and he will tell us the riddle.” In this way the pledge they had made would be nullified, since he would have disclosed the solution to them before the appointed time.
text.13_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: And she wept. Yet since it was brought about by Hashem to create enmity between Samson and the Philistines, she did not do as they requested but merely wept before him that he should tell her the riddle. She said, “You only hate me and do not love me,” for it can happen that after love one turns to hatred, as with Amnon toward Tamar; but you have not loved me at all, for you posed the riddle before the marriage and did not tell it to me. He replied that this was not out of hatred, for he had not told even his father and mother.
text.13_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: And it came to pass on the seventh day. Since it was the final day, he thought that for at least one day the matter would remain a secret with her, and he had already satisfied her by letting her know while it was still hidden from all others. But she told them, because they were her own people, and her loyalty inclined more toward them than toward her husband, who was not of her people.
text.13_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: What is sweeter than honey? This riddle contained two parts: (a) “From the eater came forth food.” This could easily be interpreted as referring to bees and honey, for in all living creatures the food they consume is transformed into their own substance and the waste is expelled; only the bee and its kind draw out the nectar of flowers and produce food from their own bodies, such that this food yields no waste but is entirely edible.
text.13_Chapter, 17_Verse, 1_Comment: The second part of the riddle — “from the strong came forth sweetness” — could not possibly have been known unless they had found the lion, and that was impossible; for had they found a lion with honey in it, such a marvel would have been reported and widely spoken of, and he would have heard of it. From this he knew that his wife had revealed it to them. Thus he said, “You have not found my riddle” — meaning, although you have declared my riddle, you have not truly found it; that is, you did not discover the lion, but rather “with my heifer you have plowed.” She was like an untrained heifer unfit for plowing, yet with her you plowed — and she did not merely plow, but revealed it.
text.13_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: And he gave the changes of garments… and his anger burned. At first he thought that when she saw them demanding the garments from him, she would defend him and reveal that she had disclosed the solution to them; but when he saw that she remained silent, he suspected that she had been unfaithful with them — as indeed was the case.
text.13_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: That she was given to his companion, for she had a bond with him — as it says, “who had been his companion,” for she had loved him previously. And although he had promised also linen garments, he gave only the changes of clothing, for he had a claim and therefore gave only half, in accordance with the rule concerning property in dispute (Abarbanel).
text.14_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: In the days of the wheat harvest. Hashem arranged it to occur at a time when the grain was still standing in the fields, so that everything would be burned.
text.14_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: Better than she. He hinted that his wife had set her eyes on others, whereas the younger one would be yours alone.
text.14_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: This time I am blameless. For surely the marriage had been conducted publicly — why, then, did they not protest when they gave a married woman to another?
text.14_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: Between the two tails in the midst. He hinted to them that just as he placed a torch between two tails, so one places fire between two companions — as it says, “Can a man take fire in his bosom…? So is he who goes in to his neighbor’s wife.”
text.14_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: If you do such a thing. That is to say, their burning of her was not truly because of her immorality, but to appease Samson’s anger. He said: I thought that a monetary penalty would suffice; but since you act in this way, imposing a punishment of death, then I too will demand lives from you according to your own custom — and this is what he meant by, “for I will surely take vengeance upon you.”
text.14_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: Do you not know that the Philistines rule over us? For the law is (according to Rambam) that if idolaters say, “Give us one of you and we will kill him,” he is not to be handed over unless he is liable to death, like Sheba son of Bichri — meaning, even if he is not liable according to Torah law but under the law of the kingdom. Likewise, if he is a pursuer whose actions endanger the many, so that through him danger comes upon all Israel, he may be handed over even if they did not single him out (as stated by the Taz in Yoreh De‘ah, siman 157).
text.14_Chapter, 10_Verse, 1_Comment: At first they said, “Do you not know that the Philistines rule over us? What is this that you have done?” — meaning, you are endangering the entire community and acting as one who pursues the many. He replied: I did not think any harm would come to you, for as they did to me, so I did to them — these were matters between me and them, not affecting the public at large.
text.14_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: And they said to him, “We have come down to bind you.” For they have singled you out, and you are liable to death under their royal law.
text.14_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: With the jawbone of a donkey, heaps upon heaps. Donkeys have fallen — a people likened to a donkey; that is, with it I struck down a thousand men.
text.14_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: You have given… and now shall I die of thirst? And it is a general principle that Hashem does not perform a miracle in vain or without purpose — since, if so, I would now fall into their hands anyway.
text.14_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: The hollow. A place formed in the shape of a mortar.
text.14_Chapter, 18_Verse, 1_Comment: Therefore he called its name. To commemorate that one who calls upon Hashem will be answered with a miracle. Some hold that when a person arrives at the place where a miracle was performed for him, he is obligated to bless; at the very least, the one for whom the miracle occurred must bless. Therefore he designated the place with a name: first he called it “Lehi” to remember the miracle of the jawbone, and when another miracle occurred there, he added the name “En HaKorei,” so that one would bless for both — as in the incident of Mar the son of Ravina (Berakhot, chapter “HaRo’eh”), who ruled that one must include both miracles.
text.15_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: And Samson went to Gaza. He was not afraid to enter a large city surrounded by walls, gates, and bars, and to lie in the house of a harlot without fear — and not only that, but…
text.15_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: To the Gazites, saying. He commanded that it be announced to the people of Gaza that Samson had come; thus he himself caused it to be proclaimed that Samson was in the city, yet he did not reveal that he himself was Samson.
text.15_Chapter, 1_Verse, 1_Comment: And they surrounded. Since they did not recognize the informer and assumed he was not Samson, they went about searching and investigating him in order to seize him when he would attempt to leave; they surrounded the city and also lay in wait at the gate, having locked it so that he could not go out. And the word “light” is in the past tense — meaning, until the morning would be light.
text.15_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: And he seized the doors. This was an even greater display of strength than if he had merely grasped the bar and broken it. (b) He placed that burden upon his shoulders. (c) And he carried them up — he bore them for the distance of a day’s journey, as the Sages said. The word “and he pulled them up” (vayissa‘em), which is in the simple form, indicates that by his own movement he caused them to be carried as well; similarly, “and he pulled up the peg of the loom” implies the ease of the action, for it would otherwise have said “and he caused them to be pulled up.”
text.15_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: And it came to pass afterward. One transgression leads to another.
text.15_Chapter, 3_Verse, 1_Comment: And her name was Delilah. The first woman converted and changed her name to a Jewish name, but this one did not convert and remained with the name Delilah. So it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud (Sotah 1:8) that in Timnah it was by way of marriage, but not in Gaza. And the Sages expounded that she “diluted” (dalelah) his strength, his deeds, and his heart.
text.15_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (5–18): They inquired about two matters — wherein lies his great strength, and how they might bind him — yet in the first instance she asked him, and he answered only how he might be bound, not wherein his strength lies. In the second and third instances she asked only about the source of his strength. By what sign did she recognize in the final instance that he had told her all his heart? And why in the earlier instances did he say, “and I shall be like one of men,” whereas in the last he said, “and I shall be like any man”?
text.15_Chapter, 4_Verse, 1_Comment: And see wherein his great strength lies, and by what means we may prevail against him. They requested two things:
text.15_Chapter, 4_Verse, 2_Comment: (a) That she discover the cause by which his strength was so great, for they assumed it was not natural but due to some special quality; and if so, they could devise a strategy to remove that cause.
text.15_Chapter, 4_Verse, 3_Comment: (b) And even if his strength were natural, she should investigate by what means he might be bound; for there are those whose strength lies in their hands but not in their feet, and he might be bound at the feet or at some other part of the body where he is not strong. And they said “and see” — meaning, examine whether his words are true. And when they said “and we will bind him to afflict him,” this was a promise that they would not kill him; and they kept their word — they did not put him to death but only put out his eyes.
text.15_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: And she said. She likewise asked him concerning the two matters mentioned.
text.15_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: And he said to her. He answered her only regarding how he might be bound, and not about wherein his great strength lay — as though he did not know any special cause for it, for it was natural to him — but he merely tested her by saying how he could be restrained.
text.15_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: And Delilah said… “Behold, you have mocked me.” That is, she believed him when he implied that he knew wherein his strength lay; but since he admitted that he knew by what means he could be bound, then why have you spoken lies? Now tell me, truly, by what you may be bound.
text.15_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: And he said to her. He replied that he had not spoken falsely at all, but had merely omitted a condition in his words.
text.15_Chapter, 10_Verse, 1_Comment: (a) That the cords must be thick — that is, braided of three strands.
text.15_Chapter, 10_Verse, 2_Comment: (b) That they must be such as have not been used for any work.
text.15_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: And he snapped them… like a thread. That is to say, not with as great ease as before, but like a thread — which a person can tear apart with a small amount of force.
text.15_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: Until now you have mocked me. That is to say, at first you justified your words, but now it is evident that you have mocked me on both occasions.
text.15_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: And she fastened it. Here it does not say, “and the ambusher was sitting in the chamber,” for after she had deceived them twice, they no longer paid attention to her words.
text.15_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: And you have not told me wherein your great strength lies. After he had already deceived her three times, she returned to ask the original question — wherein his great strength lay — since she could no longer continue asking by what means he might be bound, for he had denied her three times. If she persisted in that line of questioning, he would realize that the princes of the Philistines were conspiring with her. Therefore she asked only about the source of his strength, as though she wished merely to understand his nature and disposition, not to know how he might be bound.
text.15_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: And he told. He was enticed like a simple dove and told her both matters: (a) wherein his great strength lay — namely, through his Nazirite status; and (b) by what he might be bound — namely, if he were shaven.
text.15_Chapter, 16_Verse, 1_Comment: In the earlier instances he said, “and I shall be like one of men,” but now he said, “and I shall be like any man.” For he was careful not to speak falsehood and therefore said “like one of men,” meaning like a particular man distinguished for strength (as I have explained that the word “one,” when connected to the definite article, denotes something distinctive, as in “one of the mountains,” and the like). But now he said “like any man,” that is, like ordinary, weak men.
text.15_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: And Delilah saw that he had told her all his heart. She recognized this because he now answered both questions — wherein his strength lay and by what means he might be bound. For had he intended to deceive her, he would have told her only wherein his strength lay; in that case, even if she shaved him and his strength remained afterward, he would not be a liar, for it could be said that his strength derived from his Nazirite status and would not be removed by shaving, since he had not shaved of his own will nor willfully profaned his Nazirite vow. Yet he said, “if I be shaved,” in a form implying even if done by others. Therefore, she sent and called for the lords of the Philistines, saying, ‘Come up this time,’ for on the previous occasion they had not come up, as mentioned above.
text.15_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: And the hair of his head began to grow. It uses the intensive form of the verb to indicate that it grew rapidly, not in the usual manner; otherwise it would be difficult to understand how the Philistines were not careful to shave him repeatedly, knowing that his strength depended on his hair. Therefore it says, “when he was shaved” — meaning, immediately after the shaving it began to grow.
text.15_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: And the lords of the Philistines… and the people saw him… That is to say, the lords offered a sacrifice because he was their enemy, while the people praised (their god) for three reasons:
text.15_Chapter, 22_Verse, 2_Comment: (b) That he was the destroyer of their land, for he had burned their fields,
text.15_Chapter, 22_Verse, 3_Comment: (c) And that he had multiplied their slain, whereas to the lords he had not done these particular harms. (And “for rejoicing” is an infinitive form, like “to fear Hashem.”)
text.15_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: And he said to her: He answered that he had not spoken falsely at all, but had merely omitted a condition in his words.
text.15_Chapter, 28_Verse, 0_Comment: And he leaned. I have explained in my work *Torah ve-haMitzvah* (on Torat Kohanim) that there is a distinction between “to lean” (sha‘an) and “to press/lean with support” (samak). “Semikhah” implies with all one’s strength — as the Sages said, “semikhah requires all one’s strength” — whereas “sha‘inah” indicates only part of one’s weight. Therefore to the lad he said, “and I will lean upon them,” but in fact he pressed with all his strength.
text.16_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: And his name was Micah. At first he was righteous and was called Mikhayehu; afterward, when he served idolatry, he was called Micah. Therefore it says, “and his name was Mikhayehu,” for with the wicked their deeds precede their name — as the Sages said (Ruth Rabbah 4:3), “Nabal was his name,” and the like.
text.16_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (2): Why does it repeat, “Behold, the silver is with me; I took it”?
text.16_Chapter, 1_Verse, 1_Comment: And you uttered a curse. She pronounced an oath-curse against the thief. And you also said in my hearing, “Behold, the silver is with me,” meaning that you implied you suspected me — that the silver was with me — and thus the intent of that curse fell upon me. I confess to you that I took it, and by this I will rectify both the sin of theft and the curse. (It is explained in Choshen Mishpat 71:7 that one who imposes a curse should not say “whoever stole it,” but rather “whoever has the stolen item in his possession and does not return it”; therefore, in the curse she uttered she did not phrase it as “who took the silver,” but as “the silver is with him and he does not return it,” for the intent is not to curse for the past, but to compel the return of what is hers, as the Shach explains there.) And his mother said, “Blessed be my son to Hashem.” He passed from the category of cursed to the category of blessed.
text.16_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (3–4): Why does it say twice, “he returned the eleven hundred pieces of silver to his mother,” and again, “he returned the silver to his mother”? Did she not consecrate all the silver, yet in the end gave only two hundred pieces to the silversmith? She said, “from my hand for my son to make a graven image,” but afterward she herself gave it to the silversmith — not Micah?
text.16_Chapter, 2_Verse, 1_Comment: And he returned. He immediately restored what he had stolen, which indicates that he feared Hashem. And his mother said, “I had fully consecrated the silver to Hashem.” I stipulated two conditions in this consecration: (a) from my hand to my son, meaning that I would entrust it to my son so that he would serve as its treasurer; (b) to make a graven image and a molten image. And now I return it to you, since you are the treasurer to make the image.
text.16_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: And he returned the silver to his mother. It relates that Micah did not wish to serve as treasurer for idolatry, for he did not agree to make a graven image and a molten image. Certainly he reasoned with her not to do so, especially since according to the law the consecration did not take effect, as it was not yet in her possession (as stated in Bava Kamma 70a). As a result, she partially relented and did not make the image from the entire sum, but only from two hundred pieces of silver, and the silversmith made the image from them. And it was in the house of Micah — for although they had not yet worshiped it, he had already transgressed the word of Hashem by having the image in his house, violating the prohibition “You shall have no other gods,” which, according to Rashi (Exodus 20:3), serves as a warning even against keeping an idol in one’s home.
text.16_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: And the man Micah. From then on, one transgression led to another, and he went from bad to worse (therefore his name is called Micah, in a negative sense), until he made for himself a house of gods — a special house for the service of the idol. Afterward he made also an ephod and teraphim from his own funds, and then he ordained one of his sons to serve as priest in the service of idolatry.
text.16_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: In those days. That is to say, do not be surprised that Israel remained silent about this, for at that time there was no prince or judge in the land.
text.16_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (7): Why does it repeat, “from Bethlehem in Judah,” and “he sojourned there”?
text.16_Chapter, 6_Verse, 1_Comment: And there was a young man. This young man was from Bethlehem in Judah — for on his mother’s side he was from the family of Judah, while on his father’s side he was a Levite. Since the Levites had no portion in the land, he dwelt in his mother’s place, for he had no inheritance through his father. And according to what is stated (Bava Batra 109b) that the mother’s family is not called a “family,” he nevertheless inherited his mother’s portion, as she was an heiress of an inheritance; and in this respect he was regarded as of the family of Judah, since the inheritance was in the territory of Judah.
text.16_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (8): Why does it repeat, “and he went from the city, from Bethlehem”?
text.16_Chapter, 7_Verse, 1_Comment: And the man went from the city, from Bethlehem in Judah. Since he did not find his livelihood there, he left; and it clarifies that he did not set out toward a particular destination, but merely departed from where he had been — going from city to city seeking a place to live, as it says, “to sojourn wherever he might find.” In this way he came to the hill country of Ephraim, to the house of Micah — not because he intended to find sustenance there, but to make his way, like a traveler who turns aside to lodge.
text.16_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: “From where do you come?” For he assumed that he had a fixed residence; and he replied, I have no established place — rather, I am going to sojourn wherever I may find.
text.16_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (10): The phrase “and the Levite went” implies that he departed from him; how then does it say afterward, “and the Levite was willing to dwell”?
text.16_Chapter, 9_Verse, 1_Comment: And Micah said to him. He told him: since in any case you are wandering and have no occupation or livelihood, here you will gain in three ways: (a) “Dwell with me” — here you will remain and not wander. (b) The occupation will be an honorable one befitting your status as a Levite — “and you shall be to me a father and a priest.” (c) In terms of wages, “I will give you ten pieces of silver for the year,” that is, annually; and an allowance of clothing, meaning garments appropriate to your dignity; and also your sustenance, provisions for food. And the Levite went. It relates that at first he did not want to hire himself out for idolatry, and he departed from him.
text.16_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: And afterward, and the Levite consented. He agreed to dwell with the man, that is, not to serve as a father and priest, but merely to stay in his house for some time. And the young man was like one of his sons, eating at his table; and later, by remaining in the house of a wicked man, he was drawn after him.
text.16_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: And Micah ordained him… and he became to him… a priest, and he was in the house of Micah. That is to say, from then on he became a permanent resident in his house, to remain there continually; for until that point he had been there only temporarily. And Micah attributed this success as praise to the idol.
text.17_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (1): Is it not stated in the Book of Joshua that Zorah, Eshtaol, and Ir-Shemesh were given as an inheritance to Dan? And here too it says that they sent spies from Zorah and Eshtaol — so how can it say that no inheritance had fallen to them in which to dwell?
text.17_Chapter, 0_Verse, 1_Comment: In those days there was no king. The episode that follows was due to the absence of a king to restrain the people; had there been a king, no tribe of Israel would have engaged in idolatry. And in those days the tribe of Dan was seeking for itself an inheritance in which to dwell. The inheritance of Dan had two deficiencies: (a) it lay outside the main border of Israel, since it was the last lot cast, as it says (Joshua 19:47), “and the border of the children of Dan went out from them”; (b) for this reason they were unable to dispossess the Canaanites, and the Canaanites later reclaimed their territory (as stated above 1:35–36). Therefore they sought an inheritance in which to dwell, for their original inheritance was not fit for dwelling, since the Canaanites inhabited it. This explains the reason: for it had not fallen to them… within the tribes of Israel, but rather outside their border. Thus it says as an inheritance — meaning, the inheritance that had fallen to them was not within the tribes of Israel, but outside of them.
text.17_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (2): Why does it repeat “from their family” and “from their extremities”? Why does it repeat “to spy” and “to explore”? And why does it conclude with “go, explore,” and not say “explore and spy”?
text.17_Chapter, 1_Verse, 1_Comment: And the children of Dan sent from their family. I have explained in my commentary on the Torah (Parashat Miketz and Parashat Shelach) that there are two kinds of scouts: (a) those who first go to see whether the land is good or not, in order to determine whether it is worth fighting for; these are properly called “tourers” (tarim), for the one who tours seeks out what is good; (b) after they decide to wage war, they send spies to see the vulnerabilities of the land — from which side it is easiest to conquer it; these are called “spies” (meraglim), for the spy seeks out the weaknesses and defects. There is a distinction between them. When they first send tourers, they dispatch one from each tribe or from each family, for one tribe will not rely upon emissaries from another tribe, since a land may be good for one tribe and not for another — as the children of Reuben sought pastureland, and the children of Zebulun sought a seacoast for ships, and so on. They also send their leaders and prominent men, upon whom the people rely, who understand the needs and aims of the nation. But when they send spies, they send one or two men — even from the lesser among the people — since their task is only to see from which place the land may be most easily conquered. Furthermore, when sending spies they choose strong and valiant men, because they go to inspect fortresses and troops where they may easily be recognized as spies, and they must be brave to save themselves and skilled in military matters to observe how and from where to wage war. The tourers, however, go like merchants in the midst of the land and are not in danger; they need not be warriors. Here they sent their agents for both purposes: (a) to see whether the land was good; (b) to spy out the place easiest to conquer. Therefore, since they were sent to investigate whether the land was good or bad, they sent from their family five men — that is, one from each family — and they also sent from their extremities, meaning the leaders and chiefs among them. And since they were also sent to spy, they chose men of valor. It explains that they were sent for two purposes: (a) to spy out the land, and (b) to explore it — to see whether it was good or bad. Nevertheless, since this was the initial mission, they told them, “Go, explore the land,” for the primary command concerned the exploration — to determine whether it was good or bad — and the spying would follow the exploration. And they came… to the house of Micah. That is, they lodged at an inn near the house of Micah.
text.17_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: They were near the house of Micah. That is, since they lodged near Micah’s house, they heard the voice of the Levite and recognized him. It appears that this Levite was of the sons of Kohath, from the descendants of Moses, as the Sages received (Bava Batra 109b); and the cities of the Kohathite Levites were in the territory of Ephraim, Dan, and half of Manasseh (as explained in Joshua 21:5). Thus this Levite was born in one of the Levitical cities in Dan, and they recognized him. And they said to him. They asked him three questions: (a) “Who brought you here” — from your home — to this place? (b) “And what” — that is, what occupation do you have here? (c) “And what” — that is, what is your compensation here?
text.17_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: And he said. He replied to “Who brought you here?”: “Thus and thus has Micah done for me.” He recounted his course until he came to Micah’s house and in what manner he persuaded him to remain. In response to “What is your compensation?” — “and he hired me.” And to “What are you doing here?” — “and I have become his priest.”
text.17_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: Inquire, please. For they thought that the teraphim, through sorcery or by drawing down spiritual forces, could foretell the future.
text.17_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: And he said (after he had inquired), “Go in peace.” This means success on the journey. “Before Hashem is your way.” That is to say, the purpose of your journey stands before Hashem and under His favorable Providence, and you will attain the goal of your desire.
text.17_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (7): The entire verse appears repetitive, and the phrase “possessor of restraint” (yoresh ‘etzer) has no clear meaning. And what is meant by “and there was none who would shame them for anything in the land”?
text.17_Chapter, 6_Verse, 1_Comment: And they saw the people who were within it. That is to say, they had no reason to fear the people themselves, for they were not men of war; nor did they need to fear their neighbors or potential allies. It explains this in detail: Not from the people themselves — for a nation takes up arms for four possible reasons: (a) If it is their custom to conquer lands and their livelihood depends on war, to seize spoil and plunder. Therefore it says, “dwelling securely, after the manner of the Sidonians,” meaning that the entire kingdom dwelt securely like the Sidonians, who were merchants or herdsmen, and did not live by plunder and war. (b) If they fear an external enemy — therefore it says, “a people quiet and secure,” for no enemy’s foot came within their borders. (c) If there is internal strife, city against city or clan against clan — therefore it says, “and there was none who would shame them for anything in the land,” meaning they all lived together in peace. (d) If there is a king and sons who inherit his throne, for then they would maintain an army to preserve their monarchy. Therefore it says “and no possessor of restraint” (the word “none” applies to both: none who would shame them, and none who was heir to sovereign rule), meaning there was no heir to royal authority who imposed control over the people. Furthermore, there was no need to fear their allies coming to their aid, for the Sidonians, who were in the valley, were far from them, and they had no alliance with their neighbors, since they had no dealings with any man — they had no covenantal ties with anyone.
text.17_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: “What are you doing?” — that is, what are you saying?
text.17_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: And they said, “Rise, and let us go up.” That is, there is no need to send additional spies again; rather, we should go at once. Do not fear that the land is not good, for “we have seen the land, and behold it is very good—yet you are silent?” And do not be afraid of a difficult war, for “do not be sluggish to go and come to inherit the land”—you will not need to fight much, but simply to take possession. And he explains the reason, for:
text.17_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: “When you come” — you will come to a people secure, meaning they will not fight against you, as explained above. And they said “when you come” to mean immediately—without delay—for if you linger, the matter may become known to them and they will prepare themselves for battle. Do not think that it has other disadvantages. If you suspect it may be small in size, it says: “and the land is broad of hands”—that is, spacious. And if you think it may lack in quality or resources, it says: “a place where there is no lack of anything that is in the land”—meaning you will find there all the things found in the Land of Israel.
text.17_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: “And they set out from there.” This means that immediately they uprooted their dwelling and moved there, because they trusted in the words of the messengers.
text.17_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: “And they encamped at Kiriath-jearim.” There they prepared provisions for the long journey ahead. The camp itself did not enter the city, but remained behind Kiriath-jearim.
text.17_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: “Those who went to spy.” Since they went in order to spy, they came to know this through that mission — for through it they inquired by means of the teraphim.
text.17_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (15–20) Why does it repeat: “They came to the house of the young man” and again “the five men went up” and “these came into the house of Micah”? Why does it repeat: “they took the carved image” and again “they took the carved image,” and in verse 20 “he took the ephod”? All these phrases seem redundant, and the sequence of events appears disordered to any careful reader?
text.17_Chapter, 14_Verse, 1_Comment: “And they asked him of his welfare — and the six hundred men” etc. The meaning is that the five men and the six hundred men asked him about his welfare. That is to say: when they came to his house, they told him that they were inquiring after his peace — both in their own name and in the name of the six hundred men, who were all from the tribe of Dan and who knew him. Through this, they caused him to come out to them to the entrance of the gate. And while the priest was speaking with the six hundred men…
text.17_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: “And the five men went up.” The five men went back up into his house and entered the shrine of idolatry, and they took the carved image, the ephod, and the teraphim. Meanwhile, the priest was standing at the entrance of the gate with the six hundred men. “And in the meantime the priest noticed and returned to his house.” In the meantime, the priest became aware of what was happening and returned to his house. “But by the time the priest returned, they had already come out from the Levite’s house—where the idol was—through Micah’s house.” For the entrance to the Levite’s house was through Micah’s house.
text.17_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: “And these came to the house of Micah.” At the moment the priest returned, they were not in the priest’s house, but in Micah’s house, which was in front of the priest’s house. “And they took the carved image, the ephod…” That is, the priest saw that they were taking them out of the house. “And he said to them, ‘What are you doing?’” For if the priest had cried out at that moment, the men of Micah would have protested and stopped them, since only the five men were there.
text.17_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: “And they said to him, ‘Be silent.’” Do not cry out concerning what relates to Micah. And regarding what concerns you, “Put your hand over your mouth and come with us,” for you will benefit from this; for “Is it better for you to be a priest to the house of one man…” etc.
text.17_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: And then he took the ephod in his hand, and came into the midst of the people.
text.17_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: And the priest. For if you had not taken the priest, I would have made another idol. And why do you say to me, “What is the matter with you?” Do I not have reason to fear a loss greater than this?
text.17_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: They answered him that he should keep silent, lest he gather his own life and the lives of his household.
text.17_Chapter, 26_Verse, 0_Comment:
And they took. In this way it seemed to them that they had not oppressed or stolen, but had merely taken it as in war, since he pursued them and was unable to prevail against them.
And they came upon Laish.
And in the Midrash (Tanchuma, Ki Tisa 14) this is what is meant by the verse (Daniel 9:7), “To You, O Hashem, is righteousness, but to us shame of face”: even though they took the idol, they nevertheless succeeded in their war.
text.17_Chapter, 27_Verse, 0_Comment: And there was no deliverer. Not from the Sidonians, for it was far from Sidon; nor from their neighbors, for they had no dealings with anyone. Nor was it difficult to conquer on account of its location, for it was in a valley, which is easy to capture.
text.17_Chapter, 29_Verse, 0_Comment: And they set up for themselves the idol. At first they established only the idol itself, to draw down the spiritual influence; afterward, they set up for themselves Micah’s graven image as Micah had made it, together with the ephod and the teraphim. And it stood all the days that the House of God was in Shiloh—this corresponding to that. As for what is said that Jonathan and his sons were priests until the exile of the land, Rashi explains this as referring to the exile of Sennacherib. So too is the view of our Sages in the Jerusalem Talmud (Berakhot, ch. 9, hal. 3), which challenges Rabbi Shimon ben Nachmani, who said that Shebuel returned to God with all his heart—yet the verse states “until the exile of the land.” It answers that after the death of David, Solomon removed him, and he reverted to his former ways; and he was the old prophet in Bethel. And regarding what Radak asks—how could it be that Samuel, David, and Solomon did not destroy this idol?—it may be said that indeed in the days of Samuel it was annulled. Therefore it says, “all the days that the House of God was in Shiloh.” At that time he repented, and David appointed him over the treasuries. But in the days of Jeroboam, who set up the calf in Dan, his sons were priests there until the exile of Sennacherib.
text.18_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: And it was in those days, and there was no king in Israel. This incident as well was caused by the fact that there was no king to remove the sinners and administer justice; for at that time the people were like fuel for fire, and each man’s sword was against his brother.
text.18_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: "And his concubine acted unfaithfully toward him. It should have said “acted unfaithfully from him,” for the word “upon him” when used regarding immorality normally refers to the man with whom she committed adultery (as in “and you committed harlotry with the sons of Egypt” — Ezekiel 16:26). This indicates, according to the Sages (Gittin 6b), that she did not actually commit adultery, but only did something against his will.And she went from him. Not out to lovers, but rather to her father’s house."
text.18_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: "And her husband arose. This too indicates that she had not committed adultery, for Scripture calls him her husband; had she committed adultery, she would have been forbidden to him—according to the opinion that a concubine has kiddushin. And the young woman’s father saw him … and his father-in-law prevailed upon him. The terms are used according to the context: he rejoiced in him insofar as he was her father and wished that she not remain bound and deserted; and he pressed him to stay insofar as he was his father-in-law."
text.18_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: "And they arose early in the morning … and they drank … That is, on the first day it was still morning, but they drank, and he urged him to stay overnight because he had drunk, and the road confuses those who drink wine. On the following day, however, he was careful not to drink; only the meal extended until the day declined."
text.18_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: "Behold now, the day is waning. The Maharai”a explains that he said to him: (1) Behold, the day is slackening — it is already time to lodge. (2) Even aside from that, you will not reach your home today and will have to camp along the way; therefore, camp today and lodge here. Make your stop here, and tomorrow you may rise early and in a single day reach your tent, without needing to lodge on the road."
text.18_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: "Questions (10) What is meant by stating that with him were a pair of donkeys and his concubine? This appears unnecessary, for it was already said in verse 3, “and his servant was with him, and a pair of donkeys.” And why is his servant not mentioned here?"
text.18_Chapter, 9_Verse, 1_Comment: "And with him. This serves as an explanation for why he did not lodge in the field: for with him were a pair of saddled donkeys, carrying all his goods, and he feared bandits. Secondly, because of his concubine, for a woman is of delicate constitution and not suited to lodge in the field. For these same two reasons he did not turn aside into a foreign city—because of bandits, and because of possible violation of his concubine."
text.18_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: "Questions (12) Why the repetition: “a foreign city” — “which is not of the children of Israel”?"
text.18_Chapter, 11_Verse, 1_Comment: "To a foreign city which is not of the children of Israel. That is, there were Canaanite cities that belonged to Israel and were subject to them for tribute, and the fear of Israel was upon them. But Jebus was a foreign city that was not of the children of Israel—meaning that they were not subject to Israel, for they had not been placed under tribute (as mentioned above in 1:21)."
text.18_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: "And we will lodge in Gibeah or in Ramah. For he did not know which city was nearer. (And the word “la-lechet” here is one of three places, according to the Masorah, where a form of going is written without the final heh.)"
text.18_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: And behold, an old man. Just as the text recounts the disgrace of the men of Gibeah, who shut their doors to a traveler even though they were residents of the city and were not pressed for space, so it relates the praise of this old man: (1) though he was elderly; (2) that he had just come at that very moment; (3) that he came from his work, the hard labor in the field; (4) and that he was a sojourner in Gibeah, so the obligation of hospitality did not rest upon him more than upon the townspeople—yet nevertheless he acted as he did.
text.18_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: And he lifted up … And immediately when he saw him, he asked him, “Where are you going?” For he wondered whether perhaps he intended to continue on his way, and therefore was standing in the street.
text.18_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (18) Why does he repeat a second time, “and I am going to Bethlehem”? And why does he say, “and I am going to the House of Hashem”?
text.18_Chapter, 17_Verse, 1_Comment: And he said to him, “We are passing through.” That is, our journey is from Bethlehem of Judah to the far reaches of the hill country of Ephraim, and it is impossible to reach there while it is still day, for I am from there, and that is my home district. And lest he think that he was a peddler going about from town to town, he said that he went only as far as Bethlehem. And lest he suppose that he was one of Micah’s men who worshiped the idol (for Micah was in the hill country of Ephraim), he said, “and I am going to the House of Hashem.” Yet despite all this, there is no one who gathers me into his house, and therefore I have remained outside.
text.18_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: And lest you think that you will need to provide fodder for the donkeys, therefore he said, “There is both straw and feed for our donkeys.” And likewise, you will not need to give food to me or to the servant, for “there is also bread and wine.” Indeed, there is more than enough—so that the servant may eat with your servants from the bread and wine that I will give as his portion. And so too with other provisions, spices and the like—there is no lack of anything.
text.18_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: And he said. On the contrary, he stipulated with him that all his needs would be upon himself, for in this way he would fulfill the mitzvah properly.
text.18_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (22) What are the differences between the incident of Gibeah and the incident of Sodom? For at first glance, the two events appear similar in every respect.
text.18_Chapter, 21_Verse, 1_Comment: They were making their hearts merry, and behold, the men of the city… Scholars have already discussed this at length: What distinguishes the incident of Gibeah from the sin of Sodom, upon which brimstone and fire were rained and whose cities were overturned from their foundations? These acted as Sodom did, yet Heaven did not immediately punish them. They explain that there is a difference between the wicked and the sinful. The men of Sodom sinned out of ideology: they enacted corrupt laws and unjust civil ordinances, and accepted these as righteous statutes—that no traveler might pass through their land. Whoever transgressed was punished according to their established norms. They did not act out of mere desire, but out of perverted principles. The men of Gibeah, however, did not act from philosophical corruption nor from civic law, but from lust alone. Their refusal to host the traveler was due to stinginess and narrow-heartedness, and their desire to abuse him stemmed purely from base appetite. The distinctions are evident: (1) Lot brought the angels into his house secretly (as explained on Genesis 19:2), and the angels preferred to lodge in the street, fearing the civic law. But the old man in Gibeah brought the traveler openly into his home. (2) There it says, “the men of the city, the men of Sodom, surrounded the house, from young to old”—meaning the entire city, because hospitality violated their official law. Here it says “the men of the city, men of worthlessness”—that is, base individuals within the city, rabble who lusted after evil. Not all, and not by law, but because they were lawless men acting against justice. (3) There it says they “surrounded the house,” intending to wage battle against the homeowner for violating their law. Here it says “they surrounded the house” to prevent the guest from escaping—not to attack the old man. Therefore they did not seek his daughter, for they did not intend harm to him. Accordingly, it says they were “knocking” in a reflexive form, implying a show of force rather than actual violence; whereas in Sodom it says, “they drew near to break the door.” There, Lot shut the door behind him out of fear. Here it says, “and he went out to them,” for he knew they would not dare enter his home. (4) Here he told them that the act was “a disgrace,” showing that their moral sense remained intact—they recognized it as wickedness. But Lot did not argue that point, only that they should not do evil to guests who entered his home. For in Sodom, such conduct was considered proper under their corrupted laws.
text.18_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: Behold, my daughter. That is, to satisfy your desire, behold my daughter and his concubine. And although this too would be a disgrace, the shame involved is not as great as the disgrace of violating the man. Therefore he repeats, “but to this man you shall not do this vile thing.”
text.18_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: But they would not listen. The commentators explain that they did not desire the disgrace of the old man’s daughter. And the man seized his concubine. This too is proof that their intent was merely to satisfy their lust; therefore, when they found his concubine suitable for their desire, they were satisfied with her. And they knew her — in the usual manner. And they abused her — in an unnatural manner.
text.18_Chapter, 28_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (29) Why did he cut her into pieces and send the parts throughout all the borders of Israel? Would it not have been sufficient to send only a report of what had occurred?
text.18_Chapter, 28_Verse, 1_Comment:
And he cut her into twelve pieces. By this he demonstrated that the tribes of God are united like one body. Just as it is impossible for the spirit of life and intellect to dwell in a body once it has been dismembered—its limbs becoming lifeless corpses—so too the spirit of life and the Divine Presence cannot rest upon the nation as a whole if its parts are divided and its tribes fail to unite as the limbs of a living body must unite to sustain life.

And just as when one limb becomes infected and decay sets in, it is a grievous illness for the entire body, and efforts are made either to heal it or to amputate it lest it corrupt the whole—so too in this matter: if certain individuals within the nation become corrupted, the people must necessarily strive to bring them back to repentance or remove them from their midst.

And when he sent the pieces, he certainly also sent an account of the incident, to make known that an outrage had occurred in the land.
text.18_Chapter, 29_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (30) Why does it repeat “it has not happened” and “it has not been seen”? And why the repetition: “consider,” “take counsel,” “speak”?
text.18_Chapter, 29_Verse, 1_Comment: And it was that everyone who saw it said, “It has not happened.” And even if something like it had happened, it had not been seen, for it was done in secret. Therefore, “consider it” — investigate and inquire whether the matter is true and established. After that, “take counsel” — how to rectify the wrong, for one who gives counsel weighs all opposing factors and possibilities. And afterward, “and speak” — a decisive word, meaning the firm resolution that follows deliberation.
text.19_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (1) Why did Israel assemble for war before they fully knew the details of the incident? What concern was this to all of Israel, since each tribe had its own court to judge the members of its tribe? And why did they not first send a demand that the tribe of Benjamin remove the offenders—saying, “Deliver the men, and we will put them to death”?
text.19_Chapter, 0_Verse, 1_Comment: And all the children of Israel went out, and the congregation assembled. If they had proceeded strictly according to the judicial law of the Torah in an individual case, the men of Gibeah would not have been liable to death, as the Ramban explains. For regarding their intent to violate the man, it was only a thought and not carried out in action. Concerning their abuse of the concubine: according to Ramban, a concubine is without kiddushin; and even according to the opinion that she has kiddushin, there were no witnesses and no prior warning. As for her death, it may be said that she died from weakness, since they did not intend to kill her; perhaps she died from the cold or some other cause. Rather, Israel was aroused with zeal because the act was committed publicly and openly. In such a case, they are judged like heretics—for when many gather brazenly to commit so grave an outrage, and with all the compounded elements of this deed, they approach the status of an “ir hanidachat” (a condemned city). Therefore they could be executed as an extraordinary measure (“le-migder milta”) according to the need of the hour. Such authority could only be exercised either by the king of Israel, who may execute under the law of the monarchy, or by the entirety of Israel with the Sanhedrin at their head—who stand in place of the king and may destroy a band of evildoers as a king would, especially in a case involving great desecration of the Divine Name. Thus it says, “And all the children of Israel went out, and the congregation assembled,” for as we have explained elsewhere (in my work Torah ve-haMitzvah, Vayikra §241), the term “congregation” refers to Israel assembled with their elders at their head.
text.19_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (2–3) Why did they seek to put them to death when there were no witnesses and no prior warning? Especially according to the opinion (Sanhedrin 21a) that a concubine is without kiddushin. And her death was due to her weakness, not because they intended to kill her. Why then did they pour out their wrath upon the entire tribe of Benjamin? And the statement in verse 3, “And the children of Benjamin heard,” does not seem to belong there at all—why is it placed in that context?
text.19_Chapter, 1_Verse, 1_Comment: And the chiefs of all the people stood. That is, they took their positions according to the order of the banners—Judah and his division to the east, and so on. And among them were found all the tribes of Israel in the assembly of the people of God, for they gathered as the people of God, coming to be zealous for His honor. And there were four hundred thousand men, all of them foot soldiers, not riders on horses—who came and assembled out of zeal for the honor of the Divine Name.
text.19_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: And the children of Benjamin heard. This teaches that the matter was not hidden from Benjamin. They heard that the children of Israel had gone up to Mizpah, and they also heard that the children of Israel were saying, “How did this evil happen?” Indeed, they heard all the details that are related up to verse 12. Yet despite this, they did not take it to heart to remove the offenders themselves, nor did they come to the assembly to clear themselves. And the children of Israel said, “Speak—how did this evil happen?” For although they had already heard the account from the messengers who carried the pieces, the essential matter depended on the specific details. If this had been the act of isolated individuals who violated his concubine and she died merely as a result of the assault, that alone would not justify all Israel going to war. Rather, everything depended upon the additional elements that converged in this outrage. Perhaps she had already acted immorally, or perhaps she was not legally bound in marriage, as the Ramban argued in defense of the men of Gibeah. Or perhaps she died from the cold or some other cause. Therefore they sought clarification of the precise circumstances.
text.19_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: And the Levite, the husband of the murdered woman, answered. This is stated to clarify that she was not unmarried and had not been unfaithful to him, for he was her husband through kiddushin; she was permitted to him, since she had not committed adultery. And she did not die from the cold, but was murdered. And he said, “To Gibeah, which belongs to Benjamin, I came.” First, this sin outwardly resembles the matter of Sodom. There too, guests came to lodge, and they called to Lot, “Bring out the men that we may know them.” This was a great disgrace to all Israel. Therefore he emphasized that he came to lodge.
text.19_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment:
(2) “And they rose up against me.” He and she had had no prior dealings with them whatsoever.

(3) It was not merely individuals who rose up, but “the lords of Gibeah”—the prominent men and leaders of the city—and this openly.

(4) “And they surrounded the house against me by night,” which closely parallels the incident of Sodom.

(5) “Me they intended to kill,” for he would certainly have died from the abuse; all the more so in the case of his concubine, whom they afflicted and she died—even though a woman’s body is more accustomed to relations. And though they only intended it and did not carry it out, he was forced to save himself through his concubine.

(6) “And they afflicted my concubine,” who was a married woman.

(7) Because they intended to kill him, they therefore abused his concubine—meaning they took her against her will. This was a great public act of violence, as the Maharai”a explains.
text.19_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: For they committed lewdness and outrage. The act itself was lewdness; and insofar as it was done publicly, in a manner of brazen defiance, it was an outrage that touched the entire nation of Israel.
text.19_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: Behold, all of you… You possess the authority of a king to administer justice according to the need of the hour, in order to make a protective measure. “Give your word.” This refers to issuing the legal ruling—what is to be done with them. And afterward, “and counsel”—how to carry the ruling into effect, to remove the offenders (see what is explained on Isaiah 8:10).
text.19_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: We will not go, each man to his tent — to remain there. Nor even will we turn, each man to his house, whether temporarily or to prepare provisions. And if you should ask: Who will prepare provisions for the people? This is the thing that we shall do to Gibeah — that is, for the matter of Gibeah. Against it — meaning, for its sake, in order to remove the offenders from its midst; for they did not intend to kill all the inhabitants of Gibeah, but only the guilty ones.
text.19_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: And he was gathered … to the city — to Mizpah, until they would prepare provisions and until they would send the messengers.
text.19_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: And they sent. This highlights the wrongdoing of the children of Benjamin: Israel sent messengers to them and opened with words of peace. They said, “What is this evil?” — meaning, see how great this evil has become and what it has produced. It has arisen among you, and you are the first who should remove the offenders.
text.19_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: And now, deliver the men. Then the evil will be removed from you and transferred to the collective responsibility. And we will remove the evil — all of us together, from the midst of Israel. Yet despite this entire mission, the children of Benjamin were unwilling to listen, to surrender the offenders. Even more than that, they gathered for war and were the first to open the strife.
text.19_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: And the men of Israel. Then the children of Israel were mustered and prepared themselves for war. They appointed commanders, arranged the battle lines, and set their forces in order. Their number was again four hundred thousand, showing that they upheld their word: not one turned back to his home, nor did any who were fearful or fainthearted return. All went forth together.
text.19_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment:
Questions
(18–29) Why were Israel defeated twice before Benjamin, even though they went to contend Hashem’s cause and to be zealous for His honor? And if they inquired twice through the judgment of the Urim, how was it that the inquiry was not fulfilled and they fell slain?

After it says in verse 22 that the men of Israel strengthened themselves and again set the battle in array, how does the following verse say that they went up to Bethel and sat there—had they not already been before Gibeah and arranged the battle there?

Why in the second instance did they ask in the wording “Shall I again draw near?” and in the third instance did they ask, “Shall I again go out?”
