Why in the second instance does it say, “And the children of Israel went up and wept,” whereas in the third instance it says, “And all the children of Israel and all the people went up”? And why does it add that they fasted and offered burnt offerings?

The statement in verses 27–28—“And there was the Ark of the Covenant… and Phinehas…”—would seem to belong earlier, in verse 18, when they inquired the first time. And why is the phrase “in those days” repeated?
text.19_Chapter, 17_Verse, 1_Comment:
And they arose and went up to Bethel, and inquired of God.

Our Sages (Pirkei deRabbi Eliezer 38) said that the reason they were defeated the first two times was because they too had within their midst the sin of Micah’s idol, which was also a sin of the many. Hashem was angered with them for not protesting, for the sake of His honor, against the tribe of Dan concerning the sin of idolatry—which is more severe. Yet here they protested only in a matter of immorality and violence, which concerns social order and the settlement of the land.

However, in the verses themselves it is explained that there were three distinctions between the first two occasions, when they did not succeed in war, and the final time.
text.19_Chapter, 17_Verse, 2_Comment: The first distinction: in the beginning they asked, “Who shall go up for us first to wage war against the children of Benjamin?” They did not ask whether they should go up to war at all, nor whether they would succeed in their battle, for they relied on their own strength and on the arm of flesh. He answered them according to their manner: “Judah first.” That is, Judah precedes in all matters. It does not say “Judah shall go up,” and certainly it does not state whether they would succeed. In the second instance it says: “And the people, the men of Israel, strengthened themselves and again set the battle in array in the place where they had set it in array on the first day; and the children of Israel went up and wept before Hashem.” It is clear from this that at first they went up to battle on their own initiative and did not inquire of Hashem, and they were already positioned in the place where they had arranged themselves on the first day. Accordingly, when it says, “the children of Israel went up and wept before Hashem,” it cannot mean that all of them went up, for they were already at the battlefield before Gibeah; rather, they sent their elders and judges, and they wept. And they asked: “Shall I again draw near for battle?” They did not ask, as in the third instance, “Shall I again go out?” — because they had already gone out and were standing before Gibeah; all that remained was to approach and engage the city, as it says: “And the children of Israel drew near to the children of Benjamin.” Thus the question was only whether they were permitted to wage this war according to the law. They also did not ask whether they would succeed, for even now they relied on their strength and their great numbers. Therefore He answered them: “Go up against him.” That is, you are permitted to go up — but He did not inform them whether they would succeed, for that depends on whether they repent of their sins. Not so in the third instance: they did not even dare to go out at all. Rather: “And all the children of Israel and all the people went up and came to Bethel” — meaning, not a single man was missing. And they asked: “Shall I again go out?” And He answered: “For tomorrow I will deliver him into your hand.”
text.19_Chapter, 17_Verse, 3_Comment:
The second distinction: in the first instance they did not repent at all. In the second instance, where it says, “And the children of Israel went up and wept,” I have already explained that not all of them went up, but only their elders; and they did not weep over their sins, but over the fallen. Therefore they were again defeated in battle.

But in the third instance, when all of them went up and all of them wept—and not only that, but they preceded their request with three actions:

(1) And they sat before Hashem — to examine their deeds.

(2) And they fasted on that day — to restrain transgression and bring sin to an end.

(3) And they offered burnt offerings and peace offerings — offerings of thanksgiving for the remnant that had been spared, for they understood that all of them deserved destruction because of their sin.

Therefore they succeeded on that occasion.
text.19_Chapter, 17_Verse, 4_Comment: The third distinction: our Sages (Yoma 73b) and the commentators explain that in the first and second instances they did not inquire in the proper place nor through the proper person. Only in the third instance does it explicitly state that they inquired in the proper place, as it says, “And the Ark of the Covenant of Hashem was there in those days”—that is, now, at this time. And through the proper person, as it says, “And Phinehas the son of Eleazar stood before it in those days”—meaning now, in the third instance. Therefore they were answered. Meanwhile, the children of Benjamin increased in their wickedness. For whereas Israel’s objective was only against Gibeah—as it says in the first instance, “and they set the battle against them at Gibeah,” and in the second instance, “and they set the battle against Gibeah as at the first”—Benjamin, by contrast, intended to destroy Israel. They also grew more brazen each time: in the first instance it says, “And the children of Benjamin went out from Gibeah”; in the second, “And Benjamin went out to meet them from Gibeah”—the phrase “to meet them” implying a face-to-face confrontation; and in the third instance it adds that they were drawn away from the city.
text.19_Chapter, 28_Verse, 0_Comment: And he set ambushers. They positioned several groups of ambushers from multiple locations, as will be explained.
text.19_Chapter, 29_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (30–46) It is stated twice that twenty-five thousand of Benjamin fell. It is stated twice that the men of Israel turned back. Twice it says that the children of Benjamin struck about thirty men among them. Twice it mentions that a column of smoke rose from the city, and twice that it rose from the ambush. The entire sequence appears confused and intermingled, and the repetitions are numerous beyond count. Furthermore, the children of Benjamin numbered twenty-six thousand seven hundred, yet only twenty-five thousand one hundred fell, and six hundred remained—leaving one thousand unaccounted for.
text.19_Chapter, 29_Verse, 1_Comment: It relates that at first the children of Benjamin were drawn away from the city. Because Israel made themselves appear as though they were being struck down before them, they drew Benjamin out toward the highways. It explains that the children of Benjamin were drawn to the highways because they thought that Israel was defeated; and Israel displayed themselves as fleeing in order to pull them away from the city.
text.19_Chapter, 32_Verse, 0_Comment: And every man of Israel. At first, a portion of the camp arrayed itself in the normal manner of battle and made themselves appear to be defeated. Meanwhile, all the men—the entire camp—rose and took their position at Baal-Tamar. Israel had come from Bethel, which lies to the north of the land of Benjamin; thus their camp was to the north. And while Israel was arranging its lines, the first ambush—positioned to the west of Gibeah—emerged from its place, from the cave of Gibeah where it had been concealed in hiding.
text.19_Chapter, 33_Verse, 0_Comment: And they came opposite Gibeah. From the side of the city in the west. Thus the children of Benjamin were surrounded from the north and from the west, and the battle became heavy upon them. They did not realize that disaster was overtaking them, and the outcome of the battle was that on that day twenty-five thousand men fell from among them. All this was related in general terms; from this point onward, the text begins to explain in detail how it unfolded, and proceeds to describe the particulars of the battle.
text.19_Chapter, 35_Verse, 0_Comment: And the children of Benjamin saw that they were defeated. That is, immediately at the outset, when the ambush emerged, the children of Benjamin realized that they were being struck, and their intent was to return to the city. At that moment, the men of Israel gave place to Benjamin—meaning that the camp which stood opposite them to the north began once again to flee. And it explains why they did this: for they trusted in the ambush which they had set against Gibeah. This refers to another ambush positioned on the southern side, prepared to strike down the inhabitants of the city. The arrangement between them was that when the ambush had struck all the men of the city, they would set the city on fire; and when Israel would see the column of smoke, they would turn back against Benjamin and surround them from every side, as will be described. Therefore it says, “for they trusted in the ambush.”
text.19_Chapter, 36_Verse, 0_Comment: And the ambush. At that moment, when Israel made themselves appear to flee a second time, at that very time the ambush hastened and spread out against the city and struck down the inhabitants of the city. But since there was an appointed signal between the men of Israel and the ambush—that is, they had set a fixed time and sign between them, that the beginning of the main engagement would be when they caused a great column of smoke to rise from the city—then the ambush would move out from the city to close in on them from the third direction. This took a short time, until they finished striking the inhabitants of the city; and because of this arrangement…
text.19_Chapter, 38_Verse, 0_Comment: And the men of Israel turned in the battle. This explains what was previously stated—that they gave place to Benjamin and made themselves appear to flee. They did so because of the appointed signal they had with the ambush. At that time Benjamin began to strike down slain… about thirty men. And the children of Benjamin thought, “Surely they are utterly defeated before us.” That is, although in the midst of the fighting they themselves had also been struck, they paid no attention to this, for they assumed that even if Israel had momentarily strengthened themselves, their power had already been broken. Therefore Israel gave place to Benjamin. Thus, these three verses serve as an explanation and elaboration of what was stated earlier (in verse 36): “And the children of Israel gave place to Benjamin, for they trusted in the ambush which they had set against Gibeah.”
text.19_Chapter, 39_Verse, 0_Comment: And the column of smoke. But at the moment when the ambush finished striking the city, they set it on fire and a column of smoke rose. Then Benjamin perceived two signs of his downfall: (1) that the whole city had gone up in flames; (2) that the men of Israel had turned back. And therefore the men of Benjamin were terrified, for they saw that disaster had reached them.
text.19_Chapter, 41_Verse, 0_Comment: And they turned. For at that point they were surrounded from three directions: the main camp was to the north; the first ambush, which had emerged from the cave, was to the west; and the second ambush, which had set the city on fire, was to the south. They were therefore forced to retreat toward the way of the wilderness, to the east, which remained open. Their route led along the highways, from there before the city on its eastern side, and from there toward the wilderness. But in this movement the battle overtook them, for they were encircled and pursued from three sides. Moreover, those from the cities destroyed them in their midst—that is, the divisions of Israel that had come out from the cities penetrated into the center of Benjamin’s camp and destroyed them from within.
text.19_Chapter, 42_Verse, 0_Comment: They encircled. Now he explains each stage one by one. First, they encircled Benjamin like a crown—this occurred when the first ambush emerged, and he was surrounded from two directions. Afterward, they pursued him—this is a causative action toward a third stage, meaning that they caused him to become the pursuer by making themselves appear defeated, so that he pursued them (as stated in verse 36 and following). Then, they drove him relentlessly, when they set his cities on fire. And those from the cities destroyed him in his midst. Thus he was struck down until he reached opposite Gibeah, toward the east of the sun, for by that route he fled toward the wilderness.
text.19_Chapter, 43_Verse, 0_Comment: And they fell. Now he counts in detail how many fell in each place. First, at the place of the battle line, eighteen thousand fell. Afterward, when they fled toward the wilderness and reached the highways, as mentioned above, five thousand fell there. From there they pursued them as far as Gidom and killed another two thousand.
text.19_Chapter, 45_Verse, 0_Comment: And all who fell. The total was twenty-five thousand. And when it says on that day, this indicates that the missing eleven hundred (from the original count of twenty-six thousand seven hundred, mentioned above in verse 15) had fallen in the earlier battles, or were killed in the caves in the days that followed.
text.20_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: Questions (1) Why did they swear—after all the killing and the great destruction—that they would not give them wives? And if they swore, how did they immediately regret it? The order of the verses is very confused: it begins with the matter of the oath regarding their daughters, then speaks of how they regretted what they had done to Benjamin; afterward it discusses the inquiry concerning those who did not come to the war; then it returns to their regret for Benjamin; then again to the men of Jabesh-Gilead who did not come to the war; and again it states that the people relented concerning Benjamin. These matters appear repetitive and disordered. It would have been appropriate to address separately their regret for Benjamin and separately their grievance and actions against the men of Jabesh-Gilead. Why is each matter repeated unnecessarily? The phrase “an inheritance of survivors for Benjamin, that a tribe not be blotted out from Israel” is unclear—especially since there no longer seemed to be a danger of extinction, for they had already taken four hundred women. Why does it say three times “and they said”—“and the elders of the congregation said,” “and they said, a surviving inheritance…,” and “and they said, behold, there is a feast…”? And the words of verse 22 are obscure and difficult to understand.
text.20_Chapter, 0_Verse, 1_Comment: And the men of Israel had sworn at Mizpah. It is explained by us that when the subject precedes the verb, the matter is not being related in chronological order, but refers to something that occurred earlier (see what is explained on Joshua 1:12, on the verse “And to the Reubenites and to the Gadites…”). Thus, “and the men of Israel had sworn” refers to an oath taken previously, while they were still at Mizpah—before they went out to war—not to intermarry with Benjamin.
text.20_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: And the people came to Bethel … and they said, “Why, O Hashem God…” For had Israel not fallen in the first two battles, they would not have placed Benjamin under the ban of total destruction. They would have punished only the offenders, not killed women and children and destroyed everything. But because Benjamin caused forty thousand of Israel to fall, they exacted vengeance against him. Now they came before Hashem, sitting and weeping, searching and investigating what had caused this—why Hashem’s anger had burned against them so that they fell in the first two battles. For this became the cause of an even greater calamity: that one tribe should be lacking today from Israel. For although six hundred men remained, still the tribe was considered missing, since a mere handful cannot properly be called a tribe; they were but a remnant, not a tribe in its own standing.
text.20_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: And it was on the following day. They again sat to investigate the cause of the matter and to examine their deeds, seeking why Hashem’s anger had burned against His people. And they offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. In order to obtain favor from Hashem.
text.20_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: And the children of Israel said. As they were investigating the matter, they recalled the episode of Israel in the war against Ai, which had likewise involved a commanded battle in which they fell before the enemy. There it became known that the cause was that Achan had trespassed against the ban and Joshua’s oath. Therefore they examined whether a similar sin might be found among them. For since there had been a great oath—that whoever did not go up to Mizpah to participate in this war would surely be put to death—they concluded that there must have been some who violated this oath, and that because of this Israel had fallen in battle. Accordingly they said, “Who is there that did not go up in the assembly?” for they did not yet know who it was.
text.20_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: And they relented. Until this point he had spoken about the past—how they investigated why they had been punished and supposed that perhaps some among them had violated the oath, and that because of this they were struck. Yet it was not really incumbent upon them to pursue that matter further, for the past could not be undone. But now a new issue arose before them: they remembered that in their anger they had sworn that none of them would give his daughter to Benjamin. Accordingly, even though six hundred men of the tribe of Benjamin remained, they would find no wives—for the women of Benjamin had all been killed. In this way the entire tribe would be erased. This would be a grave blemish and deficiency for the whole nation, for the Divine Presence rests upon Israel only when they are twelve tribes; if one tribe is missing, it is a great defect for the nation as a whole, as mentioned in the words of our Sages in many places (see, for example, Bava Kamma 83a). This would be damage for generations—an irreparable loss, profaning the glory of Jacob and the sanctity of Israel forever. Thus it says, “Today one tribe has been cut off from Israel,” and they explained the reason: “What shall we do for the survivors regarding wives?”
text.20_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: And they said. When they realized that if a city or family were found that had not gone to this war and would therefore be liable to death for violating the oath, this could provide a solution for Benjamin—for the women of such a place would be permitted to them, since they had not come to Mizpah and had not sworn—they now began to search and inquire which one of the tribes of Israel had not gone up to Hashem at Mizpah, for they now needed this for the sake of Benjamin. And behold, they discovered that there was no one there from the inhabitants of Jabesh-Gilead. Accordingly, they judged that since, in their view, Jabesh-Gilead had transgressed the oath and thereby caused Hashem’s anger to burn—resulting in the destruction of Benjamin—it followed that the men of Jabesh-Gilead were the cause of this outcome. Therefore it was fitting, they reasoned, that by executing them, there would arise from among them—from the virgins of Jabesh-Gilead whom they would keep alive—a remnant for Benjamin, to become wives for them.
text.20_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: And they sent. After they found a remedy for them, they sent and proclaimed peace to them, and gave them the women. This was for the benefit of the entire nation, so that there would not be a defect in the community through the loss of a tribe; for it was accepted among them that the Divine Presence would not rest upon them if one tribe were missing from the number of the tribes.
text.20_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: And they did not find enough for them. For they did not find wives for all six hundred men.
text.20_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: And the people. That is, although their fear that a tribe would be erased from Israel had already subsided—since they had found wives for four hundred men—nevertheless, after they had reconciled with them and spoken peaceably to them, the people regretted the entire affair. They repented of what had been done, by which Hashem had made a breach among the tribes—bringing division, hatred, and war. Therefore it says, “And the people relented,” for earlier it had said, “And the children of Israel relented,” referring to the leaders, elders, and prominent figures concerned for the welfare of the nation. But now the entire people relented—they repented and returned to them in love, and did not wish that the remaining two hundred men should die without children.
text.20_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: And the elders of the congregation said, “What shall we do for the survivors regarding wives?” At that point the Sanhedrin examined whether they could annul the oath in order to provide wives for those who remained. They offered a reason: “For the women have been destroyed from Benjamin.” That is, at the time of the oath they had not intended that the women and children be killed. Their intent had only been that they themselves would not intermarry with Benjamin—not that Benjamin would be left childless, for in that case they would have taken wives from their own tribe. But now that the women of Benjamin had been destroyed and the tribe would be erased under these conditions, they had not sworn with such a circumstance in mind. Therefore there was an opening and grounds for regret (to reconsider the oath).
text.20_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: And they said. But they reconsidered and said that this was not a valid argument. It would have been correct had they found no remedy at all and the entire tribe were about to be erased—such a loss would have been a defect and deficiency for the whole nation, and then they would have had grounds to release themselves from the oath, for surely they had not sworn with the intention of obliterating an entire tribe. But now, a surviving inheritance remains for Benjamin; Benjamin already has a remnant through the four hundred young women taken from the inhabitants of Jabesh-Gilead, from whom offspring and heirs would arise. Consequently, a tribe will not be blotted out from Israel. Therefore the oath has no opening and no basis for regret. Accordingly they rendered their decision: “We cannot give them wives from our daughters, for the children of Israel have sworn.” There is no permission to release them from their oath.
text.20_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: And they said. But they again conferred for the benefit of the remaining two hundred men and devised a plan—that they should seize wives from among the dancing maidens.
text.20_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: And you shall seize. They stipulated with them: (1) that each man should seize only one woman; (2) that they should bring them to the land of Benjamin, so that their fathers would not overtake them to contend with them.
text.20_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment:
And it shall be, when they come … to us. If they come to contend with us—claiming that we have allowed the women to be taken by force—then we shall present two arguments:

(1) As for your concern about the oath—that you might say that although they seized them, we are granting them favor by remaining silent—we will say to them, “Be gracious to them?”—in astonishment. Is it an act of grace that we did not take each man’s wife from him in battle? That is, they seized them and married them with the consent of the women; they are now their wives. Are we obligated or permitted to wage war against them and take their wives from them? We are neither obligated nor permitted to do so. Therefore we are not granting them favor by refraining from taking the women back.

(2) For you did not give them, and therefore you are not now guilty. They took them on their own initiative, and you did not violate your oath.
text.20_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: And they went their ways. Although at that moment they ought to have taken heed of the stumbling block that had arisen from their own hands—while they were still gathered together, they could have repaired the breach and established a king or judge to oversee the people—nevertheless, immediately afterward each man went to his place, and the matter remained as before: there was no king in Israel, and every man did what was right in his own eyes. As for the time when these last two events—the matter of Micah’s idol and the concubine at Gibeah—took place, Scripture does not state it explicitly. According to our Sages in Seder Olam (ch. 12), it was in the days of Cushan-Rishathaim. Therefore it says, “In those days there was no king in Israel,” meaning after the death of Joshua and the elders, before a judge had yet arisen for Israel—until Othniel son of Kenaz. According to this view, it fits what is said that the tribe of Dan sought an inheritance to dwell in and captured Laish; this would have been after Joshua’s death, when each tribe went to conquer its territory, and the children of Dan captured Laish as mentioned in the book of Joshua (ch. 19). It also fits what is said regarding Jerusalem, “We will not turn aside to a foreign city which is not of the children of Israel,” for this would have been before Judah conquered its portion of Jerusalem (as stated earlier in chapter 1, verse 8). And it accords with the statement that Micah’s idol stood all the days that the House of God was in Shiloh, implying that it endured alongside the Ark’s presence in Shiloh. However, from what our Sages say (Rashi on I Samuel 20:30) regarding “son of a wayward woman,” that Saul’s wife pursued him because Saul was ashamed to seize her from among the dancers, it appears that this episode occurred after the death of Samson, before another judge arose—hence, “In those days there was no king in Israel.” According to this, it is fitting that these sections are written after the account of Samson, for that would match the chronological order. And when it says that Micah’s idol stood all the days that the House of God was in Shiloh, this would mean that it stood from that time until the destruction of Shiloh. So too it is implied by the words of the Sages (Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot 9:3), that Jonathan later became treasurer of the storehouses in the days of Solomon and that he was the old prophet in Bethel; and according to Seder Olam, he lived more than four hundred years.
